context_brief: Conformal matings in the transcendental setting
original_question: Can one develop an obstruction theory and identify structural conditions under which a transcendental map with a Herman ring can be conformally mated with the action of a Fuchsian group or a subgroup of PSL(2, Z) on the upper half-plane? More specifically, when can a topological mating between the map and the group action be defined, when can that topological mating be promoted to a conformal one, and what dynamical feature distinguishes the resulting correspondence map when the function has a Herman ring?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Let f : C → C be a transcendental meromorphic (or entire) function whose Fatou set contains a Herman ring, that is, a doubly connected periodic Fatou component on which an iterate of f is conformally conjugate to an irrational rotation of a round annulus {1 < |z| < r}. Let Γ be a Fuchsian group acting on the upper half-plane H by Möbius transformations; an important case is Γ a finite-index subgroup of PSL(2, Z). The Julia set J(f) ⊂ C carries the dynamics of f; the limit set Λ(Γ) ⊂ ∂H carries the dynamics of Γ.

A topological mating of (f, Γ) is, informally, a continuous dynamical system on a topological sphere (or appropriate quotient space) obtained by gluing the filled-in dynamical plane of f to a fundamental domain for Γ along boundary identifications that conjugate the boundary behavior of f to the action of Γ on its limit set, so that the resulting space supports a single continuous map combining the two dynamics. A conformal mating is a topological mating that can be realized so that the resulting map is holomorphic (or more generally a holomorphic correspondence) on a Riemann surface compatible with the gluing, with the conformal structures on the two pieces matching.

Problem. Develop an obstruction theory for the existence of conformal matings of transcendental maps with Herman rings and Fuchsian group actions. Specifically, address each of the following.

1. Existence of a topological mating. Identify necessary and sufficient structural conditions on f (with a Herman ring) and on Γ (a Fuchsian group, or a subgroup of PSL(2, Z)) under which a topological mating of f with the action of Γ on H can be defined. Make precise the boundary-gluing equivalence relation required, taking into account the transcendental nature of f (e.g. essential singularities, infinite-degree behavior, escaping set).

2. Promotion to a conformal mating. Determine when a topological mating, if it exists, can be promoted to a conformal one. Formulate and prove the analogue, in this transcendental setting, of obstruction-theoretic criteria (in the spirit of Thurston-type obstructions or Levy/Rees-Shishikura-Tan obstructions known for rational matings), adapted to the presence of a Herman ring and to the infinite-degree, non-compact features of transcendental dynamics.

3. Dynamical signature of the Herman ring. Identify a precise dynamical feature of the resulting holomorphic correspondence (or mated map) that distinguishes the case in which f possesses a Herman ring from the case in which it does not. In particular, characterize the image and behavior of the Herman ring under the mating construction within the correspondence dynamics.

Provide rigorous definitions, theorems with hypotheses, and proofs (or counterexamples) for each of (1)–(3).
status_search_result: Conformal mating in the transcendental setting, particularly involving maps with Herman rings and Fuchsian groups, is a recognized underdeveloped area. While conformal matings have been intensively studied for polynomials and rational maps (Bullett–Penrose, Bullett–Lomonaco, etc., and recent work on antiholomorphic matings), no general obstruction theory or existence result is known for transcendental maps with Herman rings mated with Fuchsian group actions. The problem, as posed, appears to be open.

context_brief: Infinitely many periods with stable bov
original_question: For a meromorphic function with a stable Baker omitted value, can there be infinitely many Herman rings whose periods vary, even though for each fixed period p >= 3 the number of p-periodic Herman rings is known to be finite? In particular, can this happen when the Baker omitted value is the only accumulation point of the critical values?
self_contained_problem:
Let f be a transcendental meromorphic function on the complex plane. An omitted value of f is a point a ∈ ℂ such that f(z) ≠ a for all z ∈ ℂ. An omitted value a is called a Baker omitted value (bov) of f if there exists an open disk D centered at a such that every connected component of the boundary of f^{-1}(D) is bounded in ℂ. The bov a is called stable if every iterate f^n is analytic in some neighborhood of a (equivalently, suitable iterates extend analytically across a so that a behaves as a "stable" omitted value under iteration).

A Herman ring of f is a periodic Fatou component U of period p ≥ 1 such that U is conformally an annulus and f^p restricted to U is conformally conjugate to an irrational rotation of a standard annulus. The period of the Herman ring is the smallest such p.

It is known that, for any meromorphic function f with a stable Baker omitted value and any fixed integer p ≥ 3, the number of Herman rings of f having period exactly p is finite.

Question: Does there exist a transcendental meromorphic function f possessing a stable Baker omitted value such that f has infinitely many Herman rings whose periods are not bounded (i.e., infinitely many distinct periods occur among the Herman rings of f)? In particular, can such a phenomenon occur in the case where the Baker omitted value is the unique accumulation point of the set of critical values of f?
status_search_result: The question is explicitly stated as an open problem in the recent survey on Herman rings (2025/2026). Existing results establish only finiteness of p-periodic Herman rings for each fixed p ≥ 3 under a stable bov hypothesis; no construction or obstruction is known for the case of infinitely many Herman rings of varying periods, especially when the bov is the unique accumulation point of critical values.

original_question: If a meromorphic function with an omitted value has a quasi-nested wandering domain, must that function necessarily have no Herman rings?
self_contained_problem:
Let f: ℂ → ℂ ∪ {∞} be a transcendental meromorphic function, and let F(f) denote its Fatou set, i.e., the set of points z ∈ ℂ at which the family of iterates {f^n} is normal in some neighborhood. A connected component U of F(f) is called a wandering domain if the components U_n containing f^n(U) are pairwise disjoint for n = 0, 1, 2, …. Such a wandering domain U = U_0 is called quasi-nested if every U_n is bounded and there exists a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers {n_k} such that, for each k, the component U_{n_k} surrounds the origin (i.e., 0 lies in the bounded complementary component of U_{n_k}), and the spherical/Euclidean distance from U_{n_k} to ∞ tends to 0 as k → ∞ (equivalently, U_{n_k} → ∞).

A periodic Fatou component A of period p ≥ 1 is called a Herman ring if A is conformally a round annulus and f^p restricted to A is conformally conjugate to an irrational rotation of that annulus.

Prove or disprove: every transcendental meromorphic function f that possesses a quasi-nested wandering domain has no Herman ring (in any cycle of Fatou components).
status_search_result: The statement is posed as an open conjecture in recent surveys on Herman rings of meromorphic functions. A 2022 result establishes the implication only under the additional hypothesis that f has an omitted value (showing in fact the absence of unbounded Fatou components, hence no unbounded Herman ring). The general conjecture without the omitted-value hypothesis appears not to have been resolved.

paper_title: Understanding Solar Flares and Energetic Events: Open questions, observational requirements, and instrumental needs over the coming decade
original_question: What physical process triggers magnetic reconnection that initiates a solar flare, whether flare onset is primarily caused by ideal magnetohydrodynamic instabilities such as torus or kink instabilities or by slower photospheric or coronal processes such as flux cancellation or local resistivity enhancements that build a current sheet, what generates quasi-periodic pulsations during flares, and whether directly observed pre-flare or associated quantities can be used as causal predictors of flare onset rather than merely symptomatic correlations?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a solar active region modeled as a magnetized plasma in the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) framework, in which a coronal magnetic field B(x,t) evolves under the resistive MHD equations with small but nonzero resistivity, driven from below by photospheric boundary motions. A solar flare is identified with a rapid, large-amplitude release of magnetic energy through magnetic reconnection across a thin current sheet, often accompanied by quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs): oscillatory modulations of the emitted radiation with characteristic periods of seconds to minutes.

Address the following questions about flare onset and dynamics:

(a) Triggering mechanism. Determine whether the onset of fast magnetic reconnection that produces a flare is primarily caused by an ideal MHD instability of the pre-flare magnetic configuration — for instance, the torus instability of a current-carrying flux rope (loss of equilibrium when the decay index of the external poloidal field exceeds a critical threshold near 3/2) or the kink instability of a twisted flux tube (when the magnetic twist exceeds a critical value such as 2π·1.25) — or whether it is primarily driven by slower, non-ideal processes at or near the photosphere/lower corona, such as flux cancellation along a polarity inversion line or localized enhancements of resistivity, which gradually build a thin current sheet that subsequently undergoes fast reconnection.

(b) Quasi-periodic pulsations. Identify the physical mechanism that generates QPPs during flares (e.g. magnetoacoustic eigenmodes of flare loops, repetitive/bursty reconnection, oscillatory reconnection, or wave-driven modulation of the reconnection rate), and determine whether the observed periods, amplitudes, and phase relations of QPPs provide quantitative constraints on the rate, location, and timing of magnetic energy release.

(c) Causal predictors. Among directly observable pre-flare quantities — such as photospheric magnetic free energy, magnetic helicity injection rate, decay index above a polarity inversion line, current-sheet formation indicators, and topological measures (e.g. squashing factor Q) — determine which, if any, are causal predictors of imminent flare onset, as opposed to mere symptomatic correlates, and identify the critical thresholds of such metrics that distinguish flaring from non-flaring active regions.
status_search_result: The triggering mechanism of solar flares, the origin of quasi-periodic pulsations, and the existence of genuinely causal flare predictors are widely acknowledged as outstanding open questions in solar physics. Recent reviews and community white papers (2023–2026) on flare physics and space-weather prediction continue to list these as unresolved, with competing models (ideal MHD instabilities vs. flux cancellation / tether-cutting) and multiple proposed QPP mechanisms still under active debate.

paper_title: Understanding Solar Flares and Energetic Events: Open questions, observational requirements, and instrumental needs over the coming decade
original_question: How is flare energy transported through the Sun's atmosphere from the photosphere to the corona and dissipated into heating, including how precipitating electrons and ions interact, how spatially variable non-thermal particle precipitation is in the lower atmosphere, whether that variability causes the observed small-scale flare structure, whether other transport channels such as waves, radiation, or ion beams are sometimes equally or more important than electron beams, and why observations imply heating deeper than standard non-thermal electron transport models predict?
self_contained_problem:
In the context of solar flare physics, develop a quantitative understanding of how energy released by magnetic reconnection in the solar corona is transported through the solar atmosphere — from the corona down through the chromosphere to the photosphere — and ultimately dissipated as heat. Specifically, address the following coupled questions:

1. Precipitating particles. Flare-accelerated electrons (and likely ions) stream from the acceleration region toward the lower atmosphere, where they thermalize and heat the ambient plasma. Along their trajectories, their non-thermal distribution functions and energy-deposition profiles are modified by return-current electric fields, magnetic mirroring, wave–particle interactions, and non-Maxwellian properties of the target plasma. Determine quantitatively how precipitating electrons and ions interact with one another and with the background medium under these effects.

2. Spatial variability. Characterize the spatial variability of non-thermal particle precipitation into the lower atmosphere, and decide whether such variability is sufficient to account for the observed small-scale structure within flare ribbons and kernels.

3. Alternative transport channels. Determine whether energy transport mechanisms other than electron beams — including MHD or plasma waves (e.g. Alfvén waves), thermal conduction, radiation, and ion beams — can be equally or more important than electron beams at certain times or locations during a flare, and quantify their relative contributions.

4. Deep heating problem. Observations of the lower solar atmosphere indicate heating at depths greater than those reachable by canonical non-thermal electron beams of the inferred power. Identify the additional or revised transport mechanisms (or corrections to non-thermal electron transport) needed to reconcile theoretical models with these observations of deep atmospheric heating.

Provide a self-consistent model and observational tests that simultaneously resolve (1)–(4).
status_search_result: The question of how flare energy is transported and dissipated through the solar atmosphere — including the roles of electron beams, ion beams, waves, and the unexplained deep chromospheric/photospheric heating — is a long-standing open problem in solar physics, repeatedly listed as such in recent reviews and white papers on flare physics.

paper_title: Understanding Solar Flares and Energetic Events: Open questions, observational requirements, and instrumental needs over the coming decade
original_question: What role does turbulence play in solar flares, from enabling fast reconnection and particle acceleration to modifying plasma processes, what is the connection between turbulence and particle acceleration on flare timescales, how can observations distinguish true turbulence from hot-ion broadening in spectral lines, and how should multiple acceleration sites such as the reconnection layer, termination shocks, and above-the-loop turbulence be integrated into one self-consistent flare system model?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a magnetized collisionless plasma model of a solar flare consisting of: (i) a reconnection current sheet where oppositely directed magnetic field components annihilate and convert magnetic energy into bulk flow, heat, and nonthermal particles; (ii) a fast-mode termination shock formed where the reconnection outflow impinges on the underlying magnetic loops; and (iii) a turbulent above-the-loop-top region in which magnetohydrodynamic or kinetic fluctuations are sustained. Let f_s(x, v, t) denote the phase-space distribution of species s (electrons and ions), evolving under a Vlasov–Maxwell system with a stochastic fluctuating electromagnetic component (δE, δB) whose two-point statistics define a turbulence spectrum E(k).

Provide a self-consistent quantitative theory that answers the following:

1. Fast reconnection and acceleration. Determine how the presence of turbulence modifies the reconnection rate and the efficiency η_acc(E) with which particles are injected into a nonthermal power-law tail f_s(v) ∝ v^{-(2α+1)} on the observed flare timescale (seconds to minutes). Specify the dependence of α and of the cutoff energy on the turbulence amplitude δB/B and spectral index.

2. Spectroscopic diagnostic. Spectral line emission of an ion of mass m_i at temperature T with a turbulent velocity field of one-dimensional rms amplitude v_turb produces a Doppler-broadened line width
  Δλ/λ = (1/c) · sqrt( 2 k_B T / m_i + v_turb^2 ).
A "hot-ion" hypothesis attributes the broadening to anomalously large T, while a "true turbulence" hypothesis attributes it to v_turb. Construct an observational test, based on the dependence of Δλ on m_i and on viewing angle relative to the local magnetic field, that uniquely separates the two contributions, and prove that the proposed test is well-posed (i.e., the inverse problem for (T, v_turb) admits a unique solution given multi-ion, multi-angle data).

3. Multi-stage acceleration. Model the chain of acceleration sites as a composition of three transport operators T_rec, T_shock, T_turb acting on the particle distribution, where each operator is governed by a Fokker–Planck equation with site-specific momentum-diffusion coefficient D_pp and escape time τ_esc. Derive conditions on (D_pp, τ_esc) at each stage under which the composed distribution (T_turb ∘ T_shock ∘ T_rec) f_0 reproduces the hard X-ray and gamma-ray spectra observed during impulsive flare phases, and characterize when the three-stage chain is necessary versus when a single dominant site suffices.

Determine whether such an integrated, self-consistent system model exists and is observationally identifiable.

Recent reviews and mission white papers continue to list these as outstanding open questions.

paper_title: Understanding Solar Flares and Energetic Events: Open questions, observational requirements, and instrumental needs over the coming decade
original_question: How similar are Sun-like stars to the Sun in their flare behavior, and what can observed trends across stellar populations reveal about the probability of extreme events such as superflares and about long-term changes in solar behavior?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Sun as a member of the broader population of "Sun-like stars," defined here as main-sequence stars whose effective temperature, surface gravity, metallicity, and rotation period lie within a small neighborhood of the corresponding solar values. For a star S in this class, let N_S(E) denote the long-term mean rate (events per unit time) of flares releasing bolometric radiative energy at least E, and define a superflare to be a flare with E ≥ 10^33 erg.

(a) Quantify the degree to which the flaring statistics of Sun-like stars resemble those of the Sun. Specifically, characterize, as a function of stellar parameters (effective temperature, rotation period, age, magnetic activity proxies), the distribution of cumulative flare-frequency functions N_S(E) across the population, and determine whether the Sun's observed flare-frequency distribution lies within the range exhibited by stars closely matching its parameters.

(b) Using the observed trends across the stellar population, estimate the probability that the Sun produces a superflare of energy ≥ 10^33 erg (and ≥ 10^34 erg) within a given time window (e.g., the next 100, 1000, or 10000 years), and assess what these population-level trends imply about possible long-term secular changes in solar flaring behavior over timescales exceeding the historical and instrumental record.
status_search_result: Recent Kepler-based studies (notably a 2024 Science paper) find that Sun-like stars produce superflares (≥10^34 erg) roughly once per century, an order of magnitude more frequently than previously estimated, while paleo-records (cosmogenic isotopes) show no clear evidence of such events on the Sun in the past ~10,000 years. The question of whether the Sun is statistically representative of its stellar peers, and what this implies for the probability of a solar superflare and long-term solar variability, is actively studied but not settled.

paper_title: Understanding Solar Flares and Energetic Events: Open questions, observational requirements, and instrumental needs over the coming decade
original_question: Can observations of solar flares, including X-ray and gamma-ray measurements and flare thermal, non-thermal, and magnetic parameters, be used to infer the properties and evolution of coronal mass ejections and solar energetic particles, and what is the physical relationship between particles accelerated in the flare and the solar energetic particles observed later?
self_contained_problem:
A solar flare is a sudden release of magnetic energy in the solar corona that produces electromagnetic radiation across the spectrum, including hard X-ray and gamma-ray emission generated by accelerated electrons and ions interacting with the ambient plasma. A coronal mass ejection (CME) is a large-scale eruption of magnetized plasma from the Sun's atmosphere into the heliosphere. Solar energetic particles (SEPs) are protons, electrons, and heavier ions accelerated to high energies, observed in situ near 1 AU, with sources commonly attributed both to flare reconnection sites and to CME-driven shocks.

For each flare event, define an observation vector consisting of:
(i) thermal flare parameters: peak emission measure, peak electron temperature, and their time evolution inferred from soft X-ray spectra;
(ii) non-thermal flare parameters: hard X-ray and gamma-ray photon spectra and their time evolution, including spectral index, low- and high-energy cutoffs, and inferred accelerated-electron and accelerated-ion energy content;
(iii) magnetic flare parameters: photospheric and coronal magnetic field measurements characterizing the active region, reconnection flux, and free magnetic energy.

For each associated CME, define an outcome vector consisting of its kinematic and morphological properties (mass, speed, acceleration, width, direction). For each associated SEP event, define an outcome vector consisting of peak intensity, spectral indices, elemental and isotopic composition, charge states, and onset/release times of protons, electrons, and ions at 1 AU.

Address the following questions:

1. Determine whether there exists a deterministic or statistical mapping from the flare observation vector to the CME outcome vector and the SEP outcome vector that constrains these outcomes more tightly than climatological priors, and identify which subset of thermal, non-thermal, and magnetic flare parameters yields the strongest constraint on CME and SEP evolution.

2. Characterize the physical relationship between the population of particles accelerated in the flare itself (as inferred from X-ray and gamma-ray emission) and the SEP population observed later in interplanetary space, including the extent to which the latter is composed of, reaccelerated from, or independent of the former, and quantify how this relationship depends on flare and CME properties.
status_search_result: This is a recognized open question in solar and heliospheric physics. The connection between flare-accelerated particles and SEPs, and the predictability of CME/SEP properties from flare observations, remains an active area of investigation with no consensus answer; recent reviews and decadal-survey-style documents continue to frame these as outstanding problems.

paper_title: Understanding Solar Flares and Energetic Events: Open questions, observational requirements, and instrumental needs over the coming decade
original_question: Can spectral and imaging observations of solar flares be incorporated into flare-forecasting methods, particularly to infer the build-up of turbulence before a flare, and how should that spectral information flow through a research-to-operations-to-research pipeline to improve forecasting skill?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the problem of forecasting solar flares, i.e., predicting the occurrence, timing, and magnitude of impulsive energy-release events in the solar atmosphere. Suppose one has access to two classes of observational data of active regions on the Sun:

1. Imaging observations: time-resolved two-dimensional intensity maps in selected wavelengths (e.g., extreme ultraviolet, soft X-ray, optical continuum, and chromospheric lines), which reveal the morphology and dynamical evolution of magnetic structures.
2. Spectral observations: spatially resolved line profiles (intensity as a function of wavelength) in chromospheric and transition-region diagnostic lines, from which line broadening beyond thermal and instrumental contributions — commonly attributed to unresolved nonthermal motions or turbulence — can be extracted as a function of position and time.

Define a "pre-flare turbulence build-up signature" as a statistically significant temporal increase, prior to the flare onset, in the nonthermal broadening component of selected spectral lines integrated over a flaring region.

Address the following:

(a) Construct, or prove the impossibility of, a forecasting scheme that takes as input the joint spectral-and-imaging time series of an active region and outputs a probability of flare occurrence within a specified future time window, such that the inclusion of pre-flare turbulence build-up signatures yields a statistically significant improvement in forecast skill (as measured by standard verification metrics such as the Brier skill score, the true skill statistic, or the Heidke skill score) over forecasts using imaging-only or magnetogram-only inputs.

(b) Specify a research-to-operations-to-research feedback architecture in which spectral diagnostics are continuously assimilated into operational forecasts and operational outcomes are fed back to refine the spectral diagnostics, and quantify the conditions on data latency, spectral cadence, spatial coverage, and signal-to-noise under which such a pipeline demonstrably improves forecasting skill relative to current operational baselines.

original_question: Consider the maximal immediate extensions of the valued fields Q_p(ζ_{p^∞}) and Q_p(p^{1/p^∞}) produced in Kartas's work, where some of these maximal immediate extensions have decidable elementary theories and uncountably many have distinct elementary theories. What is the structure of these maximal immediate extensions, beyond the fact that they are infinite, and which structural features distinguish the decidable extensions from the undecidable ones?
self_contained_problem:
Let p be a prime number. Consider the valued fields K_1 = Q_p(ζ_{p^∞}), the cyclotomic extension of Q_p obtained by adjoining all p-power roots of unity, and K_2 = Q_p(p^{1/p^∞}), the field obtained by adjoining all p-power roots of p, both equipped with the unique extension of the p-adic valuation. A valued field extension L/K is called immediate if it induces no extension on the value group and no extension on the residue field. A maximal immediate extension of (K, v) is one that admits no proper immediate extension.

It is known that each of K_1 and K_2 admits uncountably many maximal immediate extensions whose elementary theories in the language L_val of valued fields are pairwise distinct, and consequently uncountably many of these maximal immediate extensions have undecidable L_val-theory, while certain (specifically constructed) maximal immediate extensions are known to have decidable L_val-theory.

Problem: Beyond the fact that they are of infinite transcendence degree over K_i, describe the algebraic, valuation-theoretic, and model-theoretic structure of the maximal immediate extensions of K_1 and of K_2. In particular, identify intrinsic structural invariants or features (for instance, properties of pseudo-Cauchy sequences, Kaplansky-type defect data, generating sets, or definable subsets) that distinguish those maximal immediate extensions whose L_val-theory is decidable from those whose L_val-theory is undecidable.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a recent (2025) survey on model theory of tame valued fields. Kartas's work establishes the existence of uncountably many maximal immediate extensions of Q_p(ζ_{p^∞}) and Q_p(p^{1/p^∞}) with pairwise distinct elementary theories (so most are undecidable), while exhibiting some with decidable theory; no published structural classification distinguishing decidable from undecidable cases was found.

original_question: Kartas proves implications from decidability of the positive-characteristic perfectoid-side fields to decidability of the mixed-characteristic fields Q_p(ζ_{p^∞}), Q_p(p^{1/p^∞}), and Q_p^{ab}. self_contained_problem:
Let p be a prime number. Consider the following p-adic fields in mixed characteristic 0:
- Q_p(ζ_{p^∞}), the field obtained from Q_p by adjoining all p-power roots of unity;
- Q_p(p^{1/p^∞}), the field obtained from Q_p by adjoining all p-power roots of p;
- Q_p^{ab}, the maximal abelian extension of Q_p.

Each of these is a (non-complete) henselian valued field of mixed characteristic (0,p). Via the tilting correspondence, each is associated with a positive-characteristic perfectoid counterpart obtained from the perfect hull of F_p((t)) (or of F̄_p((t))), regarded as a valued field in the language L_val(t) of valued fields with a constant symbol for the uniformizer t.

It is known that the existential (and full first-order, in appropriate settings) decidability of the positive-characteristic perfectoid side implies decidability of the corresponding mixed-characteristic field listed above.

Establish a reverse transfer principle in the non-complete setting: prove that decidability of Q_p(ζ_{p^∞}), Q_p(p^{1/p^∞}), or Q_p^{ab} (as valued fields in their natural language) implies decidability of the corresponding positive-characteristic perfectoid field. original_question: Let F_p(t)^h denote the henselization of the t-adically valued rational function field (F_p(t),v_t). Is F_p(t)^h an elementary substructure of the Laurent series field F_p((t)) with its t-adic valuation? The paper notes that existential closedness of F_p(t)^h in F_p((t)) is known, but full elementary equivalence of the inclusion remains open.
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime number, and let $\mathbb{F}_p$ denote the field with $p$ elements. Consider the rational function field $\mathbb{F}_p(t)$ equipped with the $t$-adic valuation $v_t$, defined on $\mathbb{F}_p[t]$ by $v_t(f) = \max\{n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} : t^n \mid f\}$ and extended to $\mathbb{F}_p(t)$ in the standard way. Let $(\mathbb{F}_p(t)^h, v_t)$ denote the henselization of the valued field $(\mathbb{F}_p(t), v_t)$, i.e., the smallest henselian valued field extension of $(\mathbb{F}_p(t), v_t)$ inside a fixed algebraic closure. Let $\mathbb{F}_p((t))$ denote the field of formal Laurent series over $\mathbb{F}_p$, equipped with its natural $t$-adic valuation. There is a canonical inclusion of valued fields
$$ (\mathbb{F}_p(t)^h, v_t) \hookrightarrow (\mathbb{F}_p((t)), v_t). $$
It is known that $(\mathbb{F}_p(t)^h, v_t)$ is existentially closed in $(\mathbb{F}_p((t)), v_t)$.

Question: Is $(\mathbb{F}_p(t)^h, v_t)$ an elementary substructure of $(\mathbb{F}_p((t)), v_t)$ in the language of valued fields? Equivalently, does the inclusion above preserve and reflect the truth of every first-order formula (with parameters from $\mathbb{F}_p(t)^h$) in the language of valued fields?
status_search_result: The question of whether the henselization of $(\mathbb{F}_p(t), v_t)$ is an elementary substructure of $(\mathbb{F}_p((t)), v_t)$ is a well-known open problem in the model theory of valued fields in positive characteristic. Existential closedness is classical, but full elementary equivalence of the inclusion is not established; it is closely tied to the still-open problem of decidability/model-completeness of $\mathbb{F}_p((t))$. No solution was located in the literature search.

paper_title: Model Theory of Tame Valued Fields and Beyond: Recent Developments and Open Questions
original_question: What can be said about the model theory of the Laurent series field F_p((t))? In particular, is there a complete axiomatization of this valued field and is its full elementary theory decidable?
self_contained_problem:
Let p be a prime number, let F_p denote the field with p elements, and let F_p((t)) denote the field of formal Laurent series in one variable t over F_p, equipped with its natural t-adic valuation v: F_p((t))^× → Z (so that v(t)=1, the valuation ring is F_p[[t]], and the residue field is F_p). View F_p((t)) as a structure in the language of valued fields (for instance, the three-sorted Denef–Pas language, or the language of rings together with a binary divisibility predicate for the valuation).

Determine the first-order theory of the valued field F_p((t)). Specifically:

(a) Provide an explicit, recursive (complete) set of first-order axioms whose models are exactly the valued fields elementarily equivalent to F_p((t)).

(b) Decide whether the complete first-order theory Th(F_p((t))) of this valued field is decidable, i.e. whether there exists an algorithm that, given a first-order sentence φ in the language of valued fields, determines whether φ holds in F_p((t)).
status_search_result: The decidability and a complete axiomatization of the valued field F_p((t)) is a long-standing open problem in the model theory of valued fields. Despite substantial progress on tame, separably tame, and Kaplansky valued fields, and partial results in restricted languages, no complete axiomatization or decidability proof for the full elementary theory of F_p((t)) is known as of 2026.

original_question: Let (A) denote the elementary axiom system "henselian defectless valued field of positive characteristic with value group a Z-group and residue field F_p." If one adds the axiom scheme asserting that the valued field is extremal, does the resulting theory become complete?
self_contained_problem:
Throughout, all valued fields are considered in the language $L_{\mathrm{val}}$ of valued fields. Recall the following definitions.

A valued field $(K,v)$ with value group $vK$ and residue field $Kv$ is henselian if Hensel's Lemma holds in $(K,v)$. For a finite extension $(L,w)/(K,v)$ the fundamental inequality is $[L:K] \ge \sum_{i=1}^{g} e_i f_i$, where $e_i = (w_iL : vK)$, $f_i = [Lw_i : Kv]$, and $w_1,\dots,w_g$ are the extensions of $v$ to $L$. The extension is called defectless if equality holds; $(K,v)$ is defectless if every finite extension is defectless.

An ordered abelian group $\Gamma$ is a $\mathbb{Z}$-group if it is elementarily equivalent to $(\mathbb{Z},+,<)$, equivalently $\Gamma$ has a least positive element and $\Gamma/n\Gamma \cong \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ for all $n\ge 1$.

A valued field $(K,v)$ is extremal if for every polynomial $f(X_1,\dots,X_n) \in K[X_1,\dots,X_n]$, the set
$$\{ v(f(a_1,\dots,a_n)) : a_1,\dots,a_n \in \mathcal{O}_v \}$$
attains a maximum in $vK \cup \{\infty\}$, where $\mathcal{O}_v$ is the valuation ring of $(K,v)$.

Let $(A)$ denote the $L_{\mathrm{val}}$-theory whose axioms assert:
1. $(K,v)$ is a henselian valued field of characteristic $p > 0$ (for some fixed prime $p$),
2. $(K,v)$ is defectless,
3. the value group $vK$ is a $\mathbb{Z}$-group,
4. the residue field $Kv$ is $\mathbb{F}_p$.

It is known that $(A)$ is not complete. Let $(A)^{\mathrm{ext}}$ denote the theory obtained from $(A)$ by adjoining the axiom scheme expressing that $(K,v)$ is extremal.

Question: Is $(A)^{\mathrm{ext}}$ a complete $L_{\mathrm{val}}$-theory?
status_search_result: Available sources on extremal and tame valued fields, including Kuhlmann's notes and chapter on extremality, list the completeness of $(A)$ + "extremal" as an explicitly open problem. Partial structural results (e.g., characterizations of extremal tame fields, and the existence of both extremal and non-extremal algebraically complete fields with $\mathbb{Z}$-group value group and finite residue field) are known, but no completeness proof or counterexample appears in the literature.

original_question: Suppose a valuation v factors as v = w ◦ ̄w and v itself is extremal. It is known that the induced valuation ̄w must then be extremal. Does extremality of v also force the coarser factor w to be extremal?
self_contained_problem:
Let (K, v) be a valued field. Recall that (K, v) is called extremal if for every polynomial f ∈ K[X₁, …, X_n] the set of values
  { v(f(a₁, …, a_n)) : a₁, …, a_n ∈ O_v }
attains a maximum in vK ∪ {∞}, where O_v denotes the valuation ring of v.

Suppose that v factors as a composition v = w ∘ w̄, meaning that w is a valuation on K whose valuation ring contains O_v, and w̄ is the induced valuation on the residue field Kw of w, with v recovered as the composition of w followed by w̄. It is known that if (K, v) is extremal, then the induced valuation w̄ on the residue field Kw is also extremal.

Question: Does extremality of (K, v) imply that the coarser valuation (K, w) is also extremal?

original_question: Does hypothesis (R4) hold? Here (R4) is the assertion that for an arbitrary field K, if F|K is an extension admitting a K-rational place, then K is existentially closed in F. The paper explains that local uniformization would imply (R4), and that (R4) would in turn yield decidability of the existential Lval(t)-theory of F_p((t)).
self_contained_problem:
Let $K$ be a field and let $F\mid K$ be a field extension. A place of $F$ is a map $P:F\to L\cup\{\infty\}$ (with $L$ a field) that is a ring homomorphism on its valuation ring and sends every element outside the valuation ring to $\infty$. The place $P$ is said to be $K$-rational if $P$ is the identity on $K$ and the residue field $FP$ equals $K$ (so $P$ fixes $K$ pointwise and the image of its valuation ring under $P$ is exactly $K$). One says that $K$ is existentially closed in $F$ if every existential first-order sentence in the language of rings with parameters from $K$ that holds in $F$ already holds in $K$.

Hypothesis (R4) asserts: for every field $K$ and every field extension $F\mid K$, if $F\mid K$ admits a $K$-rational place, then $K$ is existentially closed in $F$.

Question: Does hypothesis (R4) hold?
status_search_result: Hypothesis (R4) is a known open problem in the model theory of valued fields, connected to local uniformization in positive characteristic and to the decidability of the existential theory of $\mathbb{F}_p((t))$. Recent surveys and talks by Kuhlmann list it as an open problem; no proof or counterexample for arbitrary fields $K$ has been published.

original_question: Let (K,v) be a henselian valued field. Assume that every algebraic extension of (K,v) is an independent defect field in the sense defined in the paper via Galois extensions of prime degree with nontrivial defect. Does it follow that (K,v) must already be a roughly deeply ramified field?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $(K,v)$ be a henselian valued field, with valuation ring $\mathcal{O}_v$, value group $vK$, and residue field $Kv$. For a finite extension $(L|K,v)$, write $e(L|K) = (vL : vK)$ for the ramification index, $f(L|K) = [Lv : Kv]$ for the residue degree, and define the defect $d(L|K)$ by the fundamental equality
$$[L:K] \;=\; d(L|K)\cdot e(L|K)\cdot f(L|K),$$
so $d(L|K)$ is a power of the residue characteristic $p = \mathrm{char}\,Kv$ (and equals $1$ if $p=0$).

A Galois extension $(L|K,v)$ of prime degree $p$ with nontrivial defect (i.e. $d(L|K)=p$) is called an independent defect extension if a certain canonical invariant (the "independent" type of defect, as opposed to "dependent" defect) holds; equivalently, the extension is not generated by an Artin–Schreier–type element whose defect is "linked" to a nontrivial immediate purely wild subextension. Call $(K,v)$ an independent defect field if every Galois defect extension of $(K,v)$ of prime degree has independent defect.

A henselian valued field $(K,v)$ is called roughly deeply ramified (rdr) if for every finite purely wild extension $(L|K,v)$ the trace ideal/different-type condition characterizing deeply ramified behaviour holds; equivalently, $(K,v)$ shares with deeply ramified and perfectoid fields the property that the module of relative Kähler differentials of every finite extension of its valuation ring vanishes after suitable localization. Every roughly deeply ramified henselian field has the property that all of its algebraic extensions are independent defect fields.

Question. Suppose $(K,v)$ is a henselian valued field such that every algebraic extension $(L|K,v|_L)$ of $(K,v)$ is an independent defect field (that is, every Galois extension of prime degree with nontrivial defect over any algebraic extension of $(K,v)$ has independent defect). Does it follow that $(K,v)$ is a roughly deeply ramified field?
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an explicit open conjecture in a December 2025 survey on the model theory of tame valued fields. One direction (every algebraic extension of a roughly deeply ramified field is an independent defect field) is known; the converse is stated as an open conjecture, and no resolution appears in the available literature.

status_search_result: The origin of the nitrogen-enhanced high-redshift galaxies discovered by JWST (e.g., GN-z11, CEERS-1019, GS_3073) remains an active open question as of 2026. paper_title: Open Questions in Massive Star Research across Cosmic Scales
original_question: For hot massive stars whose mass-loss rates inferred from standard ultraviolet and optical diagnostics are lower than what radiation pressure could theoretically drive, is the weak-wind problem a failure of radiation-driven wind physics or primarily a diagnostic problem caused by missing wind phases? The question requires distinguishing genuinely weak winds expected in low-density or low-luminosity regimes from cases where the real mass-loss rate is higher because a substantial hot wind component is invisible to standard ultraviolet and optical diagnostics.
self_contained_problem:
Consider hot massive stars (spectral types O and early B) whose stellar winds are believed to be driven by radiation pressure on spectral lines. For a subclass of such stars — typically late-O dwarfs of relatively low luminosity — the mass-loss rate Ṁ inferred from standard ultraviolet (e.g., C IV, Si IV, N V resonance line P Cygni profiles) and optical (e.g., Hα) diagnostics is found to be substantially smaller (often by factors of 10–100) than the rate that line-driven wind theory predicts could be accelerated by the available radiative momentum, and smaller than would be obtained by extrapolating mass-loss recipes calibrated on more luminous O stars. This is termed the "weak-wind problem."

Decide which of the following statements correctly characterizes the phenomenon, and give a quantitative criterion that distinguishes the two regimes:

(A) The weak-wind problem reflects a genuine breakdown of radiation-driven wind physics in the low-density, low-luminosity regime, so that the true total mass-loss rate is indeed close to the small value inferred from UV and optical diagnostics.

(B) The weak-wind problem is primarily a diagnostic artifact: the true total mass-loss rate is consistent with radiative driving, but a substantial fraction of the outflow resides in a hot (≳10^6 K) plasma phase that is not accessible to standard UV and optical line diagnostics and is instead detectable through X-ray spectroscopy or high-ionization infrared fine-structure lines.

Specifically, for the class of Galactic late-O dwarfs exhibiting the weak-wind signature, determine the fraction of the total mass-loss rate carried by the hot wind component as a function of stellar luminosity, effective temperature, and wind density, and identify the threshold (in terms of these parameters) below which scenario (A) rather than (B) applies.
status_search_result: Evidence supports that for at least the prototypical weak-wind star μ Columbae, X-ray spectroscopy reveals a hot wind component with a mass-loss rate roughly an order of magnitude higher than the UV/optical estimate, consistent with the wind-luminosity relation. Recent JWST mid-IR detections of high-ionization fine-structure lines in 10 Lac give additional support that mass-loss rates have been underestimated. However, a general, quantitative resolution distinguishing genuinely weak winds from diagnostic-driven underestimates across the full parameter space of late-O/early-B dwarfs has not been established, so the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Open Questions in Massive Star Research across Cosmic Scales
original_question: How should Wolf-Rayet spectral classifications be mapped to the underlying stellar structures, evolutionary states, and feedback properties of Wolf-Rayet stars? The answer must account for the fact that the same WN, WC, or WO subtype label can be produced by line ratios with different absolute line strengths, kinetic feedback, hydrostatic radii, hydrogen content, and burning stages, so treating Wolf-Rayet stars as one homogeneous group can misrepresent both evolution and feedback.
self_contained_problem:
Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars are massive, hot, evolved stars characterized by strong, broad emission lines arising in dense, fast stellar winds. They are spectroscopically classified into three principal types based on dominant emission features: WN stars (nitrogen-dominated emission), WC stars (carbon-dominated emission), and WO stars (oxygen-dominated emission). Each type is further divided into subtypes (e.g., WN2–WN11, WC4–WC9, WO1–WO4) defined by ratios of specific emission line strengths. Physically, WC and WO stars never display hydrogen in their spectra and must therefore be helium-burning ("classical") WR stars, while WN stars may be either hydrogen-burning or helium-burning depending on their hydrogen content. Two stars with very different absolute line strengths, mass-loss rates, terminal wind velocities, kinetic feedback into the interstellar medium, hydrostatic (core) radii, surface hydrogen mass fraction X_H, and current nuclear burning stage can produce identical line ratios and therefore share the same subtype label.

Construct an explicit, well-defined mapping

  Φ : {WR spectral subtype labels} ⟶ 𝒮,

where 𝒮 is a space of physical descriptors of the form

  s = (M_*, R_hydro, L_*, T_eff, Ṁ, v_∞, X_H, burning stage, evolutionary phase, Ė_kin),

(stellar mass, hydrostatic radius, luminosity, effective temperature at the hydrostatic radius, mass-loss rate, wind terminal velocity, surface hydrogen fraction, the current core nuclear burning stage, the evolutionary phase, and the wind kinetic-energy feedback rate Ė_kin = ½ Ṁ v_∞²), such that Φ is consistent with the observed degeneracies (different absolute line strengths can yield identical line ratios). Determine to what extent Φ can be made single-valued, identify the multivalued regions, and characterize the fibers Φ⁻¹(label) — that is, the full set of physically distinct stellar structures, evolutionary states, and feedback properties that can hide behind a single WN, WC, or WO subtype designation.
status_search_result: The classification-to-physics mapping for Wolf-Rayet stars remains an open problem in massive-star astrophysics. Recent reviews and modeling work (e.g., Sander, Crowther, Shenar and collaborators) emphasize that WR subtypes do not uniquely determine stellar structure, hydrogen content, evolutionary phase, or kinetic feedback, and ongoing efforts using PoWR/CMFGEN atmosphere models continue to refine but not resolve the degeneracies.

paper_title: Open Questions in Massive Star Research across Cosmic Scales
context_brief: sgB[e] stars as hidden post-common-envelope systems
original_question: Are supergiant B[e] stars a missing evolutionary link in the formation of mid-type WN Wolf-Rayet binaries, by masking post-common-envelope systems behind circumstellar material? This question includes testing whether objects such as HD 38489 in the Large Magellanic Cloud and Wd1-9 in Westerlund 1 hide Wolf-Rayet plus OB-star binary configurations beneath B[e]-type spectra or circumstellar emission.
self_contained_problem:
Supergiant B[e] stars (sgB[e]) are luminous, evolved early-type stars whose optical spectra are dominated by Balmer emission, low-excitation permitted and forbidden metallic emission lines, and a strong infrared excess attributed to hot circumstellar dust in a non-spherical (typically disk-like) envelope. It is widely held that the B[e] phenomenon reflects properties of the surrounding circumstellar material rather than of the underlying stellar object(s), so that a sgB[e] spectrum can in principle conceal the true nature of the central source(s), including the possibility that the central object is a binary system. A Wolf-Rayet (WR) star is a hot, hydrogen-depleted, high-mass-loss-rate evolved massive star; mid-type WN Wolf-Rayet stars are nitrogen-sequence WR stars of intermediate spectral subtype, and many are known to occur in close binaries with OB-type companions, where they are believed to descend from massive binaries that have undergone a common-envelope (CE) phase or other strong binary interaction.

Determine whether sgB[e] stars constitute a missing evolutionary link in the formation of mid-type WN + OB binary systems, in the sense that a non-trivial fraction of sgB[e] objects are post-common-envelope binaries whose WR + OB nature is hidden beneath optically thick circumstellar emission characteristic of the B[e] phenomenon. In particular, decide whether the sgB[e] stars HD 38489 (= LHA 120-S134) in the Large Magellanic Cloud and Wd1-9 in the young massive Galactic cluster Westerlund 1 host underlying WR + OB-star binaries concealed by their B[e]-type spectra and circumstellar emission.
status_search_result: Recent literature provides mounting but not yet conclusive evidence for the hypothesis. The X-ray spectrum of Wd1-9 has been interpreted as a WR+OB binary, and a related study of Wd1-72 frames it together with Wd1-9 as candidate post-interaction WN binaries, supporting the view that some sgB[e] stars hide post-common-envelope WR+OB systems. However, the general claim across the sgB[e] population, and the specific status of HD 38489, are not established, so the question remains only partially answered.

paper_title: Open Questions in Massive Star Research across Cosmic Scales
context_brief: Formation of WN2 and WN3h helium-ionizing sources
original_question: How can stellar-evolution and population-synthesis models reproduce observed WN2 and WN3h Wolf-Rayet stars, especially cases with no detectable companion, while also accounting for their role as strong helium-ionizing sources? A successful answer must explain the formation of early-type WN stars in subsolar-metallicity environments, the absence of plausible dark massive companions for the Small Magellanic Cloud WN3 stars, and the hard ionizing flux that such stars may contribute to low-metallicity galaxies.
self_contained_problem:
Wolf–Rayet (WR) stars are evolved, hot, massive stars that have lost most of their hydrogen-rich envelope and exhibit strong, broad emission lines from dense stellar winds. The nitrogen-sequence WN subtypes are ordered by ionization (and effective temperature), with WN2 being the hottest; the suffix "h" (as in WN3h) indicates the presence of residual hydrogen in the atmosphere. Stars of subtypes WN2 and WN3h have optically thin enough winds that they emit a hard ionizing continuum, including photons capable of doubly ionizing helium (energies ≥ 54.4 eV).

Observationally, all six known WN3h stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC, of metallicity Z ≈ 0.2 Z⊙) contain some hydrogen, while still hotter WN2 stars are found in the outer Milky Way, M33, and the Large Magellanic Cloud, suggesting an association with subsolar metallicity. Detailed multi-epoch radial-velocity monitoring of the SMC WN3 stars rules out, at the 95% confidence level, all binary companions more massive than 5 M⊙ with orbital periods shorter than one year, eliminating essentially all plausible dark massive companions (such as black holes or neutron stars) as drivers of envelope removal.

Within this setup, provide a stellar-evolution and population-synthesis framework that simultaneously:

1. Reproduces the formation of apparently single early-type WN stars (WN2 and WN3h) at subsolar metallicity, given that line-driven mass loss is too weak at such metallicities to strip the hydrogen envelope by the standard "Conti" single-star wind-stripping scenario, and that binary mass transfer or merger products with surviving companions are excluded for the SMC WN3h sample.

2. Predicts the correct relative numbers, hydrogen surface abundances, luminosities, and effective temperatures of WN2 and WN3h stars as a function of metallicity, including the direct WN-to-WO transition.

3. Quantifies the He II–ionizing photon production rate of these stars during their core helium-burning lifetimes and embeds it into a population-synthesis prescription able to account for their cumulative contribution to the hard ionizing radiation field of low-metallicity star-forming galaxies.

Identify the physical mechanism (e.g., rotationally induced chemically homogeneous evolution, envelope inflation and pulsation-driven mass loss, episodic eruptive mass loss, optically thick continuum-driven winds, or another process) that achieves all three requirements consistently.
status_search_result: Recent literature (2024–2025) confirms this remains an open problem. Schootemeijer et al. (2024) excluded companions >5 M⊙ with periods <1 year for the SMC WN3h sample, and follow-up work (e.g., Pauli et al. 2025 on metal-poor single WR stars; the SDSS-V LVM study of SMC WN3 stars, 2025) explicitly states that no current standard evolution model predicts the present population of weak-lined WN2/WN3 stars in the Magellanic Clouds, and proposes the interplay of optically thick winds and rotation as a candidate mechanism still under investigation.

paper_title: Neutrino production mechanisms in strongly magnetized quark matter: Current status and open questions
context_brief: Neutrino trapping and diffusion in early compact stars
original_question: During the early deleptonization stage of a compact star, when neutrinos are trapped and diffusion rather than free streaming controls neutrino transport, can anisotropic neutrino diffusion in strongly magnetized, lepton-rich quark matter generate momentum asymmetries that differ qualitatively from the asymmetries obtained in the free-streaming regime? A satisfactory answer requires microscopic calculations at nonzero neutrino chemical potential together with a self-consistent transport treatment of neutrino diffusion in the magnetized medium.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a region of dense quark matter in the early deleptonization stage of a newly formed compact star, modeled as a relativistic, lepton-rich plasma containing deconfined u, d, s quarks together with electrons and trapped neutrinos at finite temperature T, finite baryon chemical potential μ_B, and finite (nonzero) neutrino chemical potential μ_ν, immersed in a strong, uniform background magnetic field B = B ẑ. Assume that the mean free path of neutrinos is short compared to the macroscopic size of the system, so that neutrino transport is governed by diffusion rather than free streaming.

Using a microscopic calculation of the neutrino self-energy / opacity tensor in the magnetized, lepton-rich medium at nonzero μ_ν (including weak charged- and neutral-current interactions with quarks and leptons in Landau levels), couple the resulting anisotropic opacity to a self-consistent relativistic neutrino transport equation in the diffusion approximation, and compute the net neutrino momentum flux

  P^i = ∫ d^3k (k^i / |k|) f_ν(k, x),

where f_ν is the steady-state neutrino distribution function obtained from the diffusion equation in the magnetized medium.

Question: In this trapped/diffusive regime, does the resulting momentum asymmetry — in particular the component of P parallel to B relative to the component perpendicular to B, and its dependence on B, T, μ_B and μ_ν — differ qualitatively (in sign, scaling with B, or parametric dependence) from the asymmetry obtained in the free-streaming limit (where the same microscopic interactions are used but neutrinos escape without rescattering)? Provide a quantitative comparison of the two regimes.
category_tag: neutrino transport in magnetized quark matter
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an outlook/open direction: anisotropic neutrino diffusion in strongly magnetized, lepton-rich quark matter at nonzero neutrino chemical potential has not been worked out with a self-consistent transport treatment in the literature surveyed. No published result resolving the qualitative comparison between diffusive and free-streaming momentum asymmetries in this setting was found.

paper_title: Neutrino production mechanisms in strongly magnetized quark matter: Current status and open questions
original_question: For single-flavor spin-one color-superconducting phases of quark matter, which admit multiple pairing patterns, how does each pairing pattern affect neutrino emission, especially in phases whose superconducting gap has nodes or lines on the Fermi surface? In particular, can such gapless or nodal phases support low-energy excitations that produce non-negligible neutrino emission with observable consequences for compact-star cooling?
self_contained_problem:
Consider single-flavor spin-one color-superconducting phases of dense quark matter, in which Cooper pairing occurs between quarks of a single flavor in a spin-triplet channel. Such phases admit several inequivalent pairing patterns (for instance, the color-spin-locked phase, the polar phase, the planar phase, and the A phase), each characterized by a different angular structure of the gap function Δ(p) on the Fermi surface. In some of these patterns Δ(p) is fully gapped, while in others it has point nodes or line nodes on the Fermi surface, allowing gapless quasiparticle excitations near those nodes.

For each such pairing pattern, determine how the angular structure of the gap (in particular the presence and dimensionality of nodes) controls the temperature dependence and magnitude of the neutrino emissivity from direct Urca-like quark beta processes at temperatures T well below the critical temperature T_c. In particular:

(a) Compute the leading low-temperature behavior of the neutrino emissivity ε_ν(T) for each pairing pattern, identifying the power-law versus exponential suppression induced by full gaps, point nodes, or line nodes.

(b) Determine whether the nodal (gapless) phases can support low-energy quasiparticle excitations producing neutrino emission rates comparable to, or larger than, those of unpaired quark matter in a temperature window relevant to neutron-star cooling.

(c) Assess whether the resulting cooling curves of a compact star with a quark-matter core in such a phase exhibit observationally distinguishable signatures relative to fully gapped phases and to ordinary neutron-star cooling scenarios.
status_search_result: Neutrino emissivities for several spin-one color-superconducting pairing patterns (CSL, polar, planar, A phase) have been computed in the literature, with explicit analysis of how nodes in the gap function control the low-temperature behavior of direct Urca processes and of compact-star cooling. However, a complete pattern-by-pattern classification including all microscopic effects and the resulting observational signatures across realistic neutron-star cooling models remains an active research topic.

paper_title: Open Problems in K-Stability of Fano Varieties
original_question: For integers n and d with 3 <= d <= n + 1, is every smooth degree-d hypersurface in projective space P^{n+1} K-stable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 2$ and $d$ be integers satisfying $3 \leq d \leq n+1$, and let $X \subset \mathbb{P}^{n+1}_{\mathbb{C}}$ be a smooth hypersurface of degree $d$. Then $X$ is a Fano manifold (its anticanonical class $-K_X = (n+2-d)H|_X$ is ample, where $H$ is the hyperplane class). Recall that a Fano manifold $X$ is called K-stable if for every nontrivial test configuration $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{L})$ of $(X,-K_X)$, the generalized Donaldson–Futaki invariant $\mathrm{DF}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{L})$ is strictly positive (equivalently, in valuative terms, $\beta(E) := A_X(E) - S_X(E) > 0$ for every prime divisor $E$ over $X$, where $A_X(E)$ is the log discrepancy and $S_X(E) = \frac{1}{(-K_X)^n}\int_0^\infty \mathrm{vol}(-K_X - tE)\,dt$).

Prove that for every pair of integers $(n,d)$ with $3 \leq d \leq n+1$, every smooth hypersurface of degree $d$ in $\mathbb{P}^{n+1}$ is K-stable.
status_search_result: The general conjecture remains open. K-stability of smooth Fano hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{P}^{n+1}$ of degree $3 \leq d \leq n+1$ has been established in several special cases: when the Fano index is 1 or 2, for general hypersurfaces, for cubic fourfolds, when the dimension is at least the cube of the Fano index, and when the Fano index is at most $n/3$. The case $d=n+1$ (index 1) follows from an alpha-invariant bound $\alpha(X) \geq n/(n+1)$. A full proof for all $(n,d)$ in this range has not been established.

paper_title: Open Problems in K-Stability of Fano Varieties
original_question: Given positive integers d_1, ..., d_k with k + 2 <= sum_i d_i <= n + k, is a general complete intersection of multidegree (d_1, ..., d_k) K-stable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 1$ and $k \geq 1$ be integers, and let $d_1, \ldots, d_k$ be positive integers satisfying
$$k + 2 \;\le\; \sum_{i=1}^{k} d_i \;\le\; n + k.$$
A complete intersection of multidegree $(d_1, \ldots, d_k)$ in $\mathbb{P}^{n+k}$ is the scheme-theoretic intersection $X = H_1 \cap \cdots \cap H_k \subset \mathbb{P}^{n+k}$ of $k$ hypersurfaces $H_i$ of degree $d_i$ that meet transversally; such an $X$ is a smooth $n$-dimensional Fano variety with $-K_X = \mathcal{O}_X(n + k + 1 - \sum_i d_i)$ when the inequality is strict, and a smooth Calabi–Yau-type boundary case is excluded. (The lower bound $\sum d_i \geq k+2$ excludes projective spaces and quadrics, and the upper bound $\sum d_i \leq n+k$ ensures $X$ is Fano.)

Prove that, for every such tuple $(d_1, \ldots, d_k)$, a general complete intersection of multidegree $(d_1, \ldots, d_k)$ in $\mathbb{P}^{n+k}$ is K-stable.

Here K-stability is the algebro-geometric notion characterizing existence of Kähler–Einstein metrics on smooth Fano varieties: $X$ is K-stable if for every nontrivial test configuration $(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{L}) \to \mathbb{A}^1$ for $(X, -K_X)$ with reduced central fiber, the generalized Donaldson–Futaki invariant $\mathrm{DF}(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{L})$ is strictly positive (equivalently, by Fujita–Li, the stability threshold satisfies $\delta(X) > 1$).
status_search_result: K-stability of general Fano complete intersections is known only in restricted ranges. Zhuang and others established K-stability for index-1 Fano complete intersections via birational superrigidity, and K-stability of smooth Fano hypersurfaces of index 2 has been proved. For general multidegrees with $k+2 \le \sum d_i \le n+k$, however, K-stability of a general complete intersection remains open in higher dimensions, and surveys describe the higher-dimensional case as largely unresolved.

paper_title: Open Problems in K-Stability of Fano Varieties
original_question: Is every smooth Fano threefold X with Picard number rho(X) = 1 K-semistable?
self_contained_problem: A smooth Fano threefold is a smooth complex projective variety $X$ of dimension $3$ whose anticanonical divisor $-K_X$ is ample. Its Picard number $\rho(X)$ is the rank of the Picard group $\mathrm{Pic}(X)$. Recall that $X$ is said to be K-semistable if for every test configuration $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{L})$ of $(X,-K_X)$ the generalized Futaki invariant (equivalently, the Donaldson–Futaki invariant) satisfies $\mathrm{Fut}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{L}) \geq 0$.\n\nProve or disprove: every smooth Fano threefold $X$ with Picard number $\rho(X) = 1$ is K-semistable.
status_search_result: K-stability of smooth Fano threefolds with Picard number 1 (the "prime" Fano threefolds) is an active area of research. Although individual deformation families have been substantially analyzed, no complete classification of K-(semi)stable members exists for all such families, and recent literature (e.g., on K-moduli of prime Fano threefolds of genus twelve, 2025–2026) explicitly states that K-moduli boundaries are not described for any family of prime Fano threefolds. The conjecture that every such smooth threefold is K-semistable remains open in general.

paper_title: Open Problems in K-Stability of Fano Varieties
original_question: Let X be a Fano variety and T_X its tangent sheaf. Give a purely algebraic proof that if X is K-semistable, then T_X is semistable with respect to the polarization -K_X. Also give a purely algebraic proof that if T_X is polystable, then there exists a quasi-etale cover f: Y -> X such that Y decomposes as a product of varieties Y = \prod_i X_i and the pulled-back tangent sheaf T_Y = f^*(T_X) decomposes as a direct sum igoplus_i T_{X_i}, with each T_{X_i} stable with respect to -K_Y.
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a Fano variety over $\mathbb{C}$, that is, a normal projective variety with at worst klt singularities such that the anticanonical divisor $-K_X$ is an ample $\mathbb{Q}$-Cartier divisor. Let $T_X$ denote the tangent sheaf of $X$. Recall that a torsion-free coherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ on $X$ is slope semistable (resp. stable, polystable) with respect to the polarization $-K_X$ if for every coherent subsheaf $0 \neq \mathcal{G} \subsetneq \mathcal{F}$ of strictly smaller rank one has $\mu_{-K_X}(\mathcal{G}) \le \mu_{-K_X}(\mathcal{F})$ (resp. $<$, resp. semistable and isomorphic to a direct sum of stable subsheaves of equal slope), where $\mu_{-K_X}(\mathcal{F}) = \frac{c_1(\mathcal{F})\cdot (-K_X)^{n-1}}{\mathrm{rank}(\mathcal{F})}$ and $n = \dim X$. A finite surjective morphism $f: Y \to X$ between normal varieties is called quasi-étale if it is étale in codimension one. Prove the following two statements using only algebro-geometric methods (without invoking the existence of Kähler–Einstein metrics or other transcendental/analytic tools):

(1) If $X$ is K-semistable, then $T_X$ is slope semistable with respect to $-K_X$.

(2) If $T_X$ is slope polystable with respect to $-K_X$, then there exists a quasi-étale cover $f: Y \to X$ such that $Y$ admits a decomposition $Y = \prod_i X_i$ as a product of normal projective varieties, the pullback of the tangent sheaf decomposes correspondingly as $f^*(T_X) = T_Y = \bigoplus_i T_{X_i}$ (where each $T_{X_i}$ is identified with its pullback to $Y$), and each summand $T_{X_i}$ is slope stable with respect to $-K_Y$.
status_search_result: A purely algebraic proof of these statements is explicitly listed as an open problem in the survey on open problems in K-stability of Fano varieties. Analytic proofs via Kähler–Einstein metrics are known (Tian, Donaldson, and others), and partial algebraic results exist for log-Fano pairs and special cases (e.g., logarithmic tangent sheaf semistability), but no fully algebraic proof of (1) and (2) in the general singular Fano setting appears to have been published as of mid-2026.

paper_title: Open Problems in K-Stability of Fano Varieties
original_question: For a Fano variety X, is the Gibbs-stability invariant gamma(X) > 1 exactly when X is K-stable, and gamma(X) >= 1 exactly when X is K-semistable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano variety, that is, a normal projective variety with at worst klt singularities such that $-K_X$ is an ample $\mathbb{Q}$-Cartier divisor. For each integer $N$ such that $-NK_X$ is Cartier and very ample, choose a basis of $H^0(X, -NK_X)$ to embed $X^N := X \times \cdots \times X$ ($N$ factors), and consider the natural $\mathbb{Q}$-divisor $D_N$ on $X^N$ associated with the Vandermonde-type section
$$\det\bigl(s_i(x_j)\bigr)_{1\le i,j \le \dim H^0(X,-NK_X)}$$
(the "free-energy" divisor arising from the $N$-particle Gibbs measure with inverse temperature determined by $-K_X$). Define the Gibbs-stability invariant
$$\gamma(X) := \lim_{N\to\infty} \mathrm{lct}\bigl(X^N, \tfrac{1}{N}D_N\bigr),$$
where $\mathrm{lct}$ denotes the log canonical threshold (the limit is known to exist).

Recall that $X$ is K-stable (resp. K-semistable) if for every nontrivial special test configuration $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{L})$ for $(X,-K_X)$, the Donaldson–Futaki invariant $\mathrm{DF}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{L})$ is positive (resp. nonnegative).

Prove or disprove: $\gamma(X) > 1$ if and only if $X$ is K-stable, and $\gamma(X) \ge 1$ if and only if $X$ is K-semistable.
status_search_result: The conjecture (due to Berman) remains open in general. Fujita (2015, Compositio Math.) established that Berman–Gibbs (semi)stability implies K-(semi)stability for $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties, providing one direction. The reverse implication is still conjectural; recent work by Berman and collaborators (2025) extends the framework to Gibbs polystability and proves results in special cases (e.g., log Fano curves), but the full equivalence remains unresolved.

paper_title: Open Problems in K-Stability of Fano Varieties
context_brief: Contact Fano varieties from Lie theory
original_question: For the natural contact Fano varieties obtained as projective bases of conical symplectic singularities arising from Lie theory, is the projective base of a nilpotent orbit closure K-polystable? Is the projective base of a Slodowy slice K-polystable?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. A normal complex projective variety $X$ with at worst klt singularities and ample anticanonical class $-K_X$ is called a Fano variety. Such an $X$ is said to be K-polystable if for every test configuration $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{L}) \to \mathbb{A}^1$ of $(X,-K_X)$ with reduced central fiber, the generalized Donaldson–Futaki invariant satisfies $\mathrm{DF}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{L}) \geq 0$, with equality only when the test configuration is a product configuration.

A normal complex affine variety $Y$ with a $\mathbb{C}^*$-action and a holomorphic symplectic form $\omega$ on its smooth locus is called a conical symplectic singularity if (i) the $\mathbb{C}^*$-action contracts $Y$ to a single fixed point $0 \in Y$ and acts on $\omega$ with a positive weight $\ell$, and (ii) $\omega$ extends to a regular (possibly degenerate) $2$-form on any resolution of singularities of $Y$. The projective base of such a conical symplectic singularity $Y$ is the GIT quotient $\mathbb{P}(Y) := (Y \setminus \{0\})/\mathbb{C}^*$; under suitable conditions $\mathbb{P}(Y)$ is a Fano variety and carries a natural contact structure on its smooth locus.

Two natural classes of conical symplectic singularities arise from complex semisimple Lie theory:
(a) Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a complex semisimple Lie algebra and let $\mathcal{O} \subset \mathfrak{g}$ be a nilpotent (co)adjoint orbit. The orbit closure $\overline{\mathcal{O}} \subset \mathfrak{g}$, with the standard $\mathbb{C}^*$-scaling action, is a conical symplectic singularity.
(b) For a nilpotent element $e \in \mathfrak{g}$ embedded in an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple $(e,h,f)$, the Slodowy slice $\mathcal{S}_e := e + \mathfrak{g}^f$ inherits, after intersecting with a nilpotent orbit closure $\overline{\mathcal{O}}$ containing $e$, a conical symplectic singularity structure (with the Kazhdan $\mathbb{C}^*$-action).

Question. For each of the following, decide whether the resulting contact Fano projective base is K-polystable:
(1) Is the projective base $\mathbb{P}(\overline{\mathcal{O}})$ of a nilpotent orbit closure $\overline{\mathcal{O}}$ in a complex semisimple Lie algebra K-polystable?
(2) Is the projective base $\mathbb{P}(\overline{\mathcal{O}} \cap \mathcal{S}_e)$ of a Slodowy slice in a nilpotent orbit closure K-polystable?
status_search_result: No published resolution was found. The questions sit within the broader LeBrun–Salamon-type conjecture that contact Fano manifolds/varieties should be K-polystable, an active research area; available literature discusses singularities, resolutions, and K-stability of Fano varieties more generally, but does not establish K-polystability of the projective bases of nilpotent orbit closures or of Slodowy slices in this generality.

paper_title: Open Problems in K-Stability of Fano Varieties
original_question: If x in X is a singular point of dimension n, is its normalized volume bounded above by 2(n - 1)^n, with equality only for the A_1 singularity?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X, x)$ be an $n$-dimensional klt (Kawamata log terminal) singularity over $\mathbb{C}$, where $x \in X$ is a closed point. Recall that the normalized volume of $(X, x)$, introduced by C. Li, is defined as
$$ \widehat{\mathrm{vol}}(x, X) \;=\; \inf_{v} \; A_X(v)^n \cdot \mathrm{vol}(v), $$
where the infimum runs over all real valuations $v$ of the function field of $X$ centered at $x$, $A_X(v)$ denotes the log discrepancy of $v$ with respect to $X$, and $\mathrm{vol}(v)$ denotes the volume of $v$. The $A_1$ singularity in dimension $n$ is the hypersurface singularity defined by $x_0^2 + x_1^2 + \cdots + x_n^2 = 0$ at the origin in $\mathbb{A}^{n+1}$; its normalized volume equals $2(n-1)^n$.

Prove or disprove: for every $n$-dimensional klt singularity $(X, x)$ with $x$ a singular point,
$$ \widehat{\mathrm{vol}}(x, X) \;\leq\; 2(n-1)^n, $$
and equality holds if and only if $(X, x)$ is the $n$-dimensional $A_1$ singularity.
category_tag: K-stability and normalized volumes of klt singularities
status_search_result: The conjecture that the normalized volume of an n-dimensional klt singularity is at most 2(n-1)^n, with equality only for the A_1 singularity (often attributed to Spotti–Sun and Li–Liu–Xu), remains open in general. Recent work (e.g., Moraga 2024 on toric singularities, and Liu 2025 on optimal bounds for threefold singularities) establishes the bound in special cases, but the full conjecture in arbitrary dimension is unresolved.

paper_title: Open Problems in K-Stability of Fano Varieties
context_brief: Special valuations for Fano type morphisms
original_question: Let f : (Y, Delta) -> X be a Fano type morphism and let D be a complement. What is the structure of the special valuations LCPS(Y, Delta + D) inside the cone of log-canonical-place valuations LCP(Y, Delta + D)?
self_contained_problem:
Work over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. A morphism f : (Y, Δ) → X from a normal pair (Y, Δ) (where Δ is an effective Q-divisor with (Y, Δ) klt) to a normal variety X is called a Fano type morphism if f is projective with connected fibers and there exists an effective Q-divisor Γ on Y such that (Y, Δ + Γ) is klt and -(K_Y + Δ + Γ) is f-ample (equivalently, (Y, Δ) is relatively of Fano type over X).

A complement of f : (Y, Δ) → X is an effective Q-divisor D on Y such that K_Y + Δ + D ~_{Q,f} 0 and the pair (Y, Δ + D) is log canonical.

For a log canonical pair (Y, Δ + D), a divisorial valuation v = ord_E on the function field of Y (with E a prime divisor on some birational model of Y) is called a log canonical place of (Y, Δ + D) if the log discrepancy a_E(Y, Δ + D) = 0. Let LCP(Y, Δ + D) denote the (rational) cone of log canonical place valuations of (Y, Δ + D), i.e. the cone generated, in the space of real divisorial valuations, by such ord_E.

A log canonical place v of (Y, Δ + D) is called special if there exists a projective birational model π : Y' → Y on which v is realized as a divisor E ⊂ Y' such that E is a Fano type variety over its image (equivalently, v admits a "special" extraction in the sense that the corresponding plt-type extraction π : (Y', Δ' + E) → Y produces a Fano type fibration from E). Let LCPS(Y, Δ + D) ⊆ LCP(Y, Δ + D) denote the subset of special log canonical place valuations.

Problem. Describe the structure of LCPS(Y, Δ + D) inside LCP(Y, Δ + D). In particular: is LCPS(Y, Δ + D) a (rational polyhedral or otherwise distinguished) subcone of LCP(Y, Δ + D)? Identify, for a Fano type morphism f : (Y, Δ) → X with complement D, geometric or combinatorial conditions characterizing which log canonical place valuations of (Y, Δ + D) are special.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open research problem in the area of K-stability and birational geometry of Fano varieties, concerning the structure of special log canonical place valuations for Fano type morphisms. No published resolution was located; the question appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open Problems in K-Stability of Fano Varieties
original_question: In the same graded-ideal-sequence setting, does LCP(X, Delta + c a_•) contain a valuation v whose associated graded algebra Gr_v R is finitely generated? More strongly, does it contain a Kollár valuation?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a normal complex variety and $\Delta$ an effective $\mathbb{Q}$-divisor on $X$ such that $(X,\Delta)$ is a klt pair. Let $\mathfrak{a}_\bullet = \{\mathfrak{a}_m\}_{m\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}}$ be a graded sequence of nonzero coherent ideal sheaves on $X$ (i.e. $\mathfrak{a}_p\cdot\mathfrak{a}_q\subseteq\mathfrak{a}_{p+q}$ for all $p,q$), and let 
$$c = \mathrm{lct}(X,\Delta;\mathfrak{a}_\bullet) := \lim_{m\to\infty} m\cdot \mathrm{lct}(X,\Delta;\mathfrak{a}_m)$$
be its log canonical threshold. Define the set of log canonical places of the formal triple $(X,\Delta+c\cdot\mathfrak{a}_\bullet)$ as 
$$\mathrm{LCP}(X,\Delta+c\cdot\mathfrak{a}_\bullet) = \{\,v \in \mathrm{Val}_X^* \;:\; A_{X,\Delta}(v) = c\cdot v(\mathfrak{a}_\bullet)\,\},$$
where $A_{X,\Delta}$ is the log discrepancy and $v(\mathfrak{a}_\bullet) = \lim_m v(\mathfrak{a}_m)/m$. For a valuation $v$ on $R = \mathcal{O}_{X,x}$ (or the function field), let $\mathrm{Gr}_v R = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \{f : v(f)\geq\lambda\}/\{f : v(f)>\lambda\}$ be its associated graded algebra. A valuation $v\in\mathrm{LCP}(X,\Delta+c\cdot\mathfrak{a}_\bullet)$ is called a Kollár valuation if there exists a projective birational morphism $\pi:Y\to X$ extracting a single prime divisor $E$ such that $v = \mathrm{ord}_E$ and $(Y,\pi_*^{-1}\Delta + E)$ is plt with $-(K_Y+\pi_*^{-1}\Delta+E)$ ample over $X$.

Prove or disprove:
\begin{enumerate}
\item (Weaker version) $\mathrm{LCP}(X,\Delta+c\cdot\mathfrak{a}_\bullet)$ contains a valuation $v$ such that the associated graded algebra $\mathrm{Gr}_v R$ is finitely generated.
\item (Stronger version) $\mathrm{LCP}(X,\Delta+c\cdot\mathfrak{a}_\bullet)$ contains a Kollár valuation.
\end{enumerate}
status_search_result: Recent work has established related results: a valuation computing the lct of a graded sequence of ideals can be taken to be quasi-monomial (Jonsson–Mustaţă-type theorems), and finite generation of the associated graded algebra has been proven for quasi-monomial valuations on qdlt Fano-type models (and recently extended via extended Rees algebras in work from 2025). However, no source confirms a complete resolution of the existence of an LCP valuation with finitely generated graded algebra, nor of a Kollár valuation in LCP, in the generality stated. The problem appears to remain open.
