original_question: For every space bound S(n) with S(n) at least log n, is the class DSPACE(S(n)) of languages accepted by deterministic Turing machines using O(S(n)) work tape space equal to the class NSPACE(S(n)) accepted by nondeterministic Turing machines using O(S(n)) work tape space? In particular, does this hold in the special case S(n)=n, the linear-bounded-automaton (LBA) case?
self_contained_problem:
For a function $S:\mathbb{N}	o\mathbb{N}$, let $\mathrm{DSPACE}(S(n))$ denote the class of languages $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ accepted by some deterministic Turing machine with a read-only input tape and a separate work tape such that, on every input of length $n$, the machine uses $O(S(n))$ cells on the work tape. Let $\mathrm{NSPACE}(S(n))$ denote the analogous class defined using nondeterministic Turing machines with the same $O(S(n))$ work-tape bound.

Question: Is it true that for every space-constructible function $S(n)$ with $S(n) \geq \log n$, one has
$$\mathrm{DSPACE}(S(n)) \;=\; \mathrm{NSPACE}(S(n))?$$
In particular, in the special case $S(n) = n$ (the linear-bounded automaton, or LBA, problem), does $\mathrm{DSPACE}(n) = \mathrm{NSPACE}(n)$ hold?
status_search_result: The LBA problem (whether DSPACE(n) = NSPACE(n)) and the more general question of whether DSPACE(S(n)) = NSPACE(S(n)) for all S(n) ≥ log n remain longstanding open problems in complexity theory. Savitch's theorem gives NSPACE(S) ⊆ DSPACE(S^2), and the Immerman–Szelepcsényi theorem (1987–88) shows NSPACE(S) is closed under complement, but equality with DSPACE(S) is still unresolved.

original_question: Is the class P-TIME of polynomial-time decidable languages equal to the class P-SPACE of languages decidable by deterministic Turing machines using polynomial space?
self_contained_problem:
Let P denote the class of all languages $L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$ for which there exists a deterministic Turing machine $M$ and a polynomial $p$ such that $M$ decides membership in $L$ and, on every input $x$, halts within $p(|x|)$ steps. Let PSPACE denote the class of all languages $L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$ for which there exists a deterministic Turing machine $M$ and a polynomial $q$ such that $M$ decides membership in $L$ and, on every input $x$, uses at most $q(|x|)$ tape cells of work space.

Determine whether P = PSPACE.
status_search_result: The question of whether P equals PSPACE is a long-standing major open problem in computational complexity theory. It is widely believed that P ≠ PSPACE, but no proof of separation (or equality) is known.

original_question: Is the class 2DPDA of languages accepted by one-head two-way deterministic pushdown automata exactly equal to DLBA, the class of languages accepted by deterministic linear bounded automata?
self_contained_problem:
Let 2DPDA denote the class of languages accepted by one-head two-way deterministic pushdown automata: machines equipped with a read-only input tape (with end markers) on which a single head may move in both directions, together with a deterministic pushdown stack, that accept by entering a designated accepting state. Let DLBA denote the class of languages accepted by deterministic linear bounded automata: deterministic Turing machines whose work tape is restricted to the cells originally occupied by the input (equivalently, deterministic nondeterministic-space O(n) machines restricted to be deterministic, i.e., DSPACE(n)).

Determine whether these two classes are equal:
$$ \mathrm{2DPDA} \stackrel{?}{=} \mathrm{DLBA}. $$
That is, prove or disprove that a language is accepted by some one-head two-way deterministic pushdown automaton if and only if it is accepted by some deterministic linear bounded automaton.
status_search_result: The question of whether 2DPDA equals DLBA appears to remain open. 2DPDA is known to be contained in DTIME(n) (Cook's theorem) and hence in DLBA, but no proof of equality or separation has been reported. original_question: Is the class 2DC of languages accepted by two-way deterministic counter machines equal to the class 2NC accepted by two-way nondeterministic counter machines?
self_contained_problem:
A two-way counter machine is a finite-state device equipped with a read-only two-way input tape (with end markers) and a single counter that holds a nonnegative integer. In one step the machine reads the current input symbol and the sign-status of the counter (zero or positive), then chooses a next state, a head movement (left, stay, or right), and a counter operation (increment, decrement, or no change). The machine is deterministic if its transition function assigns at most one move to each configuration (a 2DC machine) and nondeterministic otherwise (a 2NC machine). A language is accepted by such a machine if, on input w, the machine has at least one computation that enters an accepting state.

Let 2DC denote the class of languages accepted by two-way deterministic counter machines, and 2NC the class of languages accepted by two-way nondeterministic counter machines. Decide whether
2DC = 2NC,
that is, whether every language accepted by some two-way nondeterministic counter machine is also accepted by some two-way deterministic counter machine.
status_search_result: Chrobak (MFCS 1984, "Nondeterminism is essential for two-way counter machines", LNCS 176, pp. 240–244) proved that two-way nondeterministic counter automata are strictly more powerful than two-way deterministic ones, i.e., 2DC ⊊ 2NC. Thus the equality question is settled in the negative.

(b) DLOG ⊊ 2DPDA,
(c) 2DPDA = DLOG,

original_question: Given a family consisting of 2dpda-languages or 2nc-languages of the kind constructed in the paper, does at least one language in that family belong to 2DC, the class of two-way deterministic counter-machine languages?
self_contained_problem:
Define the following classes of formal languages over a finite input alphabet, where each machine has read-only access to its input bracketed by left and right end markers and may move its input head in either direction.

- 2DPDA: the class of languages recognized by two-way deterministic pushdown automata (a finite-state control with a pushdown stack, deterministic transitions, and a two-way read-only input head).
- 2NPDA: the class of languages recognized by two-way nondeterministic pushdown automata.
- 2DC: the class of languages recognized by two-way deterministic counter machines, i.e. machines as above whose auxiliary storage is a single counter that can be incremented, decremented, and tested for zero, with deterministic transitions and a two-way input head.

Consider the following families of languages, defined for each integer n ≥ 1:

(a) L_n^{det} = { w ∈ {a, b, c, #}^* : w = x_1 # x_2 # … # x_k for some k ≥ 1 with each x_i ∈ {a,b}^*, and there exist indices 1 ≤ i < j ≤ k with j − i = n and x_i = x_j }, with deterministic recognizability witnessed by a 2DPDA.

(b) L_n^{nond} = an analogous family of 2NPDA-recognizable languages parameterized by n, obtained by allowing nondeterministic guessing of the matching index pair.

(More generally, let {F_n}_{n≥1} be any family of 2DPDA-languages, and let {G_n}_{n≥1} be any family of 2NPDA-languages.)

Question: Does there exist an integer n ≥ 1 such that L_n^{det} ∈ 2DC? Equivalently, is at least one member of the family {F_n} (respectively {G_n}) recognizable by a two-way deterministic counter machine?

Decide, for the families above, whether some member belongs to 2DC, or prove that no member of the family belongs to 2DC.

context_brief: Stability of a dimension estimate under bounded perturbations
original_question: Let S: X → Y and T: Y → Z be closed operators, and let A: X → Y and B: Y → Z be bounded operators. Define S̃ = S + A and T̃ = T + B. It is known, when X, Y, and Z are Hilbert spaces, that dim N(T̃)/R(S̃) = dim N(T)/R(S) < ∞. Does the same estimate remain valid when X, Y, and Z are Banach spaces instead of Hilbert spaces?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$, $Y$, $Z$ be Banach spaces. Let $S\colon X	o Y$ and $T\colon Y	o Z$ be closed (not necessarily bounded) linear operators with domains $\mathcal{D}(S)\subseteq X$ and $\mathcal{D}(T)\subseteq Y$, and assume that $R(S)\subseteq \mathcal{D}(T)$ and $TS=0$, so that the quotient $N(T)/R(S)$ is well defined, where $N(T)=\{y\in\mathcal{D}(T):Ty=0\}$ and $R(S)=\{Sx:x\in\mathcal{D}(S)\}$. Suppose that $\dim N(T)/R(S)<\infty$.

Let $A\colon X	o Y$ and $B\colon Y	o Z$ be everywhere defined bounded linear operators, and set $\widetilde S=S+A$ and $\widetilde T=T+B$ (so $\mathcal{D}(\widetilde S)=\mathcal{D}(S)$ and $\mathcal{D}(\widetilde T)=\mathcal{D}(T)$), and assume that $R(\widetilde S)\subseteq\mathcal{D}(\widetilde T)$ and $\widetilde T\widetilde S=0$.

It is known that when $X$, $Y$, $Z$ are Hilbert spaces one has
$$\dim N(\widetilde T)/R(\widetilde S)\;=\;\dim N(T)/R(S)\;<\;\infty.$$

Does this equality continue to hold when $X$, $Y$, $Z$ are arbitrary Banach spaces?
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface a definitive resolution (positive or negative) of the Banach-space version of this stability statement for the dimension of the cohomology $N(\widetilde T)/R(\widetilde S)$ under bounded perturbations of a pair of closed operators. Related Fredholm-type stability results exist for indices of single operators under bounded/compact perturbations, but no source clearly settles this two-step Banach-space formulation. Status is therefore recorded as unknown.

paper_title: Open Problems in Stringology
context_brief: one-way multihead automata for string matching
original_question: Let Σ be a finite alphabet and let $ be a separator symbol not in Σ. Can a one-way multihead deterministic finite automaton recognize the string-matching language {x$uxv | u, x, v are strings in Σ*}, that is, determine whether an input contains two occurrences of the same pattern x separated as x$uxv? Equivalently, can one-way multihead deterministic finite automata perform string matching?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $\$\notin\Sigma$ be a designated separator symbol. Consider the language
$$L \;=\; \{\, x\,\$\,u\,x\,v \;:\; x,u,v \in \Sigma^{*}\,\} \subseteq (\Sigma\cup\{\$\})^{*},$$
i.e. the set of strings that contain a $\$$ symbol such that some string $x$ appearing immediately before the $\$$ also occurs somewhere after the $\$$.

A one-way multihead deterministic finite automaton with $k$ heads is a finite-state machine equipped with $k$ read-only heads on a single input tape; each head moves only to the right (or stays in place) at each step, the heads cannot write, and the transition function is deterministic, depending on the current state and the tuple of symbols currently scanned by the heads.

Question: Does there exist an integer $k\ge 1$ and a one-way $k$-head deterministic finite automaton that recognizes $L$? Equivalently, can string matching be performed by a one-way multihead deterministic finite automaton?
status_search_result: The problem was settled negatively. Jiang and Li (1996), "k One-Way Heads Cannot Do String-Matching" (J. Comput. System Sci.), proved that for every k, no one-way k-head deterministic finite automaton can recognize the string-matching language, resolving the conjecture posed by Galil and Seiferas. An earlier partial result by Geréb-Graus and Li (1994) handled the case k = 3.

paper_title: Open Problems in Stringology
original_question: For string matching on an input of length n, can one design optimal parallel algorithms—meaning algorithms using p processors and time t with pt = O(n)—for larger processor ranges than were then known, specifically for ranges such as p ≤ n on a WRAM or p ≤ n/log n on a PRAM, while still solving the same string-matching problem efficiently?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the exact string matching problem: given a pattern of length m and a text of length n over some alphabet (with N = n + m the total input length), report all occurrences of the pattern in the text. We work in the standard parallel models of computation:

- A PRAM (Parallel Random Access Machine) consists of p synchronous processors sharing a common memory; concurrent reads of the same location are allowed but concurrent writes are not.
- A WRAM (also called CRCW PRAM) is the same model except that concurrent writes to the same memory location are also allowed (under some standard convention, e.g. the common-write rule).

A parallel algorithm using p processors and running in worst-case time t is called optimal if pt = O(n).

It is known that there exist optimal parallel algorithms for string matching in the ranges
  p ≤ n / log n on a WRAM, and
  p ≤ n / log² n on a PRAM.

Question: Do there exist optimal parallel string-matching algorithms (i.e. with pt = O(n)) for larger ranges of processors, in particular
  (a) for all p ≤ n on a WRAM, and
  (b) for all p ≤ n / log n on a PRAM?
status_search_result: The WRAM/CRCW-PRAM case appears resolved: Breslauer and Galil gave an optimal O(log log n)-time string-matching algorithm using n/log log n processors on a CRCW-PRAM, and Galil (STOC 1992) gave a constant-time optimal parallel string-matching algorithm, both achieving pt = O(n) in the regime p = Θ(n) on a WRAM. Subsequent randomized constant-time optimal algorithms also exist. Thus the WRAM portion (p ≤ n) of the question is solved; the corresponding PRAM (CREW) improvements have likewise been addressed in the follow-up literature.

paper_title: Some open problems of graph theory.
original_question: Given a finite set of integers, decide whether there exists a bipartite graph whose list of vertex degrees is exactly that set of integers.
self_contained_problem: For a graph $G$, let the degree set $D(G)$ denote the set of distinct vertex degrees occurring in $G$. Given a finite nonempty set $S$ of positive integers, design an algorithm (or give a characterization) that decides whether there exists a simple bipartite graph $G$ such that $D(G) = S$, i.e., the set of vertex degrees of $G$ equals exactly $S$.
status_search_result: The recognition question for bipartite degree sets is settled: it is known that for every finite nonempty set S of positive integers there exists a bipartite graph G with D(G) = S. This is established in the literature on bipartite graphs and their degree sets (e.g., Manoussakis and Patil, "Bipartite graphs and their degree sets," and subsequent works on minimum orders of such bipartite graphs). Hence the recognition problem has a trivial affirmative answer, and refinements (minimum order, connectedness, unicyclic, etc.) have also been characterized.

paper_title: Some open problems of graph theory.
original_question: Find the smallest integer k such that every k-Hamiltonian graph is Hamiltonian connected.
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finite simple graph on p ≥ 3 vertices. For an integer k with 0 ≤ k ≤ p − 3, the graph G is called k-Hamiltonian if for every set S of vertices with |S| ≤ k the graph G − S is Hamiltonian (so 0-Hamiltonian means Hamiltonian). The graph G is called Hamiltonian-connected if for every pair of distinct vertices u, v of G there exists a Hamiltonian path in G from u to v.

Determine the smallest nonnegative integer k with the property that every k-Hamiltonian graph (on a sufficiently large number of vertices, p ≥ k + 3) is Hamiltonian-connected.
status_search_result: Web searches surface the standard definitions of k-Hamiltonian graphs (Chartrand–Kapoor) and Hamiltonian-connected graphs, and references to Skupień's related work, but no source giving a definitive value of the smallest k for which k-Hamiltonicity implies Hamiltonian-connectedness was located. The status of the problem could not be conclusively determined from the available sources.

paper_title: Semantic Subtyping: Challenges, Perspectives, and Open Problems
original_question: In semantic-subtyping-based systems such as the lambda-calculus system Duce and the pi-calculus system π, deciding subtyping appears to require deciding whether certain denotable types are atomic, or more generally whether a type contains finitely many atomic types that can be enumerated. What mathematical phenomenon makes atomic types arise so persistently in semantic subtyping, how tightly is the semantic-subtyping technique tied to decidability of atomicity, and is it reasonable and possible to study semantic-subtyping systems in which atomic types are not denotable and the subtype lattice is dense?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. In the semantic-subtyping approach to designing type systems, types are interpreted as subsets of a model D, and subtyping S ≤ T is defined to hold exactly when the interpretation of S is contained in the interpretation of T. The type language is closed under the boolean connectives (union, intersection, and negation), so the set of denotable types forms a boolean algebra (modulo semantic equivalence) and the subtyping relation is the induced lattice order. A denotable type T is called atomic if T is not equivalent to the empty type and the only denotable subtypes of T are T itself and the empty type; equivalently, T is a minimal nonzero element of the subtype lattice. Concrete instances include the lambda-calculus system "CDuce" and pi-calculus systems based on semantic subtyping, in which deciding S ≤ T is reduced to emptiness checks that, in known decidability proofs, ultimately rely on enumerating the (finitely many) atomic types contained in a denotable type.

Problem. Provide a mathematical explanation of the following three intertwined questions about semantic-subtyping systems whose type interpretation lies in a model D as above.

(1) Identify the structural phenomenon that forces the recurrent appearance of atomic types in semantic-subtyping decision procedures: characterize, in terms of properties of the model D and of the boolean algebra of denotable types (e.g. atomicity, atomicness, completeness, descending chain conditions, definability of singletons, or finite-model properties), why every currently known decidability proof for semantic subtyping reduces to enumerating atoms of denotable types.

(2) Determine how tightly the semantic-subtyping technique is tied to the decidability of atomicity: exhibit either a general theorem showing that decidability of S ≤ T in a semantic-subtyping system implies decidability of "is T atomic?" (and effectiveness of an enumeration of the atoms below T), or a counterexample consisting of a semantic-subtyping system with decidable subtyping in which atomicity of denotable types is undecidable or in which atoms cannot be effectively enumerated.

(3) Construct, if possible, a non-trivial semantic-subtyping system in which no denotable type is atomic — equivalently, in which the subtype lattice (restricted to nonempty denotable types) is dense, meaning that whenever S < T are denotable and S is not equivalent to the empty type, there exists a denotable U with S < U < T — while still admitting a sound and decidable subtyping algorithm for a useful programming-language type discipline (covering, e.g., product, function, and recursive types). Alternatively, prove that no such system can exist under reasonable expressiveness assumptions.
status_search_result: The questions are posed as conceptual open challenges about semantic subtyping. Subsequent work has refined decidability results for semantic subtyping with type variables (e.g. EXPTIME decidability by Castagna et al., and logical/tableau approaches), but no source located addresses the specific structural question of why atomic types are unavoidable, or constructs a semantic-subtyping system whose subtype lattice is dense (no denotable atoms). The status of these questions therefore appears to remain open.

paper_title: Semantic Subtyping: Challenges, Perspectives, and Open Problems
context_brief: Nature and limits of semantic subtyping
original_question: Is semantic subtyping merely an alternative semantic route to type systems that could in principle also be axiomatized syntactically, or does it fundamentally yield genuinely new classes of type systems? Equivalently, what are the real limits and degrees of freedom of the semantic-subtyping approach, and to what extent can the extensional interpretation underlying the models be systematized and characterized?
self_contained_problem:
Background. In the design of typed programming languages, a subtyping relation between types is traditionally defined syntactically by a deductive system: one fixes a grammar of types (typically with constructors such as products, arrows, recursive types, and possibly Boolean combinators ∨, ∧, ¬) and gives a set of inference rules deriving judgements t ≤ s. The "semantic subtyping" approach instead proceeds as follows. One fixes a class of models in which every type t is mapped to a subset ⟦t⟧ of some domain D (an "extensional interpretation"), required to commute with the Boolean type connectives in the set-theoretic way (⟦t∨s⟧ = ⟦t⟧∪⟦s⟧, ⟦¬t⟧ = D∖⟦t⟧, etc.) and to interpret each non-Boolean type constructor in a way faithful to its operational meaning. Subtyping is then defined extensionally by

  t ≤ s  ⇔  ⟦t⟧ ⊆ ⟦s⟧  in every such model.

Problem. Address the following two interrelated questions about the expressive power and structure of this approach.

(a) Determine whether the semantic-subtyping methodology is essentially a different presentation of subtyping relations that could equivalently be obtained by a syntactic deductive system, or whether it produces type systems whose subtyping relations cannot be captured by any reasonable finite syntactic axiomatization. More precisely, give either:
  (i) a general theorem showing that for every type system arising from a semantic-subtyping construction (in a suitably formalized class) there exists an equivalent finitely axiomatized syntactic subtyping system; or
  (ii) an explicit example of a type system definable by semantic subtyping whose induced subtyping relation provably admits no such syntactic axiomatization, together with a characterization of the obstruction.

(b) Provide a systematic theory of the extensional interpretation. That is, formalize a general framework that takes as input a signature of type constructors together with their intended operational behavior and outputs a canonical extensional interpretation ⟦·⟧ together with sufficient conditions ensuring (1) soundness with respect to the operational semantics, (2) decidability of the induced subtyping relation, and (3) uniqueness or canonicity of the resulting interpretation. Identify the precise degrees of freedom (parameters, choices) available in the construction of such interpretations and characterize the boundary cases where the method fails or yields non-canonical alternatives.
status_search_result: The two questions—whether semantic subtyping yields genuinely new type systems versus alternatives to syntactically axiomatizable ones, and whether the definition of the extensional interpretation can be systematized—are stated as open problems in the semantic-subtyping literature. Subsequent work (e.g., extensions to the π-calculus, objects and classes, SMT-based decision procedures, logical approaches) has applied the methodology to new settings but, to the best of available public evidence, has not produced a general meta-theorem either equating semantic subtyping with syntactic axiomatizations or systematically characterizing all admissible extensional interpretations. Status appears still open.

paper_title: Semantic Subtyping: Challenges, Perspectives, and Open Problems
original_question: How tightly is the semantic-subtyping approach tied to the presence of a type-case construct and explicit type annotations on values such as lambda-abstractions and channels? In particular, can semantic subtyping support useful languages without type-case, or any meaningful form of partial type reconstruction, while preserving the intended semantic distinctions and the model-based account of types?
self_contained_problem:
Background. The semantic subtyping approach defines a subtyping relation on types by interpreting each type as a set of values and declaring s ≤ t whenever the interpretation of s is contained in that of t. This yields a set-theoretic account of unions, intersections, and negations of types, and is typically developed for languages featuring:
  (i) a type-case construct of the form "(x ∈ t) ? e1 : e2" that, at runtime, branches according to whether the value bound to x belongs to the type t, and
  (ii) explicit type annotations on values whose semantic type is not syntactically apparent — for instance, λ-abstractions annotated with their full intersection-of-arrows interface (λ^{⋂_i s_i → t_i} x. e) and communication channels annotated with the type of messages they carry.

These features are normally used in essential ways: the type-case is what gives observational meaning to fine-grained set-theoretic distinctions among types, and the annotations enable the model-based interpretation of values to be recovered from syntax (so that, e.g., a function annotated with Odd→Odd ∧ Even→Even is observably distinct from the same code annotated only with Int→Int).

Problem. Determine the extent to which the semantic-subtyping methodology is intrinsically tied to the presence of a type-case construct and to explicit type annotations on values such as λ-abstractions and channels. Concretely:

(a) Exhibit a useful programming language (e.g. a λ-calculus or process calculus with set-theoretic types including union, intersection, and negation) equipped with a semantic subtyping relation, in which there is no type-case construct, yet the semantic distinctions induced by the set-theoretic interpretation of types remain observable and the model-theoretic account of types is preserved; or prove that no such language exists, in the sense that without type-case the semantic-subtyping interpretation collapses to (or is indistinguishable from) a coarser, syntactic notion of subtyping.

(b) Determine whether the semantic-subtyping approach is compatible with any nontrivial form of (partial) type reconstruction — that is, a system in which type annotations on λ-abstractions and channels may be omitted (in whole or in part) and recovered by inference, while still admitting a sound and complete semantic interpretation of types as sets of values and preserving principal-type or minimum-typing-style properties.

Provide either constructions establishing the positive answers, or impossibility/lower-bound results delineating the precise dependence of semantic subtyping on type-case and on explicit annotations.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open challenge in the semantic-subtyping literature. Subsequent work (e.g., extensions of semantic subtyping with SMT-based decision procedures, logical approaches to deciding semantic subtyping, and various polymorphic extensions in the CDuce/set-theoretic types line) has refined decision procedures and added polymorphism, but no published result fully characterizes whether semantic subtyping can be sustained without a type-case construct or supports a general form of (partial) type reconstruction with set-theoretic types. The problem appears to remain open in its general form.

paper_title: Semantic Subtyping: Challenges, Perspectives, and Open Problems
original_question: What is the precise relationship between the semantic lambda-calculus system Duce and the local π-calculus system π? In particular, can one give a type-preserving encoding of Duce into π that preserves the subtyping relation and correctly handles overloaded functions, recursive types, and the channel type gap chλ(t) versus ch−(t), or do the obstacles encountered indicate a deeper mismatch that instead calls for an integrated concurrent version of Duce?
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open question about whether a faithful, subtyping- and type-preserving encoding of the semantic λ-calculus Duce into the local π-calculus exists, or whether the obstacles instead motivate an integrated concurrent Duce. No published resolution was located; later work on semantic subtyping for π-calculi (e.g., Castagna–De Nicola–Varacca and CDuce-related developments) discusses semantic subtyping for processes but does not appear to provide a complete encoding meeting all the stated requirements.

paper_title: Orthogonal polynomials and approximation theory: some open problems
context_brief: Zeros of orthogonal polynomials for singular measures
original_question: For orthogonal polynomials defined with respect to singular measures, what can be said about the fine structure of their zeros? In particular, determine detailed information about how the zeros are distributed and organized when the underlying measure is singular.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mu$ be a finite positive Borel measure on the real line (or on the unit circle) whose support is compact, and assume that $\mu$ is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure (so that its absolutely continuous part vanishes). Let $\{p_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ denote the sequence of monic orthogonal polynomials associated with $\mu$, defined by $\int p_n p_m \, d\mu = 0$ for $n\ne m$. Denote by $Z_n = \{x_{n,1},\dots,x_{n,n}\}$ the zero set of $p_n$.

It is classical (Mhaskar–Saff and others) that the global (bulk) asymptotic distribution of $Z_n$ is governed by potential-theoretic equilibrium measures. The problem is to describe the fine structure of $Z_n$ as $n\to\infty$ when $\mu$ is singular: namely, determine the local spacing and clustering behavior of consecutive zeros of $p_n$, the existence (or failure) of "clock behavior" (i.e. asymptotically equally-spaced zeros at the natural microscopic scale) at points in the support of $\mu$, and how the singular nature of $\mu$ (e.g. pure point components, singular continuous components, or singular parts supported on Cantor-type sets) is reflected in the local arrangement of the zeros.

Concretely: give a detailed description of the local distribution and organization of the zeros $\{x_{n,k}\}$ at scale $1/n$ (or the appropriate microscopic scale) for orthogonal polynomials with respect to a general singular measure $\mu$.
status_search_result: The question of the fine (microscopic) structure of zeros of orthogonal polynomials for singular measures is an active research area. Partial results exist: clock behavior has been established for random Verblunsky coefficients and under BLS-type conditions, and local zero behavior near algebraic singularities of the measure has been analyzed. However, a general description for arbitrary singular measures remains open, with progress confined to special classes.

paper_title: Analysis on Faddeev Knots and Skyrme Solitons: Recent Progress and Open Problems
original_question: In the classical three-dimensional Skyrme model, finite-energy static fields define maps from R^3 ∪ {∞} ≅ S^3 to S^3, so each field has an integer topological degree N in π3(S^3). For every integer degree N, does there exist a finite-energy static field that minimizes the Skyrme energy among all configurations with degree N?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the classical three-dimensional Skyrme model. A static field is a map φ : ℝ³ → S³ ⊂ ℝ⁴ with φ(x) → φ_∞ as |x| → ∞ for some fixed point φ_∞ ∈ S³, so that φ extends continuously to a map from the one-point compactification S³ ≅ ℝ³ ∪ {∞} into S³. The Skyrme energy is

  E(φ) = ∫_{ℝ³} ( (1/2) Σ_{i=1}^{3} |∂_i φ|² + (1/4) Σ_{1 ≤ i < j ≤ 3} |∂_i φ ∧ ∂_j φ|² ) dx,

where ∂_i φ ∧ ∂_j φ denotes the wedge product of the two ℝ⁴-valued vectors ∂_i φ and ∂_j φ in ⋀² ℝ⁴, with norm taken in ⋀² ℝ⁴. Each finite-energy configuration φ has an integer topological degree

  Q(φ) = deg(φ : S³ → S³) ∈ π₃(S³) ≅ ℤ.

For each integer N ∈ ℤ, set

  E_N = inf { E(φ) : φ : ℝ³ → S³ with E(φ) < ∞ and Q(φ) = N }.

Question: For every integer N, does there exist a finite-energy static map φ_N with Q(φ_N) = N and E(φ_N) = E_N? That is, is the infimum E_N attained for every topological degree N ∈ ℤ?
status_search_result: The existence of Skyrme energy minimizers in every degree N is a long-standing question. Partial results exist: minimizers are known to be attainable for degree ±1 and, more generally, whenever the energy levels satisfy a strict "substantial inequality" preventing energy splitting (Lin–Yang and related work). However, attainability of E_N for every integer degree N in the classical 3D Skyrme model has not been established in full generality and remains open, since concentration-compactness arguments can fail to rule out splitting into well-separated lower-degree pieces.

paper_title: Analysis on Faddeev Knots and Skyrme Solitons: Recent Progress and Open Problems
original_question: For the hyperbolic Euler-Lagrange equations governing the time-dependent Skyrme model and its Faddeev submodel in 3+1 dimensions, can one establish a mathematical well-posedness theory and determine the qualitative behavior of time-dependent solutions, including existence, uniqueness, regularity, and dynamical behavior for finite-energy data?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the time-dependent Skyrme model on Minkowski space $\mathbb{R}^{1+3}$ with metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$. The field is a map $U:\mathbb{R}^{1+3}\to SU(2)$, and the Lagrangian density is
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Sk}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{tr}(R_\mu R^\mu)+\tfrac{1}{16}\,\mathrm{tr}\big([R_\mu,R_\nu][R^\mu,R^\nu]\big),$$
where $R_\mu=U^{-1}\partial_\mu U$ takes values in $\mathfrak{su}(2)$. The corresponding Euler–Lagrange equations form a quasilinear hyperbolic system for $U$.

Consider also the Faddeev submodel, in which the field is a map $\mathbf{n}:\mathbb{R}^{1+3}\to S^2\subset\mathbb{R}^3$, $|\mathbf{n}|=1$, with Lagrangian density
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Fa}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\partial_\mu\mathbf{n}\cdot\partial^\mu\mathbf{n}-\tfrac{1}{4}\,F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu},\qquad F_{\mu\nu}=\mathbf{n}\cdot(\partial_\mu\mathbf{n}\times\partial_\nu\mathbf{n}),$$
whose Euler–Lagrange equation is a quasilinear hyperbolic equation for $\mathbf{n}$.

The associated conserved energies are
$$E_{\mathrm{Sk}}[U]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Big(-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}(R_iR_i)-\tfrac{1}{16}\mathrm{tr}([R_i,R_j][R_i,R_j])\Big)\,dx,$$
$$E_{\mathrm{Fa}}[\mathbf{n}]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}\partial_i\mathbf{n}\cdot\partial_i\mathbf{n}+\tfrac{1}{4}F_{ij}F_{ij}\Big)\,dx,$$
which are finite for the relevant Cauchy data.

Establish a mathematical well-posedness theory for the Cauchy problems associated to these two hyperbolic systems with finite-energy initial data $(U,\partial_t U)|_{t=0}$ and $(\mathbf{n},\partial_t\mathbf{n})|_{t=0}$, including:
(a) local and global existence of solutions;
(b) uniqueness in a suitable class;
(c) regularity (propagation of Sobolev regularity, persistence of smoothness);
(d) qualitative dynamical behavior such as long-time asymptotics, scattering, stability of solitons, or singularity formation.
status_search_result: A general well-posedness theory for the full (3+1)-dimensional Skyrme and Faddeev hyperbolic Euler–Lagrange systems with arbitrary finite-energy data appears to remain open. Partial progress is available: Geba–Nakanishi–Rajeev and others established global existence and scattering for Skyrme wave maps with small critical data, and Li (Duke Math. J. 2021) proved global well-posedness for equivariant (hedgehog) solutions of the (3+1) Skyrme model with large data. No comparable general result has been reported for non-symmetric finite-energy Cauchy data, nor for the Faddeev submodel.

paper_title: Analysis on Faddeev Knots and Skyrme Solitons: Recent Progress and Open Problems
original_question: Under the hedgehog ansatz in the three-dimensional Skyrme model, one obtains static critical points that minimize the energy within the radially symmetric class for each integer topological charge N. Are any of these hedgehog critical points absolute minimizers of the full Skyrme energy among all finite-energy fields of the same topological degree, rather than only within the radially symmetric subclass?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the static Skyrme energy on $\mathbb{R}^3$ for maps $U:\mathbb{R}^3 \to SU(2) \cong S^3$ satisfying $U(x) \to I$ as $|x|\to\infty$, given by
$$E(U) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{tr}(\partial_i U^{-1}\partial_i U) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{16}\,\mathrm{tr}\big([\partial_i U^{-1}\,\partial_j U,\,\partial_j U^{-1}\,\partial_i U]\big)\Big)\,dx,$$
(written here up to a positive constant normalization of the Skyrme term). Each finite-energy configuration $U$ has a well-defined integer topological degree $N \in \pi_3(S^3) \cong \mathbb{Z}$. For each integer $N$, the hedgehog ansatz takes the form
$$U_N(x) = \cos f(r)\, I + i\, \sin f(r)\, \big(\hat{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\big)^{(N)},$$
where $r=|x|$, $\hat{x}=x/r$, $\boldsymbol{\sigma}=(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3)$ are the Pauli matrices, the superscript $(N)$ denotes the standard degree-$N$ extension consistent with topological charge $N$, and $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ is a profile function with $f(0)=N\pi$ and $f(\infty)=0$. It is known that for every integer $N$ there exists a profile $f$ minimizing the Skyrme energy within the radially symmetric (hedgehog) class of degree $N$, yielding a static critical point $U_N$ of $E$.

Question: For some (or any) integer $N$, is the hedgehog critical point $U_N$ an absolute minimizer of $E$ among all finite-energy configurations $U:\mathbb{R}^3 \to SU(2)$ of topological degree $N$ (not merely among radially symmetric ones)?
status_search_result: For topological degrees $|N|\geq 2$, numerical and analytical studies (e.g., toroidal, Platonic-symmetric Skyrmions) indicate that the energy minimizers are not radially symmetric, so the hedgehog is not the absolute minimizer in those sectors. For $N=\pm 1$, the hedgehog is widely believed to be the absolute minimizer, but a rigorous mathematical proof in the full unconstrained class does not appear to be established. Thus the question is partially resolved: a clear "no" for higher $|N|$, while the $|N|=1$ case remains open in the rigorous sense.

paper_title: Analysis on Faddeev Knots and Skyrme Solitons: Recent Progress and Open Problems
original_question: Let X = {n : R^3 → S^2, E(n) < ∞} be the finite-energy Sobolev class for the Faddeev model. Does every map n in X admit approximation by smooth maps n_j ∈ C∞(R^3, S^2) with uniformly bounded energy such that n_j → n in H^1_loc(R^3, S^2)?
self_contained_problem:
For a measurable map $n:\mathbb{R}^3\to S^2$ (where $S^2$ denotes the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$), define the Faddeev energy
$$E(n)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\bigl(|\nabla n|^2+|n^{*}\omega|^2\bigr)\,dx,$$
where $n^{*}\omega$ is the pullback by $n$ of the standard area form $\omega$ on $S^2$, i.e., $(n^{*}\omega)_{ij}=n\cdot(\partial_i n\wedge\partial_j n)$, and $|n^{*}\omega|^2=\sum_{i<j}|(n^{*}\omega)_{ij}|^2$. Let
$$X=\{\,n:\mathbb{R}^3\to S^2 \ \text{measurable} : E(n)<\infty\,\}.$$
Question: Does every $n\in X$ admit a sequence of smooth maps $n_j\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3,S^2)$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\sup_{j} E(n_j)<\infty$, and
\item $n_j\to n$ in $H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^3,S^2)$ as $j\to\infty$?
\end{enumerate}
Equivalently, are smooth $S^2$-valued maps with uniformly bounded Faddeev energy $H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$-dense in the finite-energy class $X$?
category_tag: Density of smooth maps in Sobolev spaces (Faddeev model)
status_search_result: The question of $H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$-density of smooth maps with uniformly bounded Faddeev energy in the finite-energy class is highlighted as unresolved in the surveyed literature on the Faddeev model. Related works (e.g., Hang–Lin on $S^2$-valued maps and Faddeev's model, and Giaquinta–Mucci-type relaxed-energy approximations) establish density only for weaker topologies or for maps smooth away from finitely many points; no full $H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ smooth approximation result with energy bound has been reported.

paper_title: Analysis on Faddeev Knots and Skyrme Solitons: Recent Progress and Open Problems
original_question: Are absolute energy minimizers for the Skyrme and Faddeev models regular? More specifically, if one minimizes the corresponding constrained energy functional in a fixed topological class, must the resulting minimizer be smooth or otherwise enjoy strong regularity properties, rather than merely weak finite-energy regularity?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following two geometric variational problems.

(1) Skyrme model. Let $u : \mathbb{R}^3 \to S^3 \subset \mathbb{R}^4$ be a finite-energy map with $u(x) \to (1,0,0,0)$ as $|x|\to\infty$, so that $u$ extends to a map $S^3 \to S^3$ and has a well-defined topological degree $\deg(u) \in \mathbb{Z}$. The Skyrme energy is
$$E_S(u) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} \Bigl( \tfrac{1}{2} |\nabla u|^2 + \tfrac{1}{4} \sum_{i<j} |\partial_i u \wedge \partial_j u|^2 \Bigr)\, dx,$$
where $\partial_i u \wedge \partial_j u$ denotes the antisymmetric wedge product of the vector-valued partial derivatives. For a fixed integer $N \neq 0$, let $u_*$ be a minimizer of $E_S$ in the class $\{u : \deg(u) = N\}$ (assumed to exist).

(2) Faddeev model. Let $n : \mathbb{R}^3 \to S^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a finite-energy map with $n(x) \to (0,0,1)$ as $|x|\to\infty$, so that $n$ extends to a map $S^3 \to S^2$ with Hopf invariant $Q(n) \in \mathbb{Z}$. The Faddeev energy is
$$E_F(n) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} \bigl( |\nabla n|^2 + |F_n|^2 \bigr)\, dx, \qquad (F_n)_{ij} = n \cdot (\partial_i n \times \partial_j n).$$
For a fixed integer $N \neq 0$, let $n_*$ be a minimizer of $E_F$ in the class $\{n : Q(n) = N\}$ (assumed to exist).

The natural variational framework only guarantees that $u_*$ and $n_*$ lie in the finite-energy Sobolev-type space associated with the respective functional.

Question. Must any such absolute energy minimizer $u_*$ (respectively $n_*$) be smooth, or at least enjoy strong regularity (e.g., $C^\infty$, real analytic, or Hölder continuous classical solution of the Euler–Lagrange equations) on all of $\mathbb{R}^3$, beyond the weak regularity inherited from finite energy?
status_search_result: The regularity of absolute energy minimizers for the Skyrme and Faddeev models is widely cited as a fundamental open problem. Existence of minimizers is known in various topological classes (e.g., Lin–Yang results for the Faddeev model), and partial regularity results exist for related relaxed energies, but full smoothness of unconstrained absolute minimizers in arbitrary topological classes does not appear to have been established. Recent work (e.g., 2025 results on global minimality of the Hopf map in the strong-coupling regime) addresses special cases but not the general regularity question.

paper_title: Some Open Problems in the Dynamics of Quadratic and Higher Degree Polynomial ODE Systems
original_question: Give a universal definition of non-chaotic solutions for continuous autonomous dynamical systems x' = f(x) on R^N. The definition should cover non-chaotic behavior beyond the authors' criterion that excludes bounded chaos when N-2 components of every solution eventually either tend to a finite limit, are periodic or asymptotic to a periodic function, are unbounded, or exhibit one of several finite-time behaviors; in particular, it should still work for N > 3, where that criterion remains unverified and incomplete.
self_contained_problem:
Consider continuous autonomous dynamical systems
    x'(t) = f(x(t)),    x ∈ ℝ^N,  t ∈ [0, ∞),
where f : ℝ^N → ℝ^N is continuous (so that solutions exist for t ∈ [0, ∞)). Informally, a solution x(t) is called "chaotic" if it exhibits sensitive dependence on initial conditions and complicated long-term behavior, while a "non-chaotic" solution is any solution that does not display such behavior.

A known partial criterion for non-chaoticity reads as follows. Suppose the system has no cluster points in its set of isolated fixed points. Then the system has no bounded chaos provided that, for every solution, at least N − 2 of its components x_{i_1}(t), …, x_{i_{N−2}}(t) eventually satisfy at least one of the following:
 (i) tend to a finite limit as t → ∞;
 (ii) are periodic or asymptotic to a periodic function;
 (iii) are unbounded; or
 (iv) exhibit one of certain prescribed finite-time behaviors (e.g., blow-up in finite time, finite-time termination, or oscillations of unbounded frequency on a finite interval).
This criterion is widely accepted for N = 3 but remains unverified for N > 3, and even when valid it fails to capture many forms of non-chaotic behavior.

Problem. Formulate a universal definition of "non-chaotic solution" for the system x' = f(x) on ℝ^N, valid for every dimension N (in particular for N > 3), that:
 (a) reduces to or is consistent with the accepted notion of non-chaoticity in dimension N = 3;
 (b) encompasses every solution covered by the criterion above as a special case;
 (c) also includes the broad classes of non-chaotic solutions that the above criterion fails to detect; and
 (d) is intrinsic, i.e., expressible purely in terms of the qualitative dynamics of x(t) (such as its ω-limit set, recurrence structure, entropy, or sensitivity properties) without reference to the particular form of f.

Equivalently, provide a precise mathematical definition of non-chaoticity that, taken as the negation of "chaotic," yields a workable universal notion of chaotic solution for continuous autonomous ODE systems on ℝ^N.
status_search_result: The problem of giving a universal definition of non-chaotic (equivalently, chaotic) solutions for continuous autonomous ODE systems on ℝ^N is widely recognized as an open conceptual problem in dynamical systems. The Heidel–Zhang criterion is established for N = 3 but not verified for N > 3, and even there it misses many non-chaotic behaviors. No accepted universal definition has been published; the question remains open.

paper_title: Some Open Problems in the Dynamics of Quadratic and Higher Degree Polynomial ODE Systems
original_question: Let x' = f(x) be a polynomial or C^n vector field on R^3. If a trajectory is asymptotic to a two-dimensional C^r invariant manifold (r ≥ 1), can that trajectory still be chaotic, and if so how topologically complicated must the manifold be in order to contain or attract such chaos? In particular, can a quadratic differential equation on a torus exhibit chaos, and can a trajectory on a torus be more complicated than a space-filling curve?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a vector field on R^3 of the form x' = f(x), where either f is a polynomial map or f ∈ C^n(R^3, R^3) for some nonnegative integer n. Suppose a trajectory of this system is asymptotic (as t → +∞) to a two-dimensional C^r invariant manifold M ⊂ R^3, where r ≥ 1 is an integer. Address the following:

(a) Can such a trajectory be chaotic (in the sense of sensitive dependence on initial conditions together with topological transitivity, or any standard equivalent notion)?

(b) If chaotic asymptotic trajectories of this type exist, what is the minimal topological complexity required of the 2D invariant manifold M that contains or attracts them? Here topological complexity is measured in the sense that, for example, a torus is considered more complicated than a plane (e.g., via genus or other topological invariants).

(c) In particular, can a quadratic polynomial vector field on R^3 leaving a 2-torus invariant exhibit chaotic dynamics on that torus?

(d) More generally, on a 2-torus invariant under a smooth vector field, can a single trajectory be topologically more complicated than a space-filling curve (i.e., have a closure or orbit-structure exceeding that of a dense, area-filling orbit)?

Determine which of these phenomena are possible, and if possible, exhibit explicit examples; if impossible, prove the corresponding obstructions.
category_tag: Chaos on invariant 2-manifolds of polynomial ODEs
status_search_result: Classical results (Denjoy, Schwartz, Peixoto) imply that a C^2 flow on the 2-torus cannot be chaotic, so smooth trajectories confined to a 2-torus are not chaotic and orbit closures are at most the whole torus. However, the question as posed concerns trajectories in R^3 only asymptotic to a 2D invariant manifold, where the manifold need not be smoothly embedded as a flow-invariant 2-torus in the classical sense, and the question of minimal topological complexity of such 2D manifolds containing/attracting chaos remains an open problem listed in the survey of open problems on quadratic and higher-degree polynomial ODE systems. No published resolution was located.

paper_title: Positive and free boundary solutions to singular nonlinear elliptic problems with absorption: an overview and open problems
original_question: For the boundary value problem -Δu + 1/u^α = λ f(x) in Ω with u = 0 on ∂Ω, where α > 0 (mainly α < 1) and f ≥ 0, does there exist, in addition to the known maximal positive solution for sufficiently large λ, any further solution that is either another positive solution or a compact-support (free-boundary) solution?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ ($N \geq 1$) be a bounded domain with smooth boundary, let $\alpha > 0$ (with the principal interest in the range $0 < \alpha < 1$), and let $f \in L^\infty(\Omega)$ satisfy $f \geq 0$, $f \not\equiv 0$. For a parameter $\lambda > 0$, consider the singular semilinear boundary value problem
$$-\Delta u + \frac{1}{u^\alpha} = \lambda f(x) \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega,$$
where the term $1/u^\alpha$ is interpreted as $0$ on the set $\{u = 0\}$ (so that solutions may be either strictly positive in $\Omega$ or nonnegative with a free boundary $\partial\{u > 0\} \cap \Omega$).

It is known that for all sufficiently large $\lambda$ there exists a maximal positive solution $u_\lambda \in H_0^1(\Omega)$ satisfying $u_\lambda > 0$ in $\Omega$.

Question: For such $\lambda$, does the problem admit, in addition to the maximal positive solution, any further solution — either another strictly positive solution, or a nonnegative solution with compact support in $\Omega$ (i.e., a free boundary solution vanishing on a set of positive measure)?
category_tag: singular semilinear elliptic equations with absorption

original_question: For the radial solutions of problem (II) on Ω = B_r(0), where the cited work finds two radial solutions for λ* < λ < λ** and only the upper branch for λ > λ**, what mechanism explains why the lower radial branch stops at λ = λ** when the branch otherwise stays inside the positive cone and reaches zero normal derivative there?
self_contained_problem:
Let Ω = B_r(0) ⊂ ℝ^N be the open ball of radius r > 0 centered at the origin, and fix a constant β ∈ (0,1). Consider the singular semilinear elliptic problem with absorption

(II)    −Δu + u^{−β} χ_{{u>0}} = λ g(u) in Ω,    u ≥ 0 in Ω,    u = 0 on ∂Ω,

where λ > 0 is a real parameter and g : [0,∞) → [0,∞) is a fixed continuous nonlinearity (for instance g(s) = s^q with q ∈ (0,1) or another sublinear/superlinear model giving the bifurcation diagram described below). A solution u to (II) is called a free-boundary solution if the set {u = 0} ∩ Ω has nonempty interior and on its boundary one has u = 0 and ∇u = 0 simultaneously; otherwise u is called strictly positive (lying in the positive cone, with u > 0 in Ω).

Assume that the radial bifurcation diagram of (II) has the following structure: there exist 0 < λ_* < λ_{**} < ∞ such that
(a) for every λ ∈ (λ_*, λ_{**}) there exist exactly two radial solutions u_1(·;λ) < u_2(·;λ) of (II), both strictly positive in Ω;
(b) for every λ > λ_{**} only the upper radial solution u_2(·;λ) exists;
(c) as λ ↑ λ_{**}, the lower radial branch u_1(·;λ) remains strictly positive inside Ω and converges to a limit profile u_1(·;λ_{**}) which still satisfies u_1 > 0 in Ω, vanishes on ∂Ω, and has zero normal derivative on ∂Ω, i.e. ∂u_1/∂ν = 0 on ∂Ω.

Question. Determine and rigorously justify the analytic/geometric mechanism that forces the lower radial branch λ ↦ u_1(·;λ) to terminate exactly at λ = λ_{**}: that is, explain why this branch cannot be continued to values λ > λ_{**} even though, at λ = λ_{**}, u_1 still belongs to the positive cone and only meets the boundary tangentially (with simultaneous vanishing of u and of ∂u/∂ν on ∂Ω).
status_search_result: The overview where this question is posed explicitly raises it as an open problem ("we may ask why the branch stops at the value λ = λ**"). Subsequent literature on singular semilinear/quasilinear elliptic problems with absorption and free boundary (Díaz–Hernández and coauthors, and follow-up works such as the 2023 study of −Δu = λu − u^{−1} with Neumann data) discusses bifurcation diagrams with multiple radial branches, but no published result was found that rigorously identifies the precise mechanism causing the lower radial branch in problem (II) on a ball to terminate at λ**. The status appears to remain open.

paper_title: Positive and free boundary solutions to singular nonlinear elliptic problems with absorption: an overview and open problems
original_question: For the elliptic problems of the kind surveyed in this paper, how do the existence, multiplicity, and free-boundary phenomena change when measures appear in the equation not only as source data but also as coefficients of zero-order terms or in similarly singular roles?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ ($N \geq 2$) be a bounded domain with smooth boundary, and consider semilinear elliptic problems with singular absorption of the form
$$ -\Delta u + g(u) = f \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad u \geq 0 \text{ in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega, $$
where $g:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ is a continuous nondecreasing absorption nonlinearity that may be singular at $0$ (a typical model is $g(u)=u^{-\beta}\chi_{\{u>0\}}$ with $0<\beta<1$, or $g(u)=u^q$ with $0<q<1$), and where solutions may exhibit a free boundary, i.e.\ a nonempty set $\{u=0\}$ of positive measure inside $\Omega$ (compact-support or "flat" solutions).

Now allow Radon measures to enter the equation in roles beyond a mere source datum. Concretely, given a (possibly singular) Radon measure $\mu$ on $\Omega$ and a Radon measure $\nu$ on $\Omega$, study the problem
$$ -\Delta u + V \, u + g(u) = \mu \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega, $$
where the zero-order coefficient $V$ is itself a (nonnegative) Radon measure (so that the term $V u$ must be interpreted in a suitable distributional or capacity-theoretic sense), and more generally where measures appear as coefficients of zero-order or similarly singular terms.

Develop a theory of such problems analogous to the regular-coefficient case: in particular,
(a) give a precise notion of admissible solution under which $V u$ and $g(u)$ make sense (e.g.\ via $\mathrm{cap}_2$-quasi-continuous representatives and the inner-trace/outer-trace constructions for measures);
(b) determine which measures $\mu$ and $V$ are "good" in the sense that a (renormalized or distributional) solution exists, and characterize this in capacitary terms;
(c) establish multiplicity results, distinguishing between maximal/minimal solutions and intermediate solutions;
(d) analyze how the free boundary $\partial\{u>0\}$ is influenced by the singular part of $V$ and $\mu$ (concentration on sets of zero $H^1$-capacity, on lower-dimensional sets, or on the boundary), and describe the geometry/regularity of $\{u=0\}$ in this generalized setting.
category_tag: Singular semilinear elliptic equations with measure data
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a survey on singular nonlinear elliptic problems with absorption. While there is a well-developed literature on semilinear elliptic equations with measure source data and absorption (Brezis–Marcus–Ponce, Véron, and collaborators), the specific question of allowing measures as coefficients of zero-order terms (and similar singular roles) in the framework of free-boundary/compact-support solutions does not appear to have a definitive published resolution; partial results exist in adjacent settings (Schrödinger operators with measure potentials, capacity-based admissibility), but the program as stated remains open.

paper_title: Open problems in differential geometry.
context_brief: hyperbolic affine spheres asymptotic to cones
original_question: Given any convex cone, does there exist a hyperbolic affine sphere asymptotic to that cone?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Let $f: M^n \to \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ be a smooth, locally strongly convex hypersurface. There is a canonical transversal vector field $\xi$ on $M$, called the affine normal, determined (up to sign) by the requirements of equiaffine differential geometry (using the Blaschke metric induced by the second fundamental form normalized by the affine invariant). The hypersurface is called an affine sphere if all affine normals either pass through a single point (the center) or are mutually parallel. An affine sphere is called hyperbolic if the affine normals all point away from a common center on the concave side of the hypersurface; equivalently, after a suitable affine change of coordinates, $M$ can be written locally as the graph of a strongly convex function $u$ on a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ satisfying the Monge–Ampère equation
$$\det(\partial_i \partial_j u) = \left(-\frac{1}{u}\right)^{n+2},$$
with $u < 0$ in $\Omega$ and $u = 0$ on $\partial \Omega$.

A convex cone $C \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is a nonempty open convex subset such that $\lambda x \in C$ for every $x \in C$ and every $\lambda > 0$, and which contains no entire line. A complete hyperbolic affine sphere $M$ is said to be asymptotic to the cone $C$ if $M$ is contained in $C$, is properly embedded, and the closure of $M$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ has boundary equal to $\partial C \cup \{0\}$.

Problem. Prove that for every convex cone $C \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ (with vertex at the origin and containing no line), and every prescribed negative constant value of the affine mean curvature, there exists a complete hyperbolic affine sphere asymptotic to $C$ with that affine mean curvature.
status_search_result: Calabi's conjecture on the existence (and uniqueness) of a complete hyperbolic affine hypersphere asymptotic to any given non-degenerate convex cone was resolved by Cheng and Yau via their work on the real Monge–Ampère equation, with later refinements/alternative proofs by Li, Gigena, and others. The statement is now an established theorem.

paper_title: Open problems in differential geometry.
context_brief: fundamental groups of compact complete affine flat manifolds
original_question: Milnor's theorem implies that the fundamental group of a complete affine flat manifold is virtually polycyclic and torsion free, and conversely every virtually polycyclic group occurs as the fundamental group of some complete affine flat manifold. Which groups can occur as the fundamental group of a compact complete affine flat manifold?
self_contained_problem:
An affine flat manifold is a smooth manifold M equipped with a flat torsion-free affine connection; equivalently, M admits an atlas whose transition maps are restrictions of affine transformations of R^n. Such a manifold is called complete if its universal cover, with the lifted affine structure, is affinely isomorphic to R^n; equivalently, the developing map is a diffeomorphism onto R^n. In this case the fundamental group π_1(M) acts properly discontinuously and freely on R^n by affine transformations, so M = R^n / Γ for a torsion-free discrete subgroup Γ of the affine group Aff(R^n) = GL(n,R) ⋉ R^n.

It is known that for any complete affine flat manifold M (not necessarily compact), the group π_1(M) is virtually polycyclic and torsion-free, and conversely every torsion-free virtually polycyclic group arises as π_1(M) for some complete affine flat manifold M.

Problem. Characterize precisely the class of groups Γ that occur as the fundamental group of some compact complete affine flat manifold. That is, determine which torsion-free virtually polycyclic groups Γ admit a properly discontinuous, free, cocompact action on R^n by affine transformations for some n.
category_tag: Affine flat manifolds and Auslander conjecture
status_search_result: The question is closely tied to Auslander's conjecture (1964), which asserts that the fundamental group of every compact complete affine flat manifold is virtually polycyclic (equivalently virtually solvable in this setting). The conjecture is known in low dimensions: proven in dimension 3 by Fried–Goldman, and established up to dimension 6 by Abels–Margulis–Soifer, as well as in cases where the holonomy preserves a Lorentz metric. It remains open in general for dimensions ≥ 7. A complete characterization of which virtually polycyclic groups arise is therefore not known.

original_question: Can one prove that hyperbolic 3-manifolds do not admit affine flat structures?
self_contained_problem:
An affine flat structure on a smooth manifold $M^n$ is a maximal atlas of charts $\{(U_\alpha, \varphi_\alpha)\}$ with $\varphi_\alpha : U_\alpha 	o \mathbb{R}^n$ whose transition maps $\varphi_ eta \circ \varphi_\alpha^{-1}$ are restrictions of affine transformations $x \mapsto Ax + b$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (with $A \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$, $b \in \mathbb{R}^n$). paper_title: Open problems in differential geometry.
context_brief: Ricci-flow proof of the Soul theorem
original_question: Can one prove the real or complex Soul theorem by Ricci flow, rather than by the original Cheeger-Gromoll analysis via the Busemann function and Toponogov's theorem?
self_contained_problem:
Recall the Soul theorem of Cheeger–Gromoll: every complete, connected, noncompact Riemannian manifold (M, g) of nonnegative sectional curvature admits a closed, totally convex, totally geodesic embedded submanifold S (a "soul"), and M is diffeomorphic to the total space of the normal bundle of S in M. There is also a complex analogue for complete Kähler manifolds of nonnegative holomorphic bisectional (or sectional) curvature, in which the soul is a complex submanifold and M is biholomorphic to a holomorphic vector bundle over it.

The original proof of Cheeger–Gromoll proceeds by analyzing the Busemann function associated with rays in M and invokes Toponogov's triangle comparison theorem.

Problem. Give a proof of the Soul theorem — in either its real Riemannian form or its complex Kähler form — that uses the Ricci flow
   ∂g(t)/∂t = −2 Ric(g(t)),   g(0) = g,
as its main tool, in place of the Busemann function / Toponogov comparison argument of Cheeger–Gromoll. That is, construct a Ricci-flow-based argument that produces the soul S ⊂ M and establishes that M is diffeomorphic (respectively biholomorphic) to the normal bundle of S.
status_search_result: The classical Soul theorem (Cheeger–Gromoll 1972) and the Soul conjecture (Perelman 1994) have well-known proofs based on Busemann functions, Toponogov comparison, and convexity arguments. A web search did not surface a published Ricci-flow proof of the real or complex Soul theorem that replaces the Cheeger–Gromoll method; the question of finding such a Ricci-flow-based proof appears not to have been resolved in the literature.

original_question: For the recurrence x_{n+1}=a/x_n^2+1/x_{n-1} for n=0,1,2,\ldots, for which values of the parameter a is the unique positive equilibrium \bar{x} globally asymptotically stable?

$$x_{n+1} \;=\; \frac{a}{x_n^{2}} \;+\; \frac{1}{x_{n-1}}, \qquad n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots,$$
with arbitrary positive initial conditions $x_{-1}, x_{0} \in (0, \infty)$. This recurrence has a unique positive equilibrium $\bar{x} > 0$, namely the unique positive solution of $\bar{x} = a/\bar{x}^{2} + 1/\bar{x}$, equivalently $\bar{x}^{3} - \bar{x} - a = 0$.

paper_title: Some open problems of Ramsey minimal graphs.
original_question: Let F, G, and H be non-empty graphs, and write F → (G, H) to mean that every red-blue coloring of the edges of F contains either a red copy of G or a blue copy of H. A graph F is Ramsey (G, H)-minimal if F → (G, H) but, for every edge e of F, the graph F − e fails to satisfy F − e → (G, H). Let ℜ(G, H) denote the set of all Ramsey (G, H)-minimal graphs. For each integer n ≥ 4, classify all graphs in ℜ(2K2, K1,n), where 2K2 is the matching consisting of two disjoint edges and K1,n is the star with one center and n leaves.
self_contained_problem:
Let F, G, and H be non-empty simple graphs. Write F → (G, H) to indicate that for every coloring of the edges of F with two colors (red and blue), there is either a red subgraph isomorphic to G or a blue subgraph isomorphic to H. A graph F is said to be Ramsey (G, H)-minimal if F → (G, H) and, for every edge e ∈ E(F), the graph F − e satisfies (F − e) ↛ (G, H). Denote by ℜ(G, H) the class of all Ramsey (G, H)-minimal graphs (up to isomorphism).

Let 2K₂ denote the graph consisting of two vertex-disjoint edges, and let K₁,ₙ denote the star with one center vertex adjacent to n leaves.

Problem: For each integer n ≥ 4, give a complete classification (characterization) of the graphs in ℜ(2K₂, K₁,ₙ).
status_search_result: Mengersen and Oeckermann gave a characterization of graphs belonging to ℜ(2K₂, K₁,ₙ) for n ≥ 3, and determined ℜ(2K₂, K₁,ₙ) explicitly for small n (e.g. ℜ(2K₂, K₁,₂) = {2K₁,₂, C₄, C₅}). Subsequent work has continued to refine and extend these results, but a fully explicit list for general n ≥ 4 in completely closed form is not uniformly stated as settled in the literature; the structural characterization exists but explicit complete enumeration is treated as an ongoing problem.

paper_title: Lower Bounds for Unrestricted Boolean Circuits: Open Problems
original_question: For Boolean functions with multiple outputs, can one prove lower bounds that are stronger than the currently known bounds for single-output Boolean functions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider Boolean circuits over the full binary basis $B_2$ (the set of all two-input Boolean functions), with no restrictions on depth, fan-out, or topology. For a Boolean function $f:\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^m$, let $C(f)$ denote the minimum number of gates in such a circuit computing $f$. The strongest known explicit lower bound for single-output functions ($m=1$) is of the form $(3+\tfrac{1}{86})n - o(n)$.

Exhibit an explicit family of multi-output Boolean functions $\{f_n:\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^{m(n)}\}$ (with $m(n) \ge 2$, e.g., $m(n) = O(n)$) together with a proof that $C(f_n) \ge c \cdot n$ for some constant $c$ strictly larger than the best known constant for single-output functions, or more generally prove a superlinear lower bound on $C(f_n)$ for some explicit multi-output family. Equivalently: can one leverage multiple outputs to obtain circuit-size lower bounds in the unrestricted model that exceed those currently known for single-output Boolean functions?
status_search_result: Stronger lower bounds for explicit multi-output Boolean functions over the full binary basis are known: a $7n - o(n)$ bound has been established for certain explicit functions in $B_{n,n}$, exceeding the best known $\approx (3+1/86)n$ bound for single-output functions. However, no superlinear lower bound is known for any explicit (multi-output) function in the unrestricted circuit model, so the broader version of the question remains open.

paper_title: Lower Bounds for Unrestricted Boolean Circuits: Open Problems
original_question: Is there a non-gate-elimination method for proving lower bounds for unrestricted Boolean circuits that can be extended past the current 2n barrier?
self_contained_problem:
Consider Boolean circuits over the full binary basis B₂ (the set of all binary Boolean functions), where the size of a circuit is the number of gates and the input variables x₁,…,xₙ are not counted. The "gate-elimination" method is the standard inductive technique used to prove lower bounds on the size of such circuits: one fixes a small number of input variables of an alleged minimal circuit so as to force the elimination of several gates, and then applies an inductive hypothesis to the resulting smaller circuit. All current proofs of linear lower bounds of the form cn − o(n) on the B₂-circuit size of an explicit Boolean function f : {0,1}ⁿ → {0,1} (including the strongest known constants c slightly above 3) are obtained via this gate-elimination paradigm. The paradigm itself is known to be incapable of yielding lower bounds of the form 5n or larger.

Question: Is there a method other than gate elimination — i.e., a fundamentally different proof technique — that proves a lower bound of the form cn for the B₂-circuit size of some explicit family of Boolean functions, with constant c strictly greater than 2, and which can in principle be pushed beyond the 2n barrier that is currently the best achievable by known non-gate-elimination techniques?
status_search_result: As of 2026, all known strong linear lower bounds for unrestricted B₂-circuits (the strongest being 3.1n − o(n) by Li and Yang, 2022) still rely on the gate-elimination technique. Known non-gate-elimination methods (e.g., the OR-of-CNFs decomposition by Golovnev–Kulikov and related approaches) have not been pushed beyond the 2n barrier. No technique other than gate elimination has produced a super-2n lower bound for explicit functions.

paper_title: Lower Bounds for Unrestricted Boolean Circuits: Open Problems
original_question: What is the Boolean-circuit size of SUM_n, the multi-output Boolean function that returns the binary encoding of the sum of the n input bits?
self_contained_problem:
For each positive integer $n$, let $\mathrm{SUM}_n : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^{\lceil \log_2(n+1)\rceil}$ denote the multi-output Boolean function that maps an input $(x_1,\ldots,x_n) \in \{0,1\}^n$ to the binary encoding of the integer $x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n$. The Boolean circuit size of a multi-output function $f$ is the minimum number of gates in a circuit over the full binary basis $B_2$ (the set of all two-input Boolean functions) that computes $f$, where each gate has fan-in at most $2$ and fan-out is unbounded.

Determine the Boolean circuit size of $\mathrm{SUM}_n$ as a function of $n$. In particular, determine the asymptotic constant $c$ such that the circuit size of $\mathrm{SUM}_n$ equals $cn + o(n)$, or otherwise establish matching upper and lower bounds.

Known upper bounds for symmetric functions (which include SUM_n) are of the form 4.5n + o(n), while only linear lower bounds of the form (3 + 1/86)n - o(n) over the full binary basis are known, and these apply to specific functions rather than tight bounds for SUM_n. No matching upper and lower bounds have been established.

paper_title: Lower Bounds for Unrestricted Boolean Circuits: Open Problems
original_question: If there is a non-trivial satisfiability algorithm for Boolean circuits of size cn on n inputs, does that imply cn lower bounds for Boolean-circuit complexity?
self_contained_problem:
A Boolean circuit (over the standard De Morgan basis with AND, OR, NOT gates of fan-in at most 2) on n input bits is said to have size s if it consists of at most s gates. Fix a constant c > 0. A "non-trivial satisfiability algorithm" for the class of Boolean circuits of size cn on n inputs is a deterministic algorithm that, given as input a description of such a circuit C, decides whether there exists x ∈ {0,1}^n with C(x) = 1, in worst-case time 2^n / s(n) for some superpolynomial (or otherwise non-trivial) function s(n) → ∞ — that is, an algorithm that beats exhaustive search by a non-trivial factor on this circuit class.

Question: Does the existence, for every constant c > 0, of a non-trivial satisfiability algorithm for Boolean circuits of size cn on n inputs imply that there is a language in some "natural" complexity class (e.g., E^{NP}, NEXP, or similar) that, for every constant c > 0, requires Boolean circuits of size at least cn (i.e., linear lower bounds with arbitrarily large constant)?

Equivalently: prove or refute the implication

   "for every c, a non-trivial SAT algorithm exists for size-cn circuits"  ⟹  "for every c, there is an explicit function requiring circuits of size cn".
category_tag: Boolean circuit lower bounds and SAT algorithms
status_search_result: The connection between non-trivial circuit-SAT algorithms and circuit lower bounds (Williams' program) is known to yield NEXP ⊄ P/poly-style consequences from non-trivial SAT for polynomial-size circuits, and analogous results for restricted classes. However, the specific question of whether non-trivial SAT for linear-size (size cn) circuits implies linear (cn) circuit lower bounds for general unrestricted circuits remains an open problem in the area, as of recent surveys on unrestricted Boolean circuit lower bounds.

paper_title: Lower Bounds for Unrestricted Boolean Circuits: Open Problems
original_question: Which Boolean functions avoid the mass production effect, meaning that for the function r × f obtained by applying f to r independent input blocks, the circuit size of r × f is not much smaller than r times the circuit size of f?
self_contained_problem:
For a positive integer n, let B_n denote the set of Boolean functions f : {0,1}^n → {0,1}, and let gates(f) denote the minimum number of gates in an unrestricted Boolean circuit (over the full binary basis) computing f. For positive integers r and n and a function f ∈ B_n, define r × f : {0,1}^{rn} → {0,1}^r to be the function that applies f independently to r disjoint input blocks of length n, producing r output bits. One says that the "mass production effect" occurs for f when gates(r × f) is much smaller than r · gates(f); equivalently, computing r independent copies of f is significantly cheaper than computing r separate copies. 

Characterize, or exhibit explicit examples of, Boolean functions f that avoid the mass production effect: that is, families of functions f for which gates(r × f) = (1 - o(1)) · r · gates(f) (or, more strongly, gates(r × f) ≥ r · gates(f) - o(r · gates(f))) as r grows. In particular, identify structural properties of f that force the circuit complexity of r × f to grow essentially linearly in r times the circuit complexity of f, with no asymptotic savings from computing multiple independent copies in parallel.
status_search_result: The mass production phenomenon, going back to Uhlig (1974) and Paterson–Valiant, shows that for many Boolean functions r × f can be computed with only slightly more gates than f itself. Characterizing functions that avoid this effect is a recognized open problem in unrestricted circuit complexity; standard references (Jukna's "Boolean Function Complexity" and surveys on circuit lower bounds) discuss mass production but do not provide a characterization of functions for which it fails. No resolution was found in the literature.

paper_title: Lower Bounds for Unrestricted Boolean Circuits: Open Problems
original_question: Can one prove superlinear lower bounds for linear Boolean circuits that use only parity gates, especially for multi-output linear maps of the form f(x) = Ax over {0,1}?
self_contained_problem:
A linear Boolean circuit (over $\mathbb{F}_2$) is a directed acyclic graph in which every non-input gate has fan-in 2 and computes the XOR (parity) of its two inputs; the input nodes are labeled by variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$, and a designated set of $n$ output gates produces the output. The size of such a circuit is its number of gates. For a matrix $A \in \{0,1\}^{n\times n}$, the linear map $f_A: \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^n$ defined by $f_A(x) = Ax$ (with arithmetic over $\mathbb{F}_2$) can be computed by some linear Boolean circuit; let $L(A)$ denote the minimum size of any such circuit computing $f_A$.

It is known that for a uniformly random $A \in \{0,1\}^{n\times n}$ one has $L(A) = \Theta(n^2/\log n)$ with high probability, while for every explicit family of matrices $\{A_n\}$ the best known unconditional lower bound on $L(A_n)$ is only $3n - o(n)$.

Problem: Exhibit an explicit family of matrices $\{A_n\}_{n\ge1}$ with $A_n \in \{0,1\}^{n\times n}$ together with a proof that
$$L(A_n) \;=\; \omega(n),$$
i.e., prove a superlinear lower bound on the size of any linear Boolean circuit (using only parity gates of fan-in 2) computing the multi-output linear map $x \mapsto A_n x$.
status_search_result: No superlinear lower bound is known for explicit linear maps computed by XOR-only circuits. The strongest known bound for an explicit matrix family is 3n − o(n) (Chashkin), while a counting argument gives Θ(n²/log n) for random matrices. The problem is widely cited as a major open question in circuit complexity.
