paper_title: PROGRESS IN THE OPEN PROBLEMS IN THEORY OF FUNCTIONS OF BOUNDED INDEX
context_brief: Bounded directional index for PDE solutions
original_question: Let L: C^n → R_+ be a positive continuous function, and for a nonzero direction b ∈ C^n define the directional derivatives by ∂F/∂b = Σ_{j=1}^n b_j ∂F/∂z_j and ∂^kF/∂b^k by iterating this operator. An entire function F on C^n is said to have bounded L-index in the direction b if there exists m_0 such that for every m and every z, the normalized derivative (1/(m! L(z)^m))|∂^mF(z)/∂b^m| is bounded above by the maximum of the same normalized quantities for orders 0 through m_0. Suppose P_1(z_1,z_2) and P_2(z_1,z_2) are entire functions of bounded L-index in the coordinate directions e_1=(1,0) and e_2=(0,1), respectively. For which directions b, and under what additional assumptions, must every entire solution F of the first-order partial differential equation P_1(z_1,z_2) ∂F/∂z_1 + P_2(z_1,z_2) ∂F/∂z_2 = h(z_1,z_2) also have bounded L-index in the direction b?
self_contained_problem:
Let $L:\mathbb{C}^n\to\mathbb{R}_+$ be a positive continuous function. For a nonzero direction $\mathbf{b}=(b_1,\dots,b_n)\in\mathbb{C}^n\setminus\{0\}$ and an entire function $F:\mathbb{C}^n\to\mathbb{C}$, define the directional derivative $\partial_{\mathbf{b}} F(z)=\sum_{j=1}^n b_j\,\partial F(z)/\partial z_j$, and define $\partial_{\mathbf{b}}^k F$ by iterating this operator. The function $F$ is said to have bounded $L$-index in the direction $\mathbf{b}$ if there exists $m_0\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ such that
$$\frac{|\partial_{\mathbf{b}}^m F(z)|}{m!\,L(z)^m}\le \max_{0\le k\le m_0}\frac{|\partial_{\mathbf{b}}^k F(z)|}{k!\,L(z)^k}\qquad\text{for all }m\in\mathbb{Z}_+\text{ and all }z\in\mathbb{C}^n.$$
Now consider the case $n=2$ with coordinate directions $\mathbf{e}_1=(1,0)$ and $\mathbf{e}_2=(0,1)$. Let $P_1,P_2:\mathbb{C}^2\to\mathbb{C}$ be entire functions such that $P_1$ has bounded $L$-index in the direction $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $P_2$ has bounded $L$-index in the direction $\mathbf{e}_2$, and let $h:\mathbb{C}^2\to\mathbb{C}$ be entire. Determine the directions $\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{C}^2\setminus\{0\}$ and additional assumptions on $P_1,P_2,h,L$ under which every entire solution $F$ of the first-order partial differential equation
$$P_1(z_1,z_2)\,\frac{\partial F}{\partial z_1}+P_2(z_1,z_2)\,\frac{\partial F}{\partial z_2}=h(z_1,z_2)$$
necessarily has bounded $L$-index in the direction $\mathbf{b}$.
category_tag: Entire functions of bounded L-index in direction
status_search_result: Surveys on progress in problems on functions of bounded index list this as an open problem regarding first-order linear PDEs in two complex variables. Related results exist for second-order equations (Bandura–Skaskiv, Acta Comm. Univ. Tartu. Math., 2018) and linear PDEs in general, but a complete characterization of admissible directions and additional hypotheses for the stated first-order equation does not appear to have been established.

paper_title: PROGRESS IN THE OPEN PROBLEMS IN THEORY OF FUNCTIONS OF BOUNDED INDEX
context_brief: Max-min criterion for bounded directional index
original_question: Let L belong to the class Q_b^n of positive continuous functions for which the regularity quantity λ_b(η) is finite for every η > 0. Is the following criterion equivalent to bounded L-index in the direction b for an entire function F on C^n: there exist constants R > 0, P_2(R) ≥ 1, and η(R) ∈ (0,R) such that for every z_0 ∈ C^n one can choose r = r(z_0) in [η(R), R] with max{|F(z_0 + tb)| : |t| = r/L(z_0)} ≤ P_2(R) min{|F(z_0 + tb)| : |t| = r/L(z_0)}?
self_contained_problem:
Fix a direction $b \in \mathbb{C}^n \setminus \{0\}$. For a positive continuous function $L: \mathbb{C}^n \to (0,\infty)$ and $\eta > 0$, define the regularity quantity
$$\lambda_b(\eta) = \sup\!\left\{ \frac{L(z + t_2 b)}{L(z + t_1 b)} : z \in \mathbb{C}^n,\ t_1, t_2 \in \mathbb{C},\ |t_1 - t_2| \le \frac{\eta}{L(z + t_1 b)} \right\},$$
and let $Q_b^n$ denote the class of all such $L$ for which $\lambda_b(\eta) < \infty$ for every $\eta > 0$.

An entire function $F: \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ is said to be of bounded $L$-index in the direction $b$ if there exists an integer $m_0 \ge 0$ such that for every $z \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and every nonnegative integer $m$,
$$\frac{|\partial_b^m F(z)|}{m!\, L(z)^m} \le \max_{0 \le k \le m_0} \frac{|\partial_b^k F(z)|}{k!\, L(z)^k},$$
where $\partial_b F(z) = \sum_{j=1}^n b_j \partial F/\partial z_j$.

Let $L \in Q_b^n$ and let $F$ be an entire function on $\mathbb{C}^n$. Prove or disprove: $F$ is of bounded $L$-index in the direction $b$ if and only if there exist constants $R > 0$, $P_2(R) \ge 1$, and $\eta(R) \in (0, R)$ such that for every $z_0 \in \mathbb{C}^n$ there is some $r = r(z_0) \in [\eta(R), R]$ with
$$\max\{|F(z_0 + t b)| : |t| = r/L(z_0)\} \le P_2(R)\, \min\{|F(z_0 + t b)| : |t| = r/L(z_0)\}.$$
status_search_result: The conjecture (a max-min criterion for bounded $L$-index in a direction for entire functions on $\mathbb{C}^n$) has been proved in the literature on bounded index in direction by Bandura and Skaskiv, and reported as completely proved in subsequent surveys on progress in the theory of functions of bounded index.

paper_title: PROGRESS IN THE OPEN PROBLEMS IN THEORY OF FUNCTIONS OF BOUNDED INDEX
context_brief: Sharp threshold for logarithmic derivative control
original_question: Let n(r) = sup_{z∈C^n} n_z(r/L(z)), where n_z counts zeros of the slice t ↦ F(z + tb) as above, let λ(r) denote the directional regularity quantity λ_b(r), and set r_0 = sup_{r>0} r/(2 n(r) λ(r)). Do there exist an entire function F on C^n and a continuous function L: C^n → R_+ such that (1) for some r_1 > r_0 and some P > 0, every z outside G_{r_1}^b(F) satisfies (1/|F(z)|)|∂F(z)/∂b| ≤ P L(z), while (2) for every r_2 < r_0 one has sup_{z∈C^n \ G_{r_2}^b(F)} |∂F(z)/∂b|/(|F(z)|L(z)) = +∞ and n(r_2) ∈ (0,+∞)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $b \in \mathbb{C}^n \setminus \{0\}$ be a fixed direction, let $F: \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be an entire function (not identically zero), and let $L: \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{R}_+$ be a positive continuous function. For $z \in \mathbb{C}^n$ consider the slice function $g_z(t) = F(z + tb)$, $t \in \mathbb{C}$, and let $n_z(\rho)$ denote the number of zeros of $g_z$ in the disc $\{t \in \mathbb{C} : |t| < \rho\}$ (counted with multiplicities), assuming $g_z \not\equiv 0$. Define
$$n(r) \;=\; \sup_{z \in \mathbb{C}^n} n_z\!\left(\frac{r}{L(z)}\right), \qquad r > 0,$$
and the "exceptional set"
$$G^b_r(F) \;=\; \bigcup_{w \in \mathbb{C}^n : F(w)=0} \Big\{ w + tb : |t| < \tfrac{r}{L(w)} \Big\}.$$
Let $\partial F(z)/\partial b$ denote the directional derivative of $F$ along $b$, and let $\lambda_b(r)$ be the directional regularity quantity
$$\lambda_b(r) \;=\; \sup\!\left\{ \frac{L(z_1)}{L(z_2)} \,:\, z_1 = z_2 + tb,\ |t| \le \frac{r}{\min\{L(z_1),L(z_2)\}} \right\}.$$
Set
$$r_0 \;=\; \sup_{r>0} \frac{r}{2\, n(r)\, \lambda_b(r)}.$$

Question: Do there exist an entire function $F$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$ and a positive continuous function $L: \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{R}_+$ such that both of the following hold?
\begin{enumerate}
\item There exist $r_1 > r_0$ and $P > 0$ such that
$$\frac{1}{|F(z)|}\left|\frac{\partial F(z)}{\partial b}\right| \;\le\; P\, L(z) \qquad \text{for every } z \in \mathbb{C}^n \setminus G^b_{r_1}(F).$$
\item For every $r_2 < r_0$,
$$\sup_{z \in \mathbb{C}^n \setminus G^b_{r_2}(F)} \frac{1}{|F(z)|\, L(z)} \left|\frac{\partial F(z)}{\partial b}\right| \;=\; +\infty,$$
and $n(r_2) \in (0, +\infty)$.
\end{enumerate}
In other words, is the threshold $r_0$ sharp in the sense that an entire function exhibiting this exact transition between bounded and unbounded normalized directional logarithmic derivative on the complement of the tube $G^b_r(F)$ actually exists?
status_search_result: The question concerns sharpness of the threshold $r_0$ in the directional logarithmic-derivative criterion for entire functions of bounded L-index in direction. Surveys and follow-up papers by Bandura, Skaskiv and collaborators (2017–2020) have established sufficient conditions and sharper estimates of this type, but no source located definitively settles the existence of an extremal pair $(F,L)$ realizing the exact transition at $r_0$ described in the problem. The status appears to remain open or at least not publicly resolved.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: If a pattern is not k-avoidable, but is (k + 1)-avoidable, what is the minimal frequency of a letter in an infinite word over k+1 letters that avoids that pattern?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet. A pattern p is a nonempty word over an alphabet of variables E = {x_1, x_2, ...}. An infinite word w over A is said to encounter p if there exists a non-erasing morphism h : E* → A* such that h(p) is a factor of w; otherwise w avoids p. The pattern p is k-avoidable if there exists an infinite word over some alphabet of size k that avoids p, and is unavoidable on k letters otherwise.

For an infinite word w over a finite alphabet A and a letter a ∈ A, define the frequency of a in w as
    freq_w(a) = lim inf_{n → ∞} |w[1..n]|_a / n,
where |u|_a denotes the number of occurrences of a in u.

Suppose p is a pattern that is not k-avoidable but is (k+1)-avoidable. Determine
    inf { min_{a ∈ A} freq_w(a) : A is an alphabet of size k+1, and w is an infinite word over A that avoids p },
i.e., the minimal possible frequency of a letter in an infinite word over k+1 letters that avoids p.
status_search_result: Pattern avoidance and letter frequencies in infinite words is an active research area, with results known for specific patterns (e.g., square-free ternary words, abelian-square-free words). However, general results on the minimal frequency of a letter for arbitrary patterns at their avoidability threshold k+1 do not appear in the searched literature, and no comprehensive solution was found.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Is it decidable whether p is k-avoidable, given a pattern p and an integer k?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet of letters and let E = {x_1, x_2, ...} be a disjoint countable set of variables. A pattern is a nonempty word p ∈ E^+. A word w ∈ A^* is said to encounter the pattern p if there exists a non-erasing morphism h : E^+ → A^+ such that h(p) is a factor (contiguous subword) of w; otherwise w avoids p. For a positive integer k, the pattern p is called k-avoidable if there exists an infinite word over an alphabet of size k that avoids p (equivalently, infinitely many finite words over a k-letter alphabet avoid p), and p is k-unavoidable otherwise.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that, given as input an arbitrary pattern p ∈ E^+ and a positive integer k, decides whether p is k-avoidable?
status_search_result: The decidability of k-avoidability of a pattern (equivalently, computability of the avoidability index μ(p)) is widely cited as an open problem in combinatorics on words. Surveys and tutorials note no known algorithm computes μ(p), and even specific small patterns (e.g. ααββγγ) have unknown avoidability index, indicating the general decision problem remains unresolved as of recent literature.

original_question: Is there a pattern that is 6-avoidable but not 5-avoidable?
self_contained_problem:
Let A_k denote an alphabet of k letters, and let E denote a separate alphabet of pattern variables. A pattern is a nonempty word p over E. An infinite word w over A_k is said to avoid p if there is no nonerasing morphism h: E* -> A_k* such that h(p) occurs as a factor of w. The pattern p is called k-avoidable if there exists an infinite word over some alphabet of size k that avoids p; otherwise p is k-unavoidable. The avoidability index of an avoidable pattern p is the least integer k such that p is k-avoidable.

Question: Does there exist a pattern p whose avoidability index equals 6, i.e., a pattern p that is 6-avoidable but not 5-avoidable?
status_search_result: The question appears to remain open. Patterns with avoidability index 2, 3, 4, and 5 are known (a pattern of avoidability index 5 was constructed by Clark / Ochem), but no pattern with avoidability index 6 (or larger) has been exhibited, and the existence of such a pattern is listed as an open problem in the literature on combinatorics on words.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: If a pattern is k-avoidable then it is k-HD0L-avoidable (i.e. are there morphisms f : Σ*-→ A*, g : Σ*-→ Σ*, with|Σ| = k such that f (g^^ω(a)) avoids p)?
self_contained_problem:
Let A and Σ be finite alphabets, and let A* and Σ* denote the free monoids of finite words over A and Σ, respectively. A pattern is a non-empty word p over an alphabet Δ of variables. A word w over an alphabet B avoids p if there is no factor of w of the form h(p), where h : Δ* → B* is a non-erasing morphism. The pattern p is said to be k-avoidable if there exists an infinite word over an alphabet of size k that avoids p.

Given a morphism g : Σ* → Σ* and a letter a ∈ Σ such that g(a) begins with a and |g^n(a)| → ∞, let g^ω(a) denote the unique infinite word that is the limit of g^n(a). For a morphism f : Σ* → A*, the infinite word f(g^ω(a)) is called an HD0L word. The pattern p is said to be k-HD0L-avoidable if there exist an alphabet Σ with |Σ| = k, morphisms f : Σ* → A* and g : Σ* → Σ*, and a letter a ∈ Σ generating an infinite iteration, such that f(g^ω(a)) avoids p.

Prove or disprove: every k-avoidable pattern is k-HD0L-avoidable.
status_search_result: The question whether every k-avoidable pattern is k-HD0L-avoidable is stated as an open conjecture in problem collections on combinatorics on words. While it is known that every avoidable pattern is D0L-avoidable (over some alphabet), refining this to match the avoidability index k via HD0L morphic words remains an open problem. No published resolution was found.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: If p is k-avoidable, then there are arbitrary long circular words on k letters that avoid p.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A_k=\{0,1,\dots,k-1\}$ be a $k$-letter alphabet, and let $E$ be a separate alphabet of "pattern variables." A pattern is a word $p\in E^+$. A word $w\in A_k^*$ is said to encounter $p$ if there exists a non-erasing morphism $h:E^+\to A_k^+$ such that $h(p)$ is a factor of $w$; otherwise $w$ avoids $p$. A circular word of length $n$ on $A_k$ is an equivalence class of $A_k^n$ under cyclic rotation; its factors are all the factors (of every length) of the linear word $ww$ that have length at most $n$. A circular word avoids $p$ if none of its factors encounters $p$. The pattern $p$ is called $k$-avoidable if there exist infinitely many (equivalently, arbitrarily long) linear words over $A_k$ that avoid $p$.

Prove or disprove: for every pattern $p$, if $p$ is $k$-avoidable, then there exist arbitrarily long circular words on $k$ letters that avoid $p$.
status_search_result: The statement appears as a conjecture in the compilation of open problems from the WORDS conference series (listed as Conjecture 1.1.03.7). No published resolution was found in a web search; related conjectures about circular words avoiding patterns remain open.

original_question: Let p be k-avoidable. 1. If the number of p-free words on k letters of length n grows exponen- tially with n, then an integer N0 exists such that, for every n > N0, there are circular p-free words with length n on k letters. 2. If the number of p-free words on k letters of length n grows polynomi- ally with n, then the set of possible lengths for circular p-free words on k letters has density 0 in the set N\{ 0}.
self_contained_problem:
Fix an integer k ≥ 2 and let A be an alphabet of size k. A pattern is a nonempty word p over a set of variables. A word w over A is said to encounter p if there is a non-erasing morphism h from the variable alphabet to A^+ such that h(p) is a factor of w; otherwise w is p-free. The pattern p is called k-avoidable if there exist infinitely many p-free words over A. A circular word of length n over A is an equivalence class of words in A^n under cyclic rotation; equivalently, a circular word of length n is p-free if every factor (read cyclically) of every linear representative is p-free.

Let f(n) denote the number of p-free words of length n over A. Prove or disprove the following two statements for every k-avoidable pattern p:

(1) If f(n) grows exponentially in n (i.e., lim inf f(n)^{1/n} > 1), then there exists N₀ such that for every n > N₀ there is at least one circular p-free word of length n over A.

(2) If f(n) grows polynomially in n (i.e., f(n) = O(n^c) for some constant c), then the set
   S = { n ∈ ℕ \ {0} : there exists a circular p-free word of length n over A }
has density 0 in ℕ \ {0}, that is, |S ∩ {1,...,N}|/N → 0 as N → ∞.

However, no direct confirmation that the general two-part conjecture has been established in full generality was found; status is inconclusive.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: In the prefix or suffix tree of a repetition-free language, are the subtrees generated by two given words isomorphic?
self_contained_problem:
Let $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$ be a repetition-free language over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ (for example, a $k$-power-free language: the set of all finite words over $\Sigma$ that contain no nonempty factor of the form $u^k$). Order $L$ by the prefix relation: $u \le v$ iff $u$ is a prefix of $v$. The Hasse diagram of $(L, \le)$ is a rooted tree $T_{\mathrm{pref}}(L)$ (the prefix tree of $L$): its root is the empty word $\varepsilon$, and the children of a node $w \in L$ are the words $wa \in L$ with $a \in \Sigma$. For $w \in L$, let $T_w$ denote the subtree of $T_{\mathrm{pref}}(L)$ rooted at $w$, regarded as an unordered (or ordered) rooted tree. The suffix tree $T_{\mathrm{suf}}(L)$ is defined symmetrically using the suffix relation.

Question: Given two words $u, v \in L$, decide whether the subtrees $T_u$ and $T_v$ are isomorphic as rooted trees. In particular, for the binary cube-free language (the case $\Sigma = \{0,1\}$ and $k=3$), is there an algorithm that, on input $u, v$, decides whether the subtrees rooted at $u$ and $v$ in the prefix tree (respectively suffix tree) are isomorphic?
status_search_result: For the binary cube-free language, results in the literature on the tree of binary cube-free words establish that finiteness of a subtree rooted at a given word is decidable and that isomorphism of two given subtrees can be decided in linear time, so the question is answered affirmatively in this specific case. For arbitrary repetition-free / k-power-free languages the general decidability/isomorphism question does not appear to have a complete resolution, so the broader version is best regarded as partially solved.

original_question: For a conducting sequence beta in {0,1}*, let u shuffled with itself using beta denote the interleaving determined by beta. Which square-free words u can be shuffled with themselves to obtain another square-free word?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet and A* the set of finite words over A. A word w ∈ A* is square-free if it contains no non-empty factor of the form xx, i.e., there are no factorizations w = pxxq with x ≠ ε.

Given a word u = a_1 a_2 ⋯ a_n ∈ A* and a binary "conducting sequence" β = b_1 b_2 ⋯ b_{2n} ∈ {0,1}^{2n} containing exactly n zeros and n ones, define the shuffle of u with itself directed by β, denoted u ⧢_β u, to be the unique word w_1 w_2 ⋯ w_{2n} obtained as follows: read β from left to right and let i (resp. j) be the running count of 0's (resp. 1's) seen so far; if b_k = 0 set w_k = a_i (the i-th letter of the first copy of u), and if b_k = 1 set w_k = a_j (the j-th letter of the second copy of u). Equivalently, u ⧢_β u is an interleaving of two copies of u where β specifies, position by position, from which copy the next letter is drawn.

Characterize the set of square-free words u ∈ A* for which there exists a conducting sequence β ∈ {0,1}^{2|u|} (with equal numbers of 0's and 1's) such that the shuffle u ⧢_β u is again a square-free word. Combinatorics, 2015), answering a question of Harju in the affirmative. Subsequent work (e.g., Currie–Saari; Harju–Müller) studies square-free shuffles further, and recent work on shuffled-square-free words (Guégan–Ochem and successors, 2022–2023) addresses related avoidance problems. However, a complete characterization of which square-free words u admit a conducting sequence β making u ⧢_β u square-free does not appear to be fully established; the problem is partially solved.

original_question: For every k >= 5, does there exist an infinite (k/(k-1))^+-free word over k letters with letter frequency 1/(k+1), and for every k >= 6, does there exist such a word with letter frequency 1/(k-1)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma_k = \{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$ be an alphabet of size $k$. For a real number $\alpha > 1$, an $\alpha^+$-free word is an infinite word over $\Sigma_k$ that contains no factor of the form $u^e$ with rational exponent $e > \alpha$ (where $u^e$ for $|u| = p$ and $e = n/p$ denotes a factor of length $n$ which is a prefix of $u^\omega$). The repetition threshold for $k$ letters is $k/(k-1)$ for $k \geq 5$ (Dejean's theorem). The frequency of a letter $a \in \Sigma_k$ in an infinite word $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots$ is defined as
$$\mathrm{freq}_w(a) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{|\{i \leq n : w_i = a\}|}{n},$$
when the limit exists.

Prove or disprove the following two statements:

(i) For every integer $k \geq 5$, there exists an infinite $(k/(k-1))^+$-free word over $\Sigma_k$ in which some letter has frequency exactly $1/(k+1)$.

(ii) For every integer $k \geq 6$, there exists an infinite $(k/(k-1))^+$-free word over $\Sigma_k$ in which some letter has frequency exactly $1/(k-1)$.

Tunev and Shur proved related stronger versions of Dejean's conjecture for odd alphabet sizes $n = 7, 9, \ldots, 101$. The general conjecture for all $k \geq 5$ (resp. $k \geq 6$) does not appear to be fully resolved in the literature.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: What is the smallest repetition exponent that can still be avoided by an infinite word produced by iterated prefix-suffix duplication?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the set of finite words over $\Sigma$. The prefix duplication operation on a word $w \in \Sigma^*$ produces, from $w = uv$ with $u$ a nonempty prefix, the word $uuv$; the suffix duplication operation produces, from $w = uv$ with $v$ a nonempty suffix, the word $uvv$. A (finite or infinite) word $z$ is said to be obtained by iterated prefix-suffix duplication starting from a word $w_0$ if there is a (possibly infinite) sequence $w_0, w_1, w_2, \dots$ such that each $w_{i+1}$ is obtained from $w_i$ by a single prefix duplication or suffix duplication, and $z$ is the limit (or a member) of this sequence.

For a real number $\alpha > 1$, an $\alpha$-repetition (or repetition of exponent $\alpha$) in an infinite word is a nonempty factor of the form $u^k u'$ where $u'$ is a prefix of $u$ and $(k|u| + |u'|)/|u| \ge \alpha$. An infinite word $\mathbf{w}$ avoids exponent $\alpha$ (is $\alpha$-free) if it contains no factor of exponent $\ge \alpha$.

Determine the infimum of all real numbers $\alpha > 1$ such that there exists an infinite word, over some finite alphabet, that is obtained by iterated prefix-suffix duplication from some finite seed word and avoids exponent $\alpha$ (equivalently, contains no repetition of exponent $\ge \alpha$).

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Starting with a single word, does the language of ﬁ- nite words constructed by iterating prefix-suffix square completion remains semi-linear?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and $\Sigma^*$ the free monoid of finite words over $\Sigma$. For a word $w \in \Sigma^*$, define the prefix-suffix square completion relation $\Rightarrow$ on $\Sigma^*$ as follows: $w \Rightarrow w'$ if either
(i) (suffix square completion) $w$ has a suffix of the form $yx y$ for some $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ with $y \neq \varepsilon$, and $w' = w x$ (so that $w'$ ends in the square $(yx)(yx)$ when read as $\dots y\,x\,y\,x$); or
(ii) (prefix square completion) $w$ has a prefix of the form $y x y$ for some $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ with $y \neq \varepsilon$, and $w' = x w$.

Let $\Rightarrow^*$ denote the reflexive-transitive closure of $\Rightarrow$. For a single word $w_0 \in \Sigma^*$, define
$$L(w_0) = \{ w \in \Sigma^* : w_0 \Rightarrow^* w \}.$$
Recall that a language $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$ is called semi-linear if its image under the Parikh map $\Psi : \Sigma^* \to \mathbb{N}^{|\Sigma|}$ (counting the number of occurrences of each letter) is a semi-linear subset of $\mathbb{N}^{|\Sigma|}$, i.e., a finite union of sets of the form $\{ v_0 + n_1 v_1 + \cdots + n_k v_k : n_i \in \mathbb{N}\}$ with $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k \in \mathbb{N}^{|\Sigma|}$.

Question: Is $L(w_0)$ semi-linear for every starting word $w_0 \in \Sigma^*$?

The status therefore appears to be unknown/open based on available evidence.

original_question: What is the minimum number of steps of square com- pletion that are required to obtain a word from one of its factors?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and $\Sigma^*$ the set of finite words over $\Sigma$. A prefix-square completion step transforms a word $w \in \Sigma^*$ into $xw$ whenever $w$ has a prefix of the form $yxy$ for some $x,y \in \Sigma^*$ with $y$ nonempty (so that $yxy$ is a "square-like" factor $yxy$ where one repeats the bordering factor; equivalently, $w = yxy z$ and the step yields $xw = xyxyz$, which contains the square $(yx)^2$ as a prefix). Symmetrically, a suffix-square completion step transforms $w = z y x y$ into $wx = z y x y x$, which ends with the square $(xy)^2$. A prefix-suffix square completion step is either a prefix-square completion step or a suffix-square completion step. Write $u \Rightarrow^* v$ if $v$ can be obtained from $u$ by a finite sequence of prefix-suffix square completion steps; in this case $u$ is a factor (contiguous subword) of $v$.

Determine, as a function of $u$ and $v$ (with $u$ a factor of $v$ and $u \Rightarrow^* v$), the minimum number of prefix-suffix square completion steps needed to derive $v$ from $u$. In particular, give tight bounds, an exact formula, or an efficient algorithm computing this minimum.

original_question: The number of abelian cube-free ternary words grows exponentially with length. Given a n-letter alphabet, deﬁne the sequence Zn recursively by: Z1 = 1 and Zn = Zn-1nZn-1, for every n > 1.
self_contained_problem:
Two finite words u and v over a finite alphabet are said to be abelian equivalent if v is a permutation of u, i.e., each letter occurs the same number of times in u as in v. A word w contains an abelian cube if it has a factor of the form xyz where x, y, z are nonempty and pairwise abelian equivalent; otherwise w is called abelian cube-free.

Define the Zimin words over the alphabet of positive integers recursively by Z_1 = 1 and Z_n = Z_{n-1}\, n\, Z_{n-1} for every n > 1. A word w is said to encounter the abelian pattern Z_n if there exist nonempty factors w_1, w_2, …, w_k of w (where k is the number of variable occurrences in Z_n) realizing Z_n in such a way that any two factors corresponding to the same variable in Z_n are abelian equivalent.

Prove that the number of abelian cube-free words of length N over a 3-letter alphabet grows exponentially in N, i.e., establish the existence of a constant c > 1 and a positive constant C such that the count is at least C·c^N for all sufficiently large N.
status_search_result: Carpi (2004) proved that the number of ternary words of length n avoiding abelian cubes grows at least like r^n with r = 2^{1/24}, establishing exponential growth. The result is published in the Journal of Integer Sequences.

original_question: Given a pattern p and an integer n, what is the complexity of deciding whether the recursively defined word Z_n encounters p in the abelian sense?
self_contained_problem:
Define the Zimin words over an infinite alphabet of variables x_1, x_2, ... recursively by Z_1 = x_1 and Z_{k+1} = Z_k x_{k+1} Z_k for k >= 1. A pattern is a nonempty word p = p_1 p_2 ... p_m over a finite set of variables. For a finite word w over some alphabet Σ, write |w|_a for the number of occurrences of letter a in w, and call two words u, v abelian-equivalent (u ~_ab v) if they have the same length and |u|_a = |v|_a for every letter a.

Question: Determine the computational complexity of the following decision problem. Given as input a pattern p (encoded as a word over a variable alphabet) and a positive integer n (encoded in unary or binary), decide whether the Zimin word Z_n encounters p in the abelian sense.

original_question: What is the length of the longest word avoiding strongly k-abelian nth powers?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and $\Sigma^*$ the set of finite words over $\Sigma$. For a positive integer $k$, two words $u,v \in \Sigma^*$ are said to be $k$-abelian equivalent, written $u \sim_k v$, if $|u|=|v|$ and for every word $w$ with $|w|\le k$, the number of occurrences of $w$ as a factor of $u$ equals the number of occurrences of $w$ as a factor of $v$.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Is there a pure morphic binary word avoiding 2-abelian cubes?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and $\Sigma^*$ the free monoid of finite words over $\Sigma$. For an integer $k\ge 1$, two finite words $u,v\in\Sigma^*$ are said to be $k$-abelian equivalent, written $u\sim_k v$, if for every word $f\in\Sigma^*$ with $|f|\le k$, the number of occurrences of $f$ as a (contiguous) factor of $u$ equals the number of occurrences of $f$ as a factor of $v$. (For $k=1$ this is ordinary abelian equivalence, i.e.\ equality of Parikh vectors.)

A $k$-abelian cube is a non-empty word of the form $u_1 u_2 u_3$ with $u_1\sim_k u_2 \sim_k u_3$ and $|u_1|=|u_2|=|u_3|\ge 1$. An infinite word $\mathbf{w}\in\Sigma^{\mathbb{N}}$ avoids $k$-abelian cubes if no factor of $\mathbf{w}$ is a $k$-abelian cube.

A morphism is a map $h:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ satisfying $h(xy)=h(x)h(y)$. Given a letter $a\in\Sigma$ such that $h(a)=ax$ for some non-empty $x\in\Sigma^*$ and such that $|h^n(a)|\to\infty$, the unique infinite fixed point $h^\omega(a)=\lim_{n\to\infty}h^n(a)$ is called a pure morphic word. (No coding is applied; the alphabet of the infinite word equals $\Sigma$.)

Problem. Take $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$. Does there exist a pure morphic infinite binary word $\mathbf{w}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ that avoids $2$-abelian cubes?

status_search_result: It is known that 2-abelian cubes are avoidable on a binary alphabet (Rao–Rosenfeld and related works show k-abelian cubes are avoidable on binary alphabets for k ≥ 2). However, whether such an avoiding word can be realized as a pure morphic word (the fixed point of a binary morphism, with no coding) does not appear to be settled in the literature; results for the analogous ternary k-abelian-square problem show that pure morphic constructions face genuine obstructions, and no construction or impossibility proof for the binary 2-abelian-cube case was found in the search.

original_question: Is there an integer k such that 2-abelian squares of period at least k can be avoided over a binary alphabet?

For a positive integer $k$, two words $u,v \in \Sigma^*$ are said to be $k$-abelian equivalent, written $u \sim_k v$, if for every word $w \in \Sigma^*$ with $|w| \le k$, the number of occurrences of $w$ as a (contiguous) factor of $u$ equals the number of occurrences of $w$ as a factor of $v$. original_question: Do there exist infinite additive-cube-free words over the alphabets {0,1,2,3}, {0,1,4}, and {0,2,5}?
self_contained_problem:
Let an alphabet $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$ be a finite set of integers. A finite word $w=a_1a_2\cdots a_{3n}$ over $A$ (with $n\geq 1$) is called an additive cube if it can be split into three consecutive blocks of equal length whose digit sums are all equal, that is,
$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \;=\; \sum_{i=n+1}^{2n} a_i \;=\; \sum_{i=2n+1}^{3n} a_i.$$
An infinite word $\mathbf{w}=a_1a_2a_3\cdots\in A^{\mathbb{N}}$ is called additive-cube-free if no factor (contiguous subword) of $\mathbf{w}$ is an additive cube.

Determine, for each of the following three alphabets, whether there exists an infinite additive-cube-free word over it:
(i) $A=\{0,1,2,3\}$;
(ii) $A=\{0,1,4\}$;
(iii) $A=\{0,2,5\}$.
status_search_result: For the alphabet {0,1,2,3}, Lietard and Rosenfeld (extending work of Cassaigne, Currie, Schaeffer, and Shallit on {0,1,3,4}) established the existence of an infinite additive-cube-free word, in fact over every subset of {0,1,2,3}. For the alphabets {0,1,4} and {0,2,5}, the question is reported as still open: Rao constructed infinite additive-cube-free words over some size-3 integer alphabets such as {0,1,5}, {0,3,7}, {0,2,9}, but {0,1,4} and {0,2,5} remain among the unresolved cases.

original_question: (due to T. Kosciumaka, J. Radoszewski, W. Rytter and T. Waleń [43]): A word of length n contains Theta(n√n) inequivalent abelian-squares.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $w \in \Sigma^*$ be a word of length $n$. A factor (contiguous subword) of the form $uv$ with $|u|=|v|$ is called an abelian square if $v$ is a permutation of $u$, i.e. for every letter $a \in \Sigma$ the number of occurrences of $a$ in $u$ equals the number of occurrences of $a$ in $v$. Two abelian squares $u_1 v_1$ and $u_2 v_2$ (occurring as factors of $w$) are called equivalent if $|u_1|=|u_2|$ and $u_1$ is a permutation of $u_2$ (equivalently they have the same length and the same Parikh vector on each half); otherwise they are called inequivalent. Let $A(w)$ denote the number of pairwise inequivalent abelian squares occurring as factors of $w$, and define
$$ A(n) \; = \; \max_{|w|=n} A(w). $$
Prove or disprove: $A(n) = \Theta(n\sqrt{n})$, i.e. there exist constants $c_1, c_2 > 0$ such that for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$ c_1\, n\sqrt{n} \;\le\; A(n) \;\le\; c_2\, n\sqrt{n}. $$
status_search_result: The conjectured Θ(n√n) bound on the maximum number of pairwise inequivalent abelian squares in a word of length n is stated as a conjecture by Kociumaka, Radoszewski, Rytter and Waleń. Their work establishes a lower bound Ω(n^{1.5}/log n) (over a binary alphabet) but the matching upper bound O(n√n) is, to current public knowledge, not established; subsequent works on abelian-square-rich words and related extremal questions also do not appear to have closed the gap. The problem appears to remain open with partial bounds.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: How to decide whether a morphic word avoids (long) abelian power?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and $\Sigma^*$ (resp. $\Sigma^\omega$) the set of finite (resp. one-sided infinite) words over $\Sigma$. For a word $u\in\Sigma^*$ and a letter $a\in\Sigma$, let $|u|_a$ denote the number of occurrences of $a$ in $u$. Two finite words $u,v\in\Sigma^*$ are said to be abelian equivalent, written $u\sim_{\mathrm{ab}} v$, if $|u|=|v|$ and $|u|_a=|v|_a$ for every $a\in\Sigma$. For an integer $k\ge 2$, an abelian $k$-power is a nonempty finite word of the form $u_1u_2\cdots u_k$ with $u_1\sim_{\mathrm{ab}} u_2\sim_{\mathrm{ab}}\cdots\sim_{\mathrm{ab}} u_k$. An infinite word $w\in\Sigma^\omega$ is said to avoid abelian $k$-powers if no factor of $w$ is an abelian $k$-power, and to avoid long abelian $k$-powers if there exists $N$ such that no factor of $w$ of length at least $N$ is an abelian $k$-power.

A morphism is a map $h:\Sigma^*\to\Delta^*$ satisfying $h(uv)=h(u)h(v)$. Given an endomorphism $h:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ with a letter $a\in\Sigma$ such that $h(a)=au$ for some $u$ with $h^n(u)\ne\varepsilon$ for all $n$, the iteration produces a unique infinite fixed point $h^\omega(a)\in\Sigma^\omega$. A morphic word is the image $g(h^\omega(a))$ under a coding $g:\Sigma\to\Delta$.

Problem. Given as input a morphism $h:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$, a letter $a\in\Sigma$ generating an infinite fixed point $h^\omega(a)$, a coding $g:\Sigma\to\Delta$, and an integer $k\ge 2$, decide:
(a) whether the morphic word $g(h^\omega(a))$ avoids abelian $k$-powers;
(b) whether $g(h^\omega(a))$ avoids long abelian $k$-powers (i.e., contains only finitely many abelian $k$-power factors, equivalently has bounded-length abelian $k$-power factors).

Determine whether (a) and (b) are decidable problems in full generality, and if not, describe broad sufficient conditions on $(h,g)$ under which decidability holds.
category_tag: Combinatorics on words / abelian powers in morphic words
status_search_result: The general decision problem remains open, but partial results are known. Algorithms have been developed to decide whether the fixed point of a morphism avoids abelian k-powers under reasonable assumptions (e.g., for primitive morphisms with no eigenvalue of absolute value 1, and for certain classes of morphic and additive sequences in works by Rao, Rosenfeld, Currie and others). No fully general decision procedure for arbitrary morphic words has been established.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Find good heuristics to compute candidates for ques- tion 1.6.15.5.
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Let A be a finite alphabet and let E be a separate alphabet of pattern variables. A pattern is a non-empty word p ∈ E*. A morphism h : E* → A* is non-erasing if h(x) is a non-empty word for every variable x ∈ E. Two finite words u, v ∈ A* are abelian equivalent, written u ~_ab v, if they have the same length and, for every letter a ∈ A, the number of occurrences of a in u equals the number of occurrences of a in v. A word w ∈ A* is said to encounter the pattern p in the abelian sense if there exist a non-erasing morphism h : E* → A* and a factorization w = w₀ h(p₁)' h(p₂)' ⋯ h(p_n)' w₁ where p = p₁ p₂ ⋯ p_n (with p_i ∈ E) and each h(p_i)' ~_ab h(p_i) and, for every two occurrences of the same variable, the corresponding factors are abelian equivalent. Otherwise w avoids p in the abelian sense. A pattern p is abelian k-avoidable if there exists an infinite word over an alphabet of size k that avoids p in the abelian sense; p is abelian-avoidable if it is abelian k-avoidable for some k.

Problem. Provide effective heuristic procedures that, given a pattern p ∈ E* whose abelian avoidability status is unknown, produce candidate witnesses for either side of the question, namely:
(i) candidate finite or eventually periodic infinite words over a small alphabet (and candidate morphisms generating such words) that plausibly avoid p in the abelian sense, suitable for verification by direct computation up to a chosen length; and
(ii) candidate short factors or unavoidable abelian configurations that would prove p is abelian-unavoidable, suitable for a finite case analysis.

The heuristics should be efficient enough to be run on patterns of length at most a fixed modest bound and on alphabet sizes k ∈ {2, 3, 4}, and should improve substantially over exhaustive enumeration.
status_search_result: The classification of patterns with respect to abelian avoidability remains incomplete: only a partial classification of short patterns (length ≤ 7 over few variables) and of binary patterns is known, and no general decision procedure or systematic heuristic for producing avoidance/unavoidance candidates has been established. Recent works (e.g., on abelian-2-avoidability of binary patterns and on abelian/additive powers in rich words, 2016–2024) continue to use ad-hoc computer search, indicating the heuristic question is still open.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: What is the minimum k such that abelian squares of period at least k can be avoided over three letters, with 2 < k < 6?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma_3 = \{a,b,c\}$ be a three-letter alphabet. A finite nonempty word $w \in \Sigma_3^+$ is called an abelian square if $w = uv$ with $|u| = |v|$ and $v$ is a permutation of $u$ (equivalently, for every letter $x \in \Sigma_3$, the number of occurrences of $x$ in $u$ equals the number in $v$). The period of such an abelian square $w = uv$ is $|u|$.

For an integer $k \ge 1$, say that an infinite word $\mathbf{w} \in \Sigma_3^{\mathbb{N}}$ avoids abelian squares of period at least $k$ if no factor of $\mathbf{w}$ is an abelian square of period $\ge k$.

It is known that no infinite word over $\Sigma_3$ avoids all abelian squares (i.e., the case $k = 1$), and it is straightforward to show that for sufficiently large $k$ such infinite words exist. Determine the minimum integer $k$ with $2 < k < 6$ such that there exists an infinite word over the three-letter alphabet $\Sigma_3$ avoiding all abelian squares of period at least $k$.
category_tag: Combinatorics on words / abelian pattern avoidance
status_search_result: Web searches surface related results on $k$-abelian square avoidance (e.g. Rao–Rosenfeld show that 2-abelian squares of period $\ge 2$ are avoidable on three letters) and on the inavoidability of all abelian squares on three letters, but no source clearly resolves the specific question of the minimum period threshold $k\in\{3,4,5\}$ for avoiding (ordinary) abelian squares of period $\ge k$ on a ternary alphabet. The question appears in a list of open problems from the WORDS conference series, and no published resolution was located.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Is there a morphism over 5 letters with two eigenval- ues of norm smaller than 1 and an abelian-square-free ﬁxed point?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be an alphabet of $5$ letters. A morphism $h:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ has an associated incidence (Parikh) matrix $M_h\in\mathbb{Z}^{5\times 5}$ whose $(i,j)$-entry is the number of occurrences of letter $i$ in $h(j)$. A right-infinite word $w\in\Sigma^\omega$ is a fixed point of $h$ if $h(w)=w$ (taking the natural extension of $h$ to infinite words). A finite word $u_1u_2\cdots u_n\in\Sigma^*$ is called an abelian square if $n$ is even and the two halves $u_1\cdots u_{n/2}$ and $u_{n/2+1}\cdots u_n$ have the same Parikh vector (i.e., each letter occurs the same number of times in each half). A word is abelian-square-free if it contains no nonempty abelian square as a factor.

Question: Does there exist a morphism $h$ over an alphabet of $5$ letters such that the incidence matrix $M_h$ has at least two eigenvalues of modulus strictly less than $1$, and such that $h$ admits an infinite fixed point that is abelian-square-free?
status_search_result: A web search did not surface a definitive resolution of this specific question regarding the existence of a 5-letter morphism with two eigenvalues of modulus less than 1 having an abelian-square-free fixed point. Related work (e.g. Keränen's 85-uniform abelian-square-free morphism on 4 letters, and studies of fixed points avoiding abelian k-powers) is known, but no source confirming or refuting this exact statement was located.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: How to decide whether eigenvalues of norm 1 may be allowed in the result that was mentioned above?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $h:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*$ be a primitive morphism, i.e. a monoid homomorphism whose incidence (composition) matrix $M_h\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{\Sigma\times\Sigma}$, defined by $(M_h)_{a,b}=|h(b)|_a$ (the number of occurrences of letter $a$ in $h(b)$), is primitive (some power has all entries strictly positive). Suppose $a\in\Sigma$ satisfies $h(a)=au$ for some non-empty $u$, so that $h$ admits the infinite fixed point $h^\infty(a)=\lim_{n\to\infty}h^n(a)\in\Sigma^\omega$.

A template $t$ over $\Sigma$ is, in the standard sense of abelian pattern realization, a finite combinatorial object specifying constraints on the Parikh vectors of factors of an infinite word; one says that $h^\infty(a)$ realizes $t$ if there exists a factorization of some factor of $h^\infty(a)$ whose Parikh vectors satisfy the linear/affine constraints encoded by $t$ (this captures abelian repetitions, abelian-$k$-powers, additive powers, and similar abelian patterns).

It is known that whenever every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $M_h$ satisfies $|\lambda|\neq 1$, there is an algorithm that, given $h$ and any template $t$, decides whether $h^\infty(a)$ realizes $t$.

Question: Is there an algorithm which, on input a primitive morphism $h$ (with a fixed point $h^\infty(a)$) whose matrix $M_h$ is allowed to have eigenvalues of complex norm $1$, together with a template $t$, decides whether $h^\infty(a)$ realizes $t$? Equivalently, can the hypothesis "$M_h$ has no eigenvalue of norm $1$" be removed from the above decidability result?
status_search_result: The question appears as an explicitly listed open problem in the WORDS-conference open-problems compilation (arXiv:1705.04055 / hal-02355621). The underlying decidability result of Rao and Rosenfeld (2015) requires the no-eigenvalue-of-norm-1 hypothesis, and recent surveys on abelian combinatorics on words still list the eigenvalue-of-norm-1 case as unresolved. No source verifying a resolution was found.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: How do recurrence quotients behave for other families of infinite words, such as words of complexity 2n+1 or more general infinite words?
self_contained_problem:
Let $u = u_0 u_1 u_2 \cdots$ be an infinite word over a finite alphabet $A$. For an integer $n \geq 1$, let $L_n(u)$ denote the set of factors (contiguous finite subwords) of $u$ of length $n$, and let $p_u(n) = |L_n(u)|$ be its factor complexity. The recurrence function $R_u(n)$ is defined as the smallest integer $N$ (or $+\infty$ if no such integer exists) such that every factor of $u$ of length $N$ contains every factor of $u$ of length $n$ as a subfactor; $u$ is called uniformly recurrent when $R_u(n) < \infty$ for all $n$. The recurrence quotient of $u$ is then defined as
$$\rho(u) = \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{R_u(n)}{n}.$$

For Sturmian words (binary infinite words with $p_u(n) = n+1$ for all $n \geq 1$), the recurrence quotient has been completely characterized: its infimum over all Sturmian words equals $2 + \varphi$, where $\varphi = (1+\sqrt{5})/2$, attained by the Fibonacci word, and its full spectrum of values is known.

Carry out an analogous study for broader families of uniformly recurrent infinite words. In particular:

(a) Determine the set of values, the infimum, and the extremal words for the recurrence quotient $\rho(u)$ as $u$ ranges over all infinite words of factor complexity $p_u(n) = 2n+1$ (for instance, Arnoux–Rauzy words on a three-letter alphabet).

(b) More generally, describe the behavior of $\rho(u)$ for arbitrary uniformly recurrent infinite words: identify natural classes for which $\rho(u)$ admits an explicit formula or sharp lower bounds, and characterize the words attaining the extremal values within each class.
status_search_result: Recurrence functions for Arnoux–Rauzy words (which have complexity 2n+1) were explicitly computed by Cassaigne, Chekhova and others, yielding partial results for the recurrence quotient in this family. However, a complete description of the spectrum of recurrence quotients for all words of complexity 2n+1, and for general uniformly recurrent infinite words, does not appear in the literature, indicating the broader program remains only partially solved.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Give a characterization of inﬁne words whose com- plexity satisﬁes limn p(n)/n = 2.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $w \in A^{\mathbb{N}}$ be an infinite word. For each integer $n \geq 0$, let $p_w(n)$ denote the factor complexity of $w$, i.e., the number of distinct factors (contiguous finite subwords) of $w$ of length $n$.

Provide a characterization (in terms of structural / combinatorial properties such as substitutive structure, return words, S-adic representations, or similar) of all infinite words $w$ that satisfy
$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{p_w(n)}{n} = 2.$$
That is, describe explicitly the class of infinite words whose factor complexity is asymptotically equivalent to $2n$.
status_search_result: A literature search on combinatorics on words turns up many partial results on linear factor complexity (e.g., Sturmian words with p(n) = n+1, Arnoux–Rauzy words, words coming from interval exchanges and S-adic systems, and general structure theorems for words with p(n) = O(n)), but no source provides a complete characterization of infinite words satisfying lim p(n)/n = 2. The status of a full characterization of this asymptotic class appears to remain open or at least not definitively settled in the available sources.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Give characterizations of Arnoux-Rauzy words with a given balance.
self_contained_problem:
An infinite word $w$ over a finite alphabet $A$ is called Arnoux–Rauzy if, for every length $n\ge 0$, $w$ has exactly one right special factor and exactly one left special factor of length $n$, and each of these special factors can be extended (on the appropriate side) by every letter of $A$. For an infinite word $w$ and an integer $C\ge 1$, $w$ is said to be $C$-balanced if for every letter $a\in A$ and every pair of factors $u,v$ of $w$ with $|u|=|v|$ one has $\bigl||u|_a-|v|_a\bigr|\le C$, where $|x|_a$ denotes the number of occurrences of $a$ in $x$. The balance of $w$ is the smallest such $C$ (or $\infty$ if no finite $C$ works).

Problem. Give a characterization, in terms of the directive sequence (the sequence of letters generating $w$ via the Arnoux–Rauzy substitutions), of those Arnoux–Rauzy words over an alphabet of size $k\ge 3$ that have a prescribed balance $C$. In particular, for each $C\ge 1$, describe explicitly the set of directive sequences producing $C$-balanced Arnoux–Rauzy words.
status_search_result: Partial results exist: necessary and sufficient conditions for 2-balanced ternary Arnoux–Rauzy words have been obtained using the notion of strong C-balance, and it is known that for every C the set of directive sequences of C-balanced ternary Arnoux–Rauzy words is not a rational language, so no characterization purely in terms of regular languages is possible. A complete characterization for general C and arbitrary alphabet size remains open.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: For an aperiodic fixed point u of a primitive morphism whose language is closed under reversal, must the palindromic defect D(u) be either 0 or +infinity?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet and let A* denote the set of finite words over A. For a finite word w, let Pal(w) denote the number of distinct palindromic factors of w (including the empty word). For an infinite word u over A, the palindromic complexity function is P_u(n) = #{ palindromic factors of u of length n }, and the factor complexity is C_u(n) = #{ factors of u of length n }. The palindromic defect of u is defined by
   D(u) = sup_{n ≥ 0} ( n + 1 − P_u(n) − P_u(n+1) + C_u(n+1) − C_u(n) ),
equivalently, for a uniformly recurrent infinite word u whose language is closed under reversal, D(u) measures the deviation of u from being "rich" in palindromes; words with D(u) = 0 are called rich.

A morphism h : A* → A* is primitive if there exists k ≥ 1 such that for every a, b ∈ A, the letter b occurs in h^k(a). An infinite word u is a fixed point of h if h(u) = u, and u is aperiodic if it is not eventually periodic. The language L(u) of u is the set of finite factors of u, and L(u) is closed under reversal if for every w ∈ L(u), the reversal w^R also belongs to L(u).

Question: Let u be an aperiodic fixed point of a primitive morphism h such that the language L(u) is closed under reversal. Must D(u) ∈ {0, +∞}?
status_search_result: The "zero defect conjecture" of Blondin-Massé, Brlek, Garon and Labbé in its original general form has been disproved: a counterexample was given by Labbé (a primitive morphism whose aperiodic fixed point has language closed under reversal yet finite nonzero palindromic defect). The conjecture has been confirmed in restricted settings (e.g. for marked morphisms, by Pelantová–Starosta), and refinements have been proposed.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Can we decide whether two rich words are factors of a common rich word?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet and A* the set of finite words over A. For a word w of length n, let P(w) denote the set of distinct palindromic factors of w (including the empty word). It is known that |P(w)| ≤ n + 1. A word w is called rich if |P(w)| = |w| + 1, i.e., it attains the maximum number of distinct palindromic factors. For a word w, let F(w) denote the set of all factors (contiguous subwords) of w.

It is known that there exist pairs of rich words u, v such that no rich word w satisfies {u, v} ⊆ F(w).

Problem: Provide an algorithm that, given as input two rich words u, v ∈ A*, decides whether there exists a rich word w ∈ A* such that {u, v} ⊆ F(w). Equivalently, determine whether the property "u and v are factors of a common rich word" is decidable.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Does every k-automatic word have an l-abelian complexity function that is itself k-automatic?
self_contained_problem:
Let k ≥ 2 and ℓ ≥ 1 be integers, and let A be a finite alphabet. An infinite word x = x_0 x_1 x_2 … ∈ A^ω is called k-automatic if there is a deterministic finite automaton with output that, on input the base-k representation of n, outputs x_n; equivalently, the k-kernel {(x_{k^i n + j})_{n ≥ 0} : i ≥ 0, 0 ≤ j < k^i} is finite.

For two finite words u, v over A and an integer ℓ ≥ 1, write u ∼_ℓ v if u and v have the same length and, for every word w ∈ A^* with |w| ≤ ℓ, the number of occurrences of w as a (scattered or contiguous, fixed convention: contiguous factor) factor of u equals the number of such occurrences in v. The relation ∼_ℓ is an equivalence relation on words of a given length, called ℓ-abelian equivalence (so ∼_1 is ordinary abelian equivalence).

For an infinite word x, the ℓ-abelian complexity function ρ^{(ℓ)}_x : ℕ → ℕ is defined by
   ρ^{(ℓ)}_x(n) = #{ [u]_{∼_ℓ} : u is a factor of x of length n }.

A function f : ℕ → ℕ (taking finitely many values) is called k-automatic if the sequence (f(n))_{n ≥ 0} is a k-automatic sequence in the above sense.

Question: Is it true that for every integer k ≥ 2, every integer ℓ ≥ 1, and every k-automatic infinite word x over a finite alphabet, the ℓ-abelian complexity function ρ^{(ℓ)}_x is itself k-automatic?
status_search_result: The related (and standard) conjecture is that the ℓ-abelian complexity of any k-automatic word is k-regular (the appropriate notion since the values can be unbounded). Parreau, Rigo, Rowland and Vandomme established this for the 2-abelian complexity of specific 2-automatic words such as the Thue–Morse and period-doubling words, and subsequent work (e.g., on Parikh-collinear fixed points and on generalized Cantor sequences) has extended automatic/regular abelian complexity results to further families. The general statement for all k-automatic words and all ℓ remains an open conjecture.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Given a word, can its minimal and maximal regular F-factorizations, measured by the length of the index sequence, be found in polynomial time?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and $A^*$ the free monoid of finite words over $A$. Fix an indexed family $\mathcal F=(F_i)_{i\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty languages over $A$ (the family $\mathcal F$ is given by some fixed finite description, e.g. each $F_i$ is recognized by a finite automaton uniformly computable from $i$).

An $\mathcal F$-factorization of a word $w\in A^*$ is a pair consisting of a factorization
$$w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_n$$
into nonempty factors $w_j\in A^*$ together with a sequence of indices $(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)\in\mathbb N^n$ such that $w_j\in F_{i_j}$ for every $j=1,\ldots,n$. The sequence $(i_1,\ldots,i_n)$ is called the index sequence of the factorization, and its length is $n$.

An $\mathcal F$-factorization is called regular when the index sequence $(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n)$ is non-decreasing, i.e. $i_1\le i_2\le\cdots\le i_n$.

Given $w\in A^*$, a minimal (respectively maximal) regular $\mathcal F$-factorization of $w$ is a regular $\mathcal F$-factorization whose index-sequence length $n$ is as small (respectively as large) as possible among all regular $\mathcal F$-factorizations of $w$.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm which, given as input a word $w\in A^*$, computes a minimal regular $\mathcal F$-factorization of $w$ and a maximal regular $\mathcal F$-factorization of $w$ in time polynomial in $|w|$?

A targeted web search did not surface any subsequent publication or preprint resolving the polynomial-time computability of the minimal and maximal regular F-factorizations, so the current status is unclear from publicly available sources.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Is the completeness or the uniqueness undecidable, when context-freeF -factorizations are given by deterministic automata or by linear context-free grammars?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $A^*$ denote the free monoid of finite words over $A$. A factorization of a word $w \in A^*$ is a sequence $(u_1, u_2, \dots, u_k)$ of words $u_i \in A^*$ such that $w = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_k$. Fix a language $F \subseteq A^*$ (the "factor language"). An $F$-factorization of a word $w$ is a factorization $(u_1, \dots, u_k)$ in which every factor $u_i$ belongs to $F$.

Say that the language $F$ is:
 - complete (with respect to $F$-factorizations) if every word of $A^*$ admits at least one $F$-factorization;
 - unique (with respect to $F$-factorizations) if every word of $A^*$ admits at most one $F$-factorization.

Call $F$ a context-free $F$-factorization language when $F$ is a context-free language. Two natural restricted ways of presenting $F$ are:
 (i) by a deterministic (pushdown) automaton recognizing $F$;
 (ii) by a linear context-free grammar generating $F$.

Problem. Determine whether each of the following decision problems is decidable or undecidable.

(a) Given a context-free language $F \subseteq A^*$ presented by a deterministic pushdown automaton, decide whether $F$ is complete; and separately, decide whether $F$ is unique.

(b) Given a context-free language $F \subseteq A^*$ presented by a linear context-free grammar, decide whether $F$ is complete; and separately, decide whether $F$ is unique.

In other words: is completeness undecidable, and is uniqueness undecidable, in each of the settings (i) and (ii)?

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: If t is a Sturmian word of slope alpha, must the least period of every nonempty factor of t belong to Pi(alpha)?
self_contained_problem:
Let α ∈ (0,1) be an irrational number with continued fraction expansion α = [0; 1+d₁, d₂, d₃, …] (with dᵢ ≥ 1 for i ≥ 2 and d₁ ≥ 0). Define the standard sequence of finite words over {a, b} by

  s₋₁ = b,  s₀ = a,  sₙ = sₙ₋₁^{dₙ} sₙ₋₂  for n ≥ 1,

and let qₙ = |sₙ|, so q₋₁ = 1, q₀ = 1, qₙ = dₙ qₙ₋₁ + qₙ₋₂. Define

  Π(α) = { j·qₙ + qₙ₋₁ : n ≥ 0 and 1 ≤ j ≤ dₙ₊₁ } ⊂ ℤ₊,

i.e. the set of denominators of all (principal and intermediate) convergents of α.

A Sturmian word of slope α is any infinite word t over a two-letter alphabet whose factor complexity satisfies p_t(n) = n+1 for every n ≥ 1 and whose letter frequencies are α and 1−α. The least period of a nonempty finite word w = w₁w₂…w_m is the smallest positive integer p such that wᵢ = wᵢ₊ₚ for every 1 ≤ i ≤ m − p.

Question: For every Sturmian word t of slope α, and every nonempty factor w of t, does the least period of w belong to Π(α)?
status_search_result: Currie and Saari, in "Least Periods of Factors of Infinite Words" (RAIRO – Theor. Inform. Appl., 2008), explicitly characterize the set of least periods of factors of a Sturmian word of slope α, confirming that every such least period belongs to the set of denominators of (semi)convergents of α (and that for the Fibonacci word this set is exactly the Fibonacci numbers). Subsequent work (e.g., "Standard factors of Sturmian words", 2010) builds on this characterization.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: If a morphism f generates a quasiperiodic infinite word and f(a) is not a power of a, must f be weakly quasiperiodic on every infinite word?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and $A^*$ (resp. $A^\omega$) the set of finite (resp. right-infinite) words over $A$. A morphism is a map $f: A^* \to A^*$ satisfying $f(uv) = f(u)f(v)$ for all $u, v \in A^*$; it extends naturally to $A^\omega$ when $|f^n(a)| \to \infty$ for some letter $a$.

An infinite word $w \in A^\omega$ is said to be quasiperiodic if there exists a finite word $q$ (a quasiperiod) such that every position of $w$ lies inside an occurrence of $q$ in $w$; equivalently, $w$ can be written as an overlapping concatenation of occurrences of $q$. A morphism $f$ is called weakly quasiperiodic if there exists at least one non-quasiperiodic infinite word $w \in A^\omega$ such that $f(w)$ is quasiperiodic.

Suppose that $f: A^* \to A^*$ is a morphism such that, for some letter $a \in A$, the infinite word $f^\omega(a) = \lim_{n \to \infty} f^n(a)$ is well-defined and quasiperiodic, and such that $f(a)$ is not a power of $a$ (i.e., $f(a) \notin \{a^k : k \geq 0\}$).

Prove or disprove: under these hypotheses, $f$ must be weakly quasiperiodic on every infinite word, in the sense that for every non-quasiperiodic infinite word $w \in A^\omega$, the image $f(w)$ is quasiperiodic.
status_search_result: Searches surface foundational work on (weakly/strongly) quasiperiodic morphisms by Levé and Richomme and related papers on quasiperiodic Sturmian words, but none of the readily available sources explicitly resolve the stated implication in full generality. Partial answers exist in the original framework, but no definitive proof or counterexample for the general conjecture was located.

original_question: If a non-periodic bi-infinite word w has k disjoint X-factorizations for a finite set X of words with k <= |X|, must the combinatorial rank satisfy r(X) <= |X|-k+1?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $A^*$ denote the free monoid of finite words over $A$. A bi-infinite word over $A$ is a sequence $w = \cdots a_{-2}a_{-1}a_0 a_1 a_2 \cdots$ with $a_i \in A$ for all $i \in \mathbb{Z}$. Such a word $w$ is called periodic if there is an integer $p \geq 1$ such that $a_{i+p} = a_i$ for all $i \in \mathbb{Z}$, and non-periodic otherwise.

Given a finite set $X \subseteq A^*\setminus\{\varepsilon\}$ of nonempty words, an $X$-factorization of a bi-infinite word $w$ is a factorization $w = \cdots x_{-1} x_0 x_1 \cdots$ with each $x_i \in X$, specified together with the sequence of cutting positions $(p_i)_{i \in \mathbb{Z}} \subset \mathbb{Z}$ between consecutive factors. Two $X$-factorizations of $w$ are called disjoint if their sets of cutting positions are disjoint.

The combinatorial rank $r(X)$ of $X$ is defined as
$$r(X) = \min\{\,|F| : F \subseteq A^* \text{ and } X \subseteq F^*\,\}.$$

Question: Suppose $X \subseteq A^*$ is a finite set of nonempty words and $w$ is a non-periodic bi-infinite word over $A$ that admits $k$ pairwise disjoint $X$-factorizations, where $k \leq |X|$. Must the combinatorial rank satisfy
$$r(X) \leq |X| - k + 1\,?$$

context_brief: Defect e ﬀect and independent systems of equations
original_question: Is there a positive integer k such that the system (S ) is equivalent to one of its subsystems induced by k equations?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $X = \{x_1, \dots, x_n\}$ be a finite set of unknowns. A word equation over $X$ is a pair $(u,v) \in X^* \times X^*$, usually written $u = v$. A solution of the equation $u=v$ in the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ is a morphism $h : X^* \to \Sigma^*$ such that $h(u) = h(v)$.

Two systems $S_1$ and $S_2$ of word equations over $X$ are said to be equivalent if they have exactly the same set of solutions $h : X^* \to \Sigma^*$. A subsystem of a system $S$ is any subset of the equations in $S$.

By the compactness property of free monoids (the Ehrenfeucht conjecture, proved by Albert–Lawrence and by Guba), every system $S$ of word equations over the finitely many unknowns $X$ is equivalent to some finite subsystem of itself.

Question: Does there exist a positive integer $k$, depending only on the number $n$ of unknowns (and not on the system $S$), such that every system $S$ of word equations over $n$ unknowns is equivalent to one of its subsystems consisting of at most $k$ equations? Equivalently, is the maximal cardinality of an independent system of word equations on $n$ unknowns finite, and if so, can a uniform bound $k = k(n)$ be given?
category_tag: Combinatorics on words / independent systems of word equations
status_search_result: The general question — whether the size of an independent system of word equations on n unknowns is bounded — is open for n ≥ 3. It is trivial for n = 2. For n = 3, an upper bound of 18 has been established (Holub and others), while constructions give independent systems of size Θ(n^4). The compactness property (Ehrenfeucht conjecture) guarantees a finite equivalent subsystem exists for each system, but no uniform bound k = k(n) is known in general.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Is the Post Correspondence Problem decidable for unique-equality-continuation instances?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the free monoid of finite words over $\Sigma$. An instance of the Post Correspondence Problem (PCP) is a finite list of pairs of nonempty words
$$P = \{(u_1,v_1),(u_2,v_2),\dots,(u_n,v_n)\}\subset \Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*,$$
and a solution of $P$ is a finite sequence of indices $i_1,i_2,\dots,i_k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ (with $k\ge 1$) such that
$$u_{i_1}u_{i_2}\cdots u_{i_k}=v_{i_1}v_{i_2}\cdots v_{i_k}.$$
For words $x,y\in\Sigma^*$, write $x\le y$ if $x$ is a prefix of $y$. Given an instance $P$, call a pair $(x,y)\in\Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*$ with $x\le y$ or $y\le x$ an admissible configuration if it can arise as $(u_{i_1}\cdots u_{i_j},\,v_{i_1}\cdots v_{i_j})$ for some sequence of indices. Say that $P$ is a unique-equality-continuation instance if for every admissible configuration $(x,y)$ with $x\ne y$ there is at most one index $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ such that the configuration obtained after appending $(u_i,v_i)$ remains admissible (i.e., one of the two resulting words is a prefix of the other).

Question: Is there an algorithm that, given a unique-equality-continuation instance $P$ as input, decides whether $P$ has a solution?

Related work by Halava, Harju and collaborators establishes decidability of the marked PCP and of PCP for instances with unique blocks, and decidability of the existence of infinite solutions under uniqueness-of-continuation conditions, but the specific question of decidability of PCP for unique-equality-continuation instances does not appear to be settled in the sources found.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Must every aperiodic infinite word have factors of arbitrarily large palindromic length?
self_contained_problem:
Definitions. Let A be a finite alphabet. A finite word over A is a palindrome if it reads the same from left to right as from right to left. The palindromic length PL(w) of a nonempty finite word w is the least integer k ≥ 1 such that w can be written as a concatenation w = p_1 p_2 ··· p_k of nonempty palindromes p_1, …, p_k over A. A factor of an infinite word u = u_0 u_1 u_2 ··· (u_i ∈ A) is any finite word of the form u_i u_{i+1} ··· u_{j-1} with 0 ≤ i ≤ j. An infinite word u is called periodic if there exists T ≥ 1 such that u_{n+T} = u_n for all n ≥ 0, and is called aperiodic otherwise.

Question. Prove or disprove: for every aperiodic infinite word u over a finite alphabet A and every integer N ≥ 1, there exists a factor w of u with PL(w) ≥ N. Equivalently, must the set {PL(w) : w is a factor of u} be unbounded for every aperiodic infinite word u?
status_search_result: The conjecture (originating with Frid, Puzynina and Zamboni, 2013) remains open in full generality. It has been proven in several substantial cases: for all k-power-free words, for Sturmian words, and for a class covering "almost all" aperiodic infinite words; further partial results concern prefix palindromic length of automatic words such as the Thue–Morse and Sierpinski words. No complete proof or counterexample for arbitrary aperiodic infinite words is known.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Are there words all of whose prefixes have palindromic length at most n but some factor has palindromic length 2n?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and $A^*$ the free monoid of finite words over $A$. A word $w \in A^*$ is a palindrome if it equals its reversal. The palindromic length of a word $w$, denoted $\mathrm{PL}(w)$, is the least integer $k \geq 0$ such that $w$ can be written as a concatenation $w = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k$ of palindromes $p_i \in A^*$ (with $\mathrm{PL}(\varepsilon) = 0$). For an infinite word $\mathbf{w} = w_1 w_2 w_3 \cdots$ over $A$, a prefix is any word of the form $w_1 \cdots w_m$ ($m \geq 0$), and a factor is any word of the form $w_i w_{i+1} \cdots w_j$ ($1 \leq i \leq j+1$).

Question: Does there exist a positive integer $n$ and an infinite word $\mathbf{w}$ (or a finite word) such that every prefix of $\mathbf{w}$ has palindromic length at most $n$, yet some factor of $\mathbf{w}$ has palindromic length equal to $2n$?

Equivalently, is the bound $\mathrm{PL}(\text{factor}) \leq 2n$ — given that all prefixes satisfy $\mathrm{PL}(\text{prefix}) \leq n$ — tight, or can it always be improved?
status_search_result: Saarela established that if every prefix of a word is a product of at most n palindromes, then every factor is a product of at most 2n palindromes, showing the 2n bound. Whether this bound is attained — i.e., whether there exist words with prefix palindromic length at most n but some factor of palindromic length exactly 2n — does not appear to be settled in the available literature, so the tightness question is recorded as unknown.

paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: Does there exist an aperiodic infinite word whose factors all have FG-palindromic length bounded by a constant?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet and let A* denote the free monoid of finite words over A. A finite word w ∈ A* is called a palindrome if it equals its reversal. Embed A* into the free group F(A) generated by A. For a finite word w ∈ A*, define the FG-palindromic length of w to be the least integer k ≥ 0 such that w, viewed as an element of the free group F(A), can be written as a product of k palindromes (each palindrome being an element of A* that reads the same forwards and backwards), where the equality is taken in F(A) (so cancellations between the palindromic factors are allowed). 

An infinite word u ∈ A^ℕ is called periodic if u = v^ω for some finite nonempty word v, and aperiodic otherwise. A factor of u is any finite contiguous subword of u.

Question: Does there exist an aperiodic infinite word u over some finite alphabet A such that the set {FG-palindromic length of f : f is a factor of u} is bounded by a constant?

The free-group (FG) variant of the palindromic length was introduced and studied by Saarela and others around 2017; the boundedness question for aperiodic infinite words in the FG-setting does not appear to have been resolved in the literature retrieved.

original_question: If Γ is the permutation on words over {a,b} defined in the source, must cycles containing odd-length words have odd length, cycles containing even-length words with an odd number of a letters have even length, and cycles containing even-length words with an even number of a letters be allowed to have either parity?

Consider the binary alphabet $\{a,b\}$ and the set $\{a,b\}^*$ of all finite words on this alphabet. For each word $w$ associate a non-crossing partition by the following factorization: write $w = w_0\, c_1\, w_1\, c_2\, w_2 \cdots c_k\, w_k$ where the letters $c_i$ are matched in the unique non-crossing way that pairs each $a$ with a $b$ to its right (when possible), and let $\Gamma$ be the permutation on $\{a,b\}^*$ induced by cyclically rotating this factorization (so that $\Gamma$ preserves the length of $w$ and the number of occurrences of each letter; in particular $\Gamma$ restricts to a permutation $\Gamma_n$ on words with $n$ occurrences of $a$ and $n+1$ occurrences of $b$, and more generally to a permutation on each class of words of fixed length $\ell$ and fixed number of $a$'s).

(i) Every cycle of $\Gamma$ that contains a word of odd length has odd length.

(ii) Every cycle of $\Gamma$ that contains a word of even length whose number of occurrences of $a$ is odd has even length.

(iii) Cycles of $\Gamma$ containing words of even length with an even number of occurrences of $a$ may have either odd or even length (i.e., both parities actually occur).

paper_title: Solutions to four open problems on quorum colorings of graphs
original_question: Find an infinite family of graphs, other than the odd complete graphs K_(2n+1) and the joins K_r + K_s with r + s odd and r ≥ 2, for which the quorum coloring number ψ_q(G) equals 1.
self_contained_problem:
Let G=(V,E) be a finite simple graph. For a vertex v∈V, let N[v]=N(v)∪{v} denote its closed neighborhood. A coloring c:V→{1,2,…,k} of the vertices of G (not required to be proper) is called a quorum coloring if for every vertex v∈V at least half of the vertices in N[v] receive the same color as v, i.e.
   |{u∈N[v] : c(u)=c(v)}| ≥ |N[v]|/2.
The quorum coloring number ψ_q(G) is defined as the maximum number of colors used in any quorum coloring of G (equivalently, the maximum number of nonempty color classes in such a coloring).

Two known infinite families of graphs G with ψ_q(G)=1 are:
 (a) the odd complete graphs K_{2n+1} for n≥1, and
 (b) the joins K_r + K_s (the complete bipartite-type join, i.e. take disjoint copies of K_r and K_s and add all edges between them) with r+s odd and r≥2.

Exhibit an infinite family of graphs, distinct from the two families (a) and (b) above, every member G of which satisfies ψ_q(G)=1.

original_question: If a graph G satisfies ψ_q(G) = 1, must its diameter diam(G) be at most 2?
self_contained_problem:
Let G=(V,E) be a finite simple connected graph. For a vertex v∈V, let N[v] denote the closed neighborhood of v (i.e., v together with its neighbors). A partition π={V_1,V_2,…,V_k} of V into nonempty color classes is called a quorum coloring of G if for every vertex v∈V, at least half of the vertices of N[v] lie in the same class as v; that is, |N[v]∩V_i| ≥ |N[v]|/2 whenever v∈V_i. paper_title: Open problems on classical de Sitter solutions
original_question: For classical 10-dimensional string backgrounds with a 4-dimensional de Sitter spacetime, D-brane sources, and orientifold sources, must every classical de Sitter solution that contains intersecting sources be perturbatively unstable, equivalently having at least one tachyonic 4-dimensional scalar mode?
self_contained_problem:
Consider classical ten-dimensional string backgrounds of type II supergravity whose spacetime is a warped product of four-dimensional de Sitter spacetime $dS_4$ with a six-dimensional internal manifold, and whose only localized sources are D$p$-branes and O$p$-orientifold planes (treated in the smeared or localized supergravity approximation, with the standard NSNS and RR field content satisfying the equations of motion and Bianchi identities). Say that such a solution "contains intersecting sources" if there exist at least two source stacks (D-branes and/or orientifolds) whose internal worldvolume directions are not all parallel, i.e. they wrap distinct, transversely-intersecting cycles in the internal manifold. A solution is called perturbatively unstable if the spectrum of four-dimensional scalar fluctuations around it contains at least one mode whose squared mass $m^2$ satisfies $m^2/H^2 < 0$ (a tachyonic mode), where $H$ is the de Sitter Hubble scale; equivalently, the slow-roll-type parameter $\eta_V = \min(\nabla^2 V)/V$ is negative at the critical point.

Prove or disprove: every classical de Sitter solution of the above form that contains intersecting sources is perturbatively unstable.
status_search_result: The statement is a conjecture supported empirically: all known classical de Sitter solutions with intersecting D-brane/orientifold sources (typically on group manifolds) are tachyonic, often with η_V < -1. Subsequent works (e.g. Andriot 2021 on tachyonic de Sitter solutions of 10d type II supergravities) develop sufficient conditions and identify a systematic tachyon under assumptions, but no general proof exists. The conjecture is therefore still open.
