paper_title: From P systems to morphogenetic systems: an overview and open problems
original_question: Consider Monte Carlo M systems, meaning probabilistic morphogenetic systems that accept an instance if a distinguished floating object yes appears within polynomially many steps with probability at least 1/2 and reject if yes never appears. What is the exact computational complexity class of decision problems solvable by such systems in polynomial time in the semi-uniform sense? In particular, does this class include PSPACE?
self_contained_problem:
Morphogenetic systems (M systems) are a class of computational devices generalizing membrane (P) systems, in which "tiles" (geometric objects) and "floating objects" interact in a Euclidean space according to local probabilistic rules that allow tiles to attach, detach, and form structures, with floating objects diffusing among compartments.

A Monte Carlo M system is a probabilistic M system used as a decision device in the following way. Fix a distinguished floating object, denoted yes. For an input instance x of a decision problem, a family {Π_x} of M systems is constructed (the semi-uniform setting: a separate system Π_x is built for each instance x by a deterministic polynomial-time construction). The system Π_x is run for at most p(|x|) computation steps, where p is a fixed polynomial. The acceptance convention is:
  • If x is a yes-instance, then with probability at least 1/2 the object yes appears in a designated output region within p(|x|) steps.
  • If x is a no-instance, then the object yes never appears in the output region during the computation.

Let MCM-P denote the class of decision problems decidable in this semi-uniform Monte Carlo polynomial-time sense by M systems.

Question: Determine the exact characterization of MCM-P in terms of standard complexity classes. In particular, decide whether PSPACE ⊆ MCM-P.
status_search_result: No published characterization of the complexity class of polynomial-time semi-uniform Monte Carlo morphogenetic (M) systems was found. The problem is stated as an open problem in surveys on morphogenetic systems and no subsequent paper resolving it (in particular settling whether PSPACE is contained in this class) appears in the literature.

paper_title: From P systems to morphogenetic systems: an overview and open problems
original_question: Do there exist morphogenetic systems that are computationally universal in the Turing sense and at the same time self-healing for injuries of degree strictly greater than 1, where the degree of an injury is the graph-theoretic distance between the pre-injury and post-injury configurations in the configuration digraph?
self_contained_problem:
A morphogenetic system (M system) is an abstract computational model whose configurations are finite arrangements of abstract tiles in a discrete d-dimensional space, evolving by a fixed set of local rewriting/assembly rules. The set of all reachable configurations together with the one-step transition relation forms the configuration digraph of the system, whose vertices are configurations and whose directed edges are one-step transitions.

An injury to such a system M is a pair (x, y) of configurations where y cannot be reached from x in a single legitimate step of M. The degree of the injury (x, y) is defined as the graph-theoretic distance between x and y in the underlying undirected graph of the configuration digraph.

The system M is called self-healing of degree k if, after any injury (x, y) with degree at most k that occurs during a computation, M is still able to continue and complete its intended computation correctly (i.e., reach the same final result it would have reached without the injury).

The system M is called Turing-universal if it can simulate the computation of an arbitrary Turing machine on arbitrary input.

Question: Does there exist a morphogenetic system M that is simultaneously
(i) Turing-universal, and
(ii) self-healing of degree strictly greater than 1?
status_search_result: Existing literature establishes Turing-universal M systems that are self-healing of degree 1, but no construction or impossibility result has been reported for degree strictly greater than 1. The question therefore appears to remain open.

paper_title: From P systems to morphogenetic systems: an overview and open problems
context_brief: Virus spread in M-system cell populations
original_question: Model viruses as geometrically simple agents inside a population of cells represented by a morphogenetic system, and use the model to simulate and analyze how viral infection spreads through that cell population. Develop the model so that its predictions are meaningful at the level of macro-observables rather than only at the level of microscopic simulation details.
self_contained_problem:
A morphogenetic system (M-system) is a discrete spatial computational model in which a population of agents — called cells — is represented by collections of geometrically embedded tiles (e.g., polygons or polyhedra) that interact through local rules governing self-assembly, division, signaling, and degradation. Each cell occupies a bounded region of Euclidean space, has a membrane composed of tiles, and evolves under stochastic local interaction rules that may produce, consume, or transform tiles based on geometric contact and local concentrations of signal objects.

Within this framework, model viruses as additional agents of simple geometry and behavior (for example, small rigid tiles or compact tile assemblies) that diffuse in the spatial environment, attach to compatible cell membrane tiles, enter cells, replicate inside them by consuming intracellular resources to produce copies of themselves, and are released upon cell lysis or by budding through the membrane.

Tasks:
1. Formally define such a virus-augmented M-system, specifying the tile types representing virions, the rules for virion–cell attachment, entry, intracellular replication, and release, and the spatial diffusion mechanism for free virions.
2. Use this model to simulate the spread of viral infection through a population of cells.
3. Establish that the model yields predictions that are meaningful at the level of macro-observables — for instance, the time evolution of the number of infected cells, the basic reproduction number, total viral load, or spatial infection front speed — and not merely at the level of microscopic simulation traces. In particular, derive or empirically validate relationships between the local M-system parameters (rates of attachment, entry, replication, lysis, diffusion) and macroscopic epidemiological quantities, comparing them where possible to classical compartmental (e.g., SIR-type) descriptions of viral spread in tissue.
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not find any published work that explicitly models virus spread within morphogenetic (M-)systems and validates predictions at the level of macro-observables. The problem appears as an open challenge in the morphogenetic systems literature, and no resolution was located.

paper_title: Dense ideals in topological algebras: some results and open problems
original_question: If A is an F-algebra that is also a division algebra, must A be isomorphic to the complex field C?
self_contained_problem:
Define an F-algebra to be a complex associative algebra A equipped with a topology making A a completely metrisable topological vector space and such that the multiplication A × A → A is jointly continuous (equivalently, an associative complex algebra whose underlying topological vector space is a complete metrisable t.v.s., with separately or jointly continuous multiplication in the standard sense used for completely metrisable topological algebras). Assume A has a unit element. Recall that A is called a division algebra if every nonzero element of A has a (two-sided) multiplicative inverse in A.

Question: Must every F-algebra that is also a division algebra be isomorphic, as a complex algebra, to the field ℂ of complex numbers?
status_search_result: The question of whether the Gelfand–Mazur theorem extends to F-algebras (i.e., whether every completely metrisable topological division algebra over ℂ is isomorphic to ℂ) is a long-standing open problem. Partial results exist: Turpin–Waelbroeck showed it holds under the additional assumption of continuity of inversion together with a continuous p-homogeneous seminorm, but the general case remains unresolved.

paper_title: Dense ideals in topological algebras: some results and open problems
original_question: Let A be a commutative complex unital F-algebra, meaning a completely metrizable topological algebra. Does it follow that every multiplicative linear functional on A is continuous?
self_contained_problem:
An F-algebra is a topological algebra over $\mathbb{C}$ whose underlying topological vector space is completely metrizable (equivalently, a Fréchet space) and whose multiplication is jointly continuous. Let $A$ be a commutative unital F-algebra (with unit $e$). A multiplicative linear functional on $A$ is a linear map $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{C}$ such that $\varphi(xy) = \varphi(x)\varphi(y)$ for all $x, y \in A$ and $\varphi(e) = 1$. 

Question: Must every multiplicative linear functional on $A$ be continuous?
status_search_result: This is the classical Michael problem (E. Michael, 1952), asking whether every character on a commutative unital Fréchet algebra is automatically continuous. It is widely cited as still open in the literature; while several claimed solutions have appeared (e.g. an arXiv preprint by Patel and others), these have not been generally accepted, and the problem continues to be referenced as a famous open question in automatic continuity theory and in recent work such as Esterle's 2023 paper on Picard–Borel ideals.

paper_title: Dense ideals in topological algebras: some results and open problems
original_question: Suppose a topological algebra A has a dense finitely generated ideal I = x1 A + · · · + xn A. Must A contain a proper topologically invertible element? More strongly, must the ideal I itself contain a topologically invertible element?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a topological algebra over $\mathbb{C}$ with identity $e$ (i.e., a complex algebra equipped with a Hausdorff topology making the multiplication separately continuous). Denote by $G(A)$ the group of (two-sided) invertible elements of $A$. An element $x \in A$ is called topologically invertible if there exist nets $(a_\alpha), (b_\alpha)$ in $A$ such that $x a_\alpha \to e$ and $b_\alpha x \to e$; let $G_t(A)$ denote the set of topologically invertible elements. An element of $G_t(A) \setminus G(A)$ is called a proper topologically invertible element.

Suppose that $A$ contains a dense, finitely generated right ideal

self_contained_problem:
A topological algebra is a (complex) associative algebra $A$ equipped with a Hausdorff vector-space topology making the multiplication separately (equivalently, jointly, in the metrizable complete case) continuous. An $F$-algebra is a topological algebra whose underlying topological vector space is a complete metrizable topological vector space (an $F$-space). A $B_0$-algebra is an $F$-algebra whose topology can be defined by a countable family of submultiplicative seminorms (equivalently, a complete metrizable locally convex algebra with continuous multiplication).

A two-sided ideal $I \subseteq A$ is called proper if $I \neq A$, and dense if its closure in $A$ equals $A$.

Question: Does there exist an $F$-algebra $A$ — or even a $B_0$-algebra — such that every proper (two-sided) ideal of $A$ is dense in $A$?
